News.title: Man, 66, admits murdering missing mum-of-seven and dumping her skeleton in the bin nearly 30 years ago
News.content:
KILLER'S CONFESSION Man, 66, admits murdering missing mum-of-seven and dumping her skeleton in the bin nearly 30 years ago

A MAN has admitted murdering a mum-of-seven and dumping her body in the bin after she vanished nearly 30 years ago.

Patricia Lashley, 33, disappeared from her West Midlands flat in 1998 and has not been seen since.



Trevor Dunkley has now pleaded guilty to the mother-of-seven’s murder 28 years on.

He also admitted to a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing in Wolverhampton Crown Court today.



Appearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday, Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister, Balbir Singh, told a judge that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

Asked by Judge Michael Chambers KC if the victim’s body had been found, Mr Singh answered: “No, because this is 28 years ago and the body was put into the cellar downstairs.

“It decomposed.

“When he was moving about nine months to a year later the skeleton was disposed of into the bins.”



Asked if there was a basis of plea, Mr Singh said of the case: “It is down to what the defendant told the police when there was no evidence in reality of what had happened.”

Patricia, who also used the names Vanessa and Tricia as well as the surname Bradford, moved to Dudley in the mid 1990s.

It is believed the victim and Dunkley were known to one another.

The man was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on November 6.

Detective Inspector Michelle Cordell said: “Even if you already spoke to us at the time Patricia went missing, we still want to hear from you as we gather as much information as we can to help her family find some closure after nearly 30 years.”

News.title: Shocking moment passenger is almost dragged to his death after getting trapped between moving train and platform
News.content:
THIS is the dramatic moment a passenger was dragged 50 metres alongside a moving train after slipping into the gap beside the platform.

Heart-stopping CCTV footage shows the helpless commuter desperately struggling to escape as the Sabarmati Express continues rumbling through the station.



The man, wearing a blue button-down shirt, was attempting to board the train at Agra Cantt Railway Station in Uttar Pradesh, India.

But the journey almost ended in disaster when he suddenly lost his footing at around 9:35pm local time on September 8.



CCTV shows his foot plunging towards the ground as he became trapped in the moving carriage and the platform.

The train is seen continuing along the platform as the stricken passenger is dragged beside it.



He desperately battles to keep himself away from the tracks as stunned travellers spot the unfolding nightmare.

Several passengers immediately sprinted alongside the train, frantically trying to haul him free.

A huge crowd quickly gathered as the terrifying rescue attempt unfolded inches from the moving carriages.

Passengers aboard the train can even be seen poking their heads through windows to watch the chaos below.



Seconds later, members of the Government Railway Police‘s Quick Response Team race towards the trapped man and assist fellow travellers with the rescue.

Officers finally managed to drag the passenger clear and haul him to safety.

Remarkably, the man reportedly escaped the terrifying ordeal without suffering any injuries.



GRP inspector Sandeep Tomar said the passenger’s life was saved by the alertness and courage of police personnel and fellow travellers who immediately sprung into action.

India’s vast railway network has been plagued by deadly accidents blamed on a combination of ageing infrastructure, overcrowding and human error.

Outdated tracks and signalling systems have been cited as major safety concerns, while packed services place further strain on the sprawling network.

Mistakes including misread signals and fatigue among workers have also been linked to crashes across the country.

News.title: Plan to move 600 migrants into huge detention centre next to homes now facing public inquiry in win for furious locals
News.content:
PLANS to move 600 migrants into a detention centre next to homes that have been met with fury will now face a public inquiry in a win for locals.

The Government faced backlash over its plans to re-open Haslar Immigration Removal Centre and expand its operations.



According to locals, the site – which is used to house detained migrants – is one of the closest to people’s homes in the country.

Locals living by the immigration removal centre [IRC] in Gosport, Hampshire, publicly slammed the Government’s plans – raising concerns over security and infrastructure.



Work is ongoing to bring Haslar Immigration Removal Centre [IRC] back into use after its closure in 2015, with the first phase creating 130 beds and second phase expanding this to 600 beds.

However, the Home Office used the Crown Development route to plan the second phase – bypassing the local council’s usual decision-making process and ignoring locals’ voices.





But now the Planning Inspectorate has announced a public inquiry of the “highest level of scrutiny” will be heard on November 17 before Haslar is opened.

The Inspectorate said an inquiry was necessary because the application has generated “considerable local interest” and because “some of the issues raised are complex and the evidence would benefit from formal cross-examination.”

The decision came just a day after a meeting between the residents most affected by the Haslar plans, MP for Gosport Dame Caroline Dinenage and Leader of Gosport Borough Council Cllr Zoe Huggins BEM.

Dame Caroline, who has been at the forefront of opposing the plans, accused the Home Office of doing “its utmost to avoid engaging with local people.”

She said at the meeting: “I was disappointed that given the tragic record of engagement by the Home Office they decided to refuse this opportunity to meet the people living closest to Haslar and hear what they had to say.



“Residents spoke very powerfully about the impact this is already having on their daily lives, whether that is construction traffic passing their front doors, concerns about security or simply not knowing who at the Home Office they are supposed to contact when something goes wrong.”

Dame Caroline has now praised the decision to launch an inquiry into the site’s expansion.

She said: “This is an important victory for local residents whose opposition has been vindicated. An inquiry is exactly what I called for in my objection.

“The Planning Inspectorate has recognised that there is considerable local interest in these proposals and, crucially, that some of the issues we have raised are sufficiently complex that they need to be properly tested.

“The Government chose to pursue this development through the Crown Development process rather than the normal local planning system.



“It is therefore particularly important that the Planning Inspectorate has now agreed that its proposals should face the highest level of scrutiny available.”

Residents said it was “tragic” and added that they felt their objections to the site’s development were being ignored.

But now they say they have been “vindicated” with the plans for the site set to face a public inquiry with the “highest level of scrutiny.”



Cllr Huggins also welcomed the news and said it meant that residents were being heard.

She said: “This decision vindicates the concerns that Gosport Borough Council and local residents have been raising throughout this process.

“We have consistently argued that an application of this significance cannot simply be pushed through without the proper opportunity for the evidence to be scrutinised and local concerns to be heard.

“I wrote directly to the Home Secretary to raise our further concerns about both the proposals themselves and the process being used. The Planning Inspectorate has now agreed that the complexity of the issues warrants a full Inquiry where the evidence can be properly tested.

“The council will continue to stand up for Gosport and ensure that our residents’ voices are heard throughout what happens next.”



When The Sun visited Gosport last week homeowners said they were concerned that the three storey blocks will directly overlook their properties and allow the migrants to see into their gardens and windows.

Others said that the detained migrants would be suddenly introduced into the neighbourhood with no integration, raising security concerns.

People living just metres away from the 600-person immigration centre said they feared they’ll be the “first targets” when migrants move in.

They claim their concerns about security and privacy have been completely overlooked.

Concerns about the 600 migrants themselves were joined by the three-year issues from constant construction, including traffic, dust and noise polluting the neighbourhood.



The Home Office claimed plans for the site always detailed a 600-person capacity.

Angela Bryant, 88, says her garden backs onto the centre and she worries people will be able to see into her home.

While David Robinson, 65, is a retired civil servant at the MoD who has lived at his home opposite the site for 20 years.

He said he had worries about security, adding: “There will be 600 detainees – I’ll refer to them as detainees. The Home Office refers to them as residents but they’re not.

“We have got worries about the security for us all. It’s not like prison where the inmates have work like joinery or mail to keep them occupied. There will be 600 of them with nothing to do.”



Dame Caroline previously said: “Since announcing the expansion of Haslar to 600 beds the Government has done its utmost to avoid engaging with local people.

“Last week I invited the Home Office to a public meeting with residents but they failed to attend.

“The height of the buildings is a serious concern compounded by the fact it was revealed without warning at a small engagement session last year.

“Since then all planning decisions have been taken away from the local authority and there are limited opportunities for local people to have their say, something I have raised repeatedly with Ministers.”

An inquiry is the highest level of scrutiny available when examining the application and is currently due for November 17, 2026, with the details to be confirmed.



A Home Office spokesperson said: “All Crown Development planning applications require extensive engagement, and a public inquiry of this kind is a standard part of the process.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We encourage residents and stakeholders to share their views through the formal process.

“Since the election we have returned or deported over 80,000 individuals, including 11,733 foreign national offenders, and these investments are essential to continue ramping up these removals.”

News.title: Major UK water supplier warns hosepipe ban may last until WINTER in blow to over 6million customers
News.content:
A HOSEPIPE ban that is currently enforced for over six million Brits could last until winter, a major water supplier has warned.

The water company first introduced restrictions in July, but significantly more rain is needed to replenish water supplies.

Anglian Water has told councillors that a temporary use ban for its customers is “not going to be stopping anytime soon.”



Prolonged dry weather has left over six million of the water company’s customers under restrictions for over two months.



Earlier this week, at a Norfolk County Council meeting Grant Tufts from Anglian Water told councillors that the hosepipe ban could even continue untilwinter.

Tufts reportedly said: “I can’t give you a date but it’s going to be well into the autumn, maybe even the winter”.

“I think we need several more downpours and consistent rain to recharge those supplies,” he continued.

Anglian Water supplies drinking and wastewater services to swathes of the East of England, including parts of Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Essex.

According to the water company, water use dropped by around nine per cent when restrictions were introduced, making a “real difference at a time when most of our region is in drought“.

Under a temporary use ban, customers cannot use a hosepipe, sprinkler or pressure washer for various activities, with anyone caught breaking the rules at risk of facing a £1,000 fine.

News.title: Married headmaster, 53, ‘set up cameras in girls’ locker rooms and watched them undress on livestream’
News.content:
SCHOOL SHAME Married headmaster, 53, ‘set up cameras in girls’ locker rooms and watched them undress on livestream’

A MARRIED headmaster set up cameras in the girls locker rooms before watching them undress on a livestream, according to a criminal complaint.

Eric James, 53, was arrested over allegations he installed four hidden recorders while he was principal at Brooke High School in West Virginia.



He is being sued by 11 students over the alleged secret filming.

The devices were found at the school in Wellsburg, Brooke County, on September 2 after a custodian discovered a device that looked like an ink pen.



They realised it was a recording device before immediately alerting authorities.

Police rushed to the scene and found two cameras in the dance team’s changing space, one in the varsity locker room and a fourth in the P.E. changing facilities.

read more us news UNSEEN HORROR I sat near Lindsay Clancy at trial - what I saw in her town made me feel sick



Investigators identified James as the suspect before arresting him on September 3.

One of the children from a previous school said the teacher would “wait for her at the locker room door, let her in, and then disappear”, according to a criminal complaint.



The student believed James was “disappearing to go view the live camera footage” while she changed inside.

Eight students filed a class action lawsuit together last week, before another three filed civil complaints, the Daily Mail reported.

Another one of the accusers who attended a different school said she had to use the locker rooms at Brooke High School during an away sports fixture.

She alleged James would view the camera footage while the girl was inside the locker room, the complaint says.

One student aged 17 who attended Brooke High claimed she “reasonably believes” James caught her undressing on livestream through one of his alleged hidden cameras.



Reports and complaints were made concerning the educator’s conduct while he taught at another school, Cameron High, between 2000 and 2018, one of the accusers claims.

All three civil lawsuits and the class action lawsuit are asking for monetary damages to be determined by a jury.

The class action says: “The resulting invasion of the bodily privacy of Plaintiffs and other students was not momentary.

“Every day that the devices remained concealed and operational exposed children to additional secret observation and recording.”

James was suspended last Wednesday and is being held in the Northern Regional Jail on a £75,000 bond.



The teacher has been charged with two counts of breaking and entering and one count related to intercepting electronic communications.

He is scheduled to appear in court on September 16.

News.title: Is it wrong to impose tourist taxes for holidays in UK? VOTE NOW
News.content:
POLL OF THE DAY Is it wrong to impose tourist taxes for holidays in UK? VOTE NOW

BRIT holidaymakers could soon have to pay a tourist tax for staycations under controversial new plans announced by the government.

Local leaders are set to be allowed to slap an “overnight visitor levy” on families staying in hotels, B&Bs and holiday lets.



And reports last night suggested there will be no national cap on how high they can set the charge – although it’s thought the amount won’t exceed 5 per cent.

It means holidaymakers could be forced to cough up extra cash for every night of their trip – potentially piling £100 or more onto the cost of a family break.



There are more than 130 million overnight stays in England each year, all of which would be liable for the charge when it is introduced.

News.title: Mystery over death of woman, 21, found in boatyard as man arrested for her ‘murder’ is released
News.content:
DEATH RIDDLE Mystery over death of woman, 21, found in boatyard as man arrested for her ‘murder’ is released

MYSTERY surrounds how a woman who was found in a boatyard died, as cops release a man arrested on suspicion of her murder.

Corinna Baker, 21, was found dead at a former boat-building yard in a South Wales coastal town.



Corinna was last seen entering Netpool Boat Yard in Cardigan on the night of November 13 last year.

Her body was found two days later on November 15.



Shortly after the tragic find, detectives arrested a 29-year-old man on suspicion of murder.

Nearly a year on, cops have now released the man and said he will face no further action.

But it is still not known what the 21-year-old was doing in the boat shed so late at night.

Her cause of death still hasn’t been revealed either.



The cops haven’t said whether her death has been declared non-suspicious after they released the man.

They have closed their criminal investigation into Corinna’s death.

Witnesses at the time report seeing a boat covered in black tarpaulin being taken away by police.

Dyfed-Powys Police said the decision comes following a review of the evidence and results of the post-mortem examination.

In a heartbreaking tribute last year, Corinna’s sister Caitlyn said: “Heaven has the most beautiful, funny, stubborn angel entering the gates.



“I can’t believe I have to write this post. I’d give anything not to post this, for it to not be true… For it to be a cruel joke..

“But I’m so sorry to say my baby sister Corinna Rose has suddenly gained her wings this morning at 21.”

Her family also urged anyone with information to come forward.

They said: “We as a family are distraught at the loss of our beloved Corinna.”

“She was much loved, and she will be greatly missed by her whole family and all those who were blessed to have known her.



“We appeal to anyone who has any information however small to please come forward.”

A police spokesperson said: “Following a comprehensive review of the evidence in this case, including the findings of the post-mortem examination, the police investigation into the death of Corinna Baker has been closed.

“No further action is being taken against the 29-year-old man who had been arrested on suspicion of murder, and the criminal investigation has been finalised.

“A file of evidence is now being prepared for HM Coroner in preparation of an inquest.

“Corinna’s family have been informed of this decision, and our thoughts remain with them at this difficult time.”

News.title: I was MI6 spy inside Al Qaeda – I’m haunted by 9/11 tip that came too late… but I saved thousands from another attack
News.content:
WHILE thousands have suffered from Al Qaeda’s brutality, few understand its inner workings as well as Aimen Dean, a former operative turned British spy.

The dad-of-one was working undercover for the secret service in 2001 when he was called to meet one of bin Laden’s closest lieutenants.



He feared his cover had been blown, but was instead asked to deliver a message to four “brothers” in London, instructing them to “leave the country”.

The message read: “They must leave the country and come here before September 1.



“Something big is going to happen and we expect the Americans to come to Afghanistan.”

Aimen was walking along Oxford Street later that year when he learned of the terror attack on America’s Twin Towers and remembered those haunting words: “something big”.

Aimen was just 17 when he met Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the mastermind behind the 9/11 attacks, which killed almost 3,000 civilians.

He had just emerged from a year battling the Serbs in the Bosnian war, where he was exposed to “charred remains, mutilated bodies, and mass graves”.

Speaking exclusively to The Sun, Aimen revealed he was lured in by the promise of fighting a “villainous” America who he blamed for the lengthy war.

But he turned on them when he saw the true face of the terror group – appalled by how they would indiscriminately slaughter civilians.



“He was so convincing, he was so eloquent that I believed what I now know were delusions,” he said.

Aged 18, Aimen travelled to a secluded mountainous spot in Afghanistan where he would spend the next 11 months learning how to build bombs.

As a self-confessed bookworm and “nerd”, the intellectual rigour and mathematical precision required for bomb making proved an exciting – albeit risky – endeavour for the teenager.



“I remember thinking this is so much fun, why didn’t they teach chemistry like this at school?” he said.

Joined by three other men – including Moez Fezzani, now an ISIS leader in Libya – he spent his days mixing highly toxic chemicals under the watchful leadership of vengeful chemist and terror mastermind Abu Khabab.

Khabab was in charge of developing Al Qaeda’s mass-casualty weapons and was linked to a series of terror plots before being killed in a CIA drone strike in 2008.

Outside of building bombs, the group spent their time debating and listening to the radio.

“We would just sit down and discuss everything endlessly. We would talk about what is wrong with the world.



“We would reinforce each other’s negative views and talk about the need for change and how this could only come if we tear the system down,” Aimen recalled.

With just a mattress on the floor to sleep on and little else but books to keep him occupied, the bunker was basic at best.

Bombs and extremely toxic chemicals were stored in wooden shelves, which Aimen joked would have given any British health and safety inspector a heart attack.

He said: “We were dealing with chemicals all the time so they gave us lots of fruit to build up our resilience.”



“Khabab told us that your first mistake is your last mistake. He had two missing fingers to which I said, well you are testament of living to make another mistake.

“He said: ‘it’s idiots who came before you who did this. They are no longer here anymore – I was just collateral damage'”.

But just under a year after Aimen joined the terror group, his life took a drastic turn when news of a suicide bomb attack in East Africa upended his views and beliefs.

The devastating assault on US embassies in Nairobi, Kenya and Tanzania resulted in 200 deaths and an estimated 4,000 wounded.



According to Aimen, some 150 civilians were also blinded because the vans were “loaded with shrapnel” to maximise death and destruction.

“This is when I started to have doubts and I realised things were going in the wrong direction.

“I realised it was about making gas canisters full of hydrogen cyanide to attack nightclubs and cinemas,” he said.

“My good moral compass and critical thinking kicked in.

“I thought, what if I build something for someone that is then used on civilians? I disagreed completely with this,” he added.



When he raised his concerns with Khaleb, the terror leader replied: “The world is not the Disney movies that you watch.

“This is a jungle. Kill or be killed. The world only respects one language: terror.”

Feigning sickness, Aimen was sent to Qatar where he renounced his oath to the terror group and decided he would never go back.



Arriving in the country, he was questioned by security services as a suspected Al-Qaeda member.

He cooperated by giving them a number he had memorised for an Al-Qaeda bank account.

Delighted at having landed on an treasure trove of intelligence, the Qataris offered him the choice of being handed over to America, France or Britain.

“I felt little cultural affinity with the French and didn’t speak the language. And I didn’t trust the Americans either,” said Aimen.

Within nine days he had “landed in the lap” of MI5, who he said enthusiastically whisked him back to the UK after quickly recognising his impressive knack for map reading and photographic memory.



Arriving in the UK, he was offered a Coca-Cola which he tried for the first time (now, his favourite drink) and a Harry Potter book.

The next six months were filled with long training days and getting to grips with English before being sent to live in a flat with an Al Qaeda operative in London.

On becoming an informant for the British Secret Intelligence Service he said the best piece of advice he received was to just “go and have fun”.

During this time, Aimen hopped between homes and became close with his roommates by leaning on his superior intellect and offering them religious guidance.

He said: “I am generally theologically better trained than the average Al Qaeda person so I ended up being kind of like a spiritual coach.



“It’s a bit brutal but it means they will open their hearts and minds to me, which made my espionage much easier.”

It wasn’t long before Aimen was asked if we would go back to Afghanistan and acquire intelligence for the MI6.

After rigorous training, he returned to the Middle East pretending his return was so he could get back in touch with his spirituality.

He spent the next eight years spying for MI5 and MI6, becoming one of the secret service’s most audacious spies.

Not long after, he caught wind of a worrying plot engineered by his former leader Khabab to bomb the New York Subway.



Thanks to Aimen’s tip, news of the planned attack was passed to the Oval office and successfully foiled.

When asked about any close calls, he recalled the time he was cooking at the military camp and suddenly felt the cold end of a pistol against his lower spine.

“Someone said, that’s it confess, we know who you are. We know who you are working with,” he said.

His thorough training had taught him how to detect a bluff, so he held his nerve.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It later transpired the incident was a routine test. Did he ever feel scared? Nervous, yes, he said.



But the trick is to always “forget you’re spying”.

News.title: Spies, strategies and missed opportunities: How the lessons of 9/11 are still being learnt
News.content:
No one can question that 9/11 was a colossal intelligence failure, or to be more specific, a failure of imagination in the US intelligence community. At the time both the CIA and the FBI were in possession of information which, if shared properly, could have prevented what happened.

The 9/11 Commission Report that followed blamed "failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management" on the US government. The CIA and FBI, the report concluded, failed to properly assess intelligence and share information with each other and take sufficient steps to disrupt the plot.

This most basic of lessons has since been largely â although not completely â learnt, and sharing between Western intelligence agencies is infinitely better than it was in 2001.

The old rivalries between say, MI5 and Police Counter Terrorism have dissolved, first with regional 'fusion centres' dotted around the UK and now, most recently, with the establishment of the high-security Counter Terrorism Operations Centre in London. Here MI5 intelligence officers might find themselves sitting literally right next to police officers whose job it is to take the executive action to stop a terrorist plot. Equally, they might find themselves sitting next to a US federal agent from the FBI or a language specialist seconded from GCHQ.

Since 9/11, there has also been a root-and-branch reorganisation of US intelligence with the establishment of a National Counter Terrorism Center just outside Washington DC and a Director of National Intelligence to ensure that information is shared where it needs to be between the 18 separate US intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and its UK counterpart, the Secret Intelligence Service (better known as MI6) is perhaps the closest one in the world. This is supplemented by the Five Eyes alliance that pools intelligence between the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Yet disastrous failures of intelligence, assessment and strategic planning have still occurred since the planes hit the Twin Towers. In the run-up to the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, MI6 unwisely allowed its intelligence to be politicised, leading to the organisation suffering its worst reputational setback since the days of betrayal by the double agent Kim Philby and other Soviet moles in the 1950s and 60s.

News.title: AI boom helps drive surprise UK growth in July
News.content:
Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.

He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.

He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.

Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".

However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.

The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty".

"Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added.

"But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."

Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy, despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures.

"Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."

News.title: New hurricane season record as 'historic' El Niño leaves Atlantic eerily quiet
News.content:
A new hurricane season record will be set this week as a historic and still strengthening El NiÃ±o stifles tropical development in the Atlantic.

To date, no hurricanes have formed in the basin, despite this week marking the peak of the season on average - and there's no sign of development in the near future.

It means a new record will be be set for the latest date in the satellite era (1960s onward) without an Atlantic hurricane forming.

Currently, the record is 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.

In an average season, there would have been eight named tropical storms and three hurricanes by this point.

This year, however, there have only been five tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly and Edouard.

With few indications that there will be any development in the next week, this will mean the longest stretch into in a season where no hurricane has formed in the modern satellite era.

News.title: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next
News.content:
Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.

Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.

Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night.

"We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds.

"Then we'll worry about what comes next."

His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.

Over the two-day event, party activists were split on the wisdom of holding a midterm convention featuring a president who has record low approval ratings, and amid public frustration over the economy and war with Iran.

"I think it will make a difference. If anything it allows us to test the [campaign] message in front of a large audience," Jeff Ryer, the Virginia Republican Party chairman, told the BBC.

Others said the president's rambling, nearly two-hour convention speech on Wednesday wouldn't sway voters weighing whether to keep Republicans in power in Congress.

Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance to retake control of the House and the Senate is also in play, though viewed as more of a long shot for the party.

"Do I wish Trump gave a shorter speech? Sure, but that's not who he is," said one Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer a blunt view of Trump's convention appearance.

The source added that Trump's plea for voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot would fall flat.

"I don't think saying 'pretend I'm on the ballot' will work. He's not," the person said.

News.title: Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
News.content:
It is so dangerous now in Slovyansk and Kramatorsk that police say it is time for civilians to get out. These neighbouring cities are the biggest still under full Ukrainian control in the eastern Donbas region.

In the worst affected areas, forced evacuations of families with children have already begun, says Pavlo Dyachenko of Donetsk police.

"This is the only way to save your life," he says, because security has deteriorated so much.

"If you take Slovyansk, it used to be hit by glide bombs roughly once a week, but now it's almost every day."

Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka, to the south, form part of what is known as Ukraine's "fortress belt" â a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the east.

However, Kostyantynivka only has a limited presence of Ukrainian troops left, reports say, while Russia claims to be in full control of it.

News.title: Polanski selected as Green Party candidate for Starmer's former seat
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has been selected as the party's candidate in the by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's former seat in Parliament.

Polanski, who is a London Assembly member, will stand in Holborn and St Pancras on 8 October as he seeks to become an MP.

He was voted to be the party's candidate by members of the Camden Green Party ahead of local councillor Hamza Chowdhury.

Polanski said the Greens "might be the underdog in this election but we have the momentum and we can win".

Labour has held the inner London seat since it was created in 1983 and the party's candidate for the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali.

The seat became vacant after former Prime Minister Sir Keir announced he was standing down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

News.title: I watched as a hijacked plane flew over my home - moments later my wife was killed
News.content:
Charles first met Katherine in New York in 1988, when he was singing with a theatre group and she was a piano accompanist.

"We met quite accidentally outside the rehearsal hall and we fell in love with each other in about two minutes, and that was it," he said.

Charles said he "hit the jackpot" when he met her, adding: "There was no parting us."

Katherine took Charles back to the UK for a visit in 1989, as well as trips to parts of Wales that he admitted he "could not pronounce", including Machynlleth and Llanfairpwllgwyngyll.

"It was just the beginning," said Charles.

"We had a wonderful, wonderful relationship."

At 08:06 EDT, on September 11, 2001, Charles kissed Katherine goodbye from their New York City apartment for the last time.

Exactly 40 minutes later, a jet smashed into the 97th floor of the tower - the very floor she had been working on, in a new job she had started less than a fortnight earlier.

"I knew instantly when it flew over my building - our apartment building - that it was a twin engine jet at full throttle," said Charles, a trained pilot.

"I knew it so well that I called the FBI and told them... 'That was no accident, that was deliberate'."

A year later, when Charles met the FBI agent who took that call, he said the agent told him: "You were the first person to get us on to the fact that that was not an accident."

News.title: Brother of Muslim policeman killed in attacks 'disappointed' by calls for Mamdani to sit out memorial
News.content:
This yearâs 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks has become embroiled in divisive politics. There are controversial calls for the cityâs first Muslim Mayor to sit out the commemorative event, including from Rudy Giuliani who was New Yorkâs mayor on the morning of 9/11.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he will attend and his focus will be on the families who lost loved ones.

Zeshan Hamdani lost his older brother Salman, a Muslim American New York police cadet, in the North Tower. He spoke to the BBC's Nada Tawfik over his thoughts on this anniversary.

Video filmed and edited by Andrew Blum; produced by Pratiksha Ghildial

News.title: Assisted dying bill for England and Wales faces new vote in Commons
News.content:
The legalisation of assisted dying in England and Wales could move a step closer on Friday when MPs vote on a proposal to introduce it.

The bill would allow adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards, the bill's sponsor, said there was a "real human cost to the delay" in passing the legislation - but opponents say it lacks sufficient safeguards, particularly for vulnerable people.

The last effort to change the law was supported by MPs but stalled in the House of Lords earlier this year after peers tabled more than 1,200 amendments.

Edwards said she was asking MPs to send the same law "back to the House of Lords so that they can finish what they started".

If an identical bill passes the Commons, peers can still suggest changes, but cannot halt its progress.

Edwards said the Lords has an "important role in scrutinising, refining and often improving legislation" sent to them by the Commons, adding: "Let them amend this bill if they choose to and send it back to MPs for a final decision.

"That is how our democratic decisions are made and what should happen now.

"There is a real human cost to the delay in passing this legislation and correcting the injustices and cruelty of the current law."

Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen, a high-profile campaigner for assisted dying, called on MPs to support the bill, saying her own life with terminal cancer had become "unbearable".

The 86-year-old said she was too frail to travel to an assisted suicide clinic in Switzerland as she had planned to, saying: "Everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now."

News.title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
News.content:
Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.

The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.

Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted dying in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.

She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer.

"Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said.

"And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

"So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."

Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.

The prominent assisted dying campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".

Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Jersey legalised assisted dying for terminally ill adults earlier this year.

MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.

While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-Thompson

They fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.

The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.

The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.

It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used, meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time.

Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.

Assisted dying is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

News.title: Labour mayors in England vow to cap tourist tax at 5%
News.content:
Labour's regional mayors in England have pledged to cap a new fee on visitors' overnight stays at 5%, after hospitality bosses warned it could put jobs at risk.

Local leaders are set to gain new powers to charge an uncapped levy, dubbed a "tourist tax", as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

But the Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge if they do apply it, adding that they had listened to concerns over costs.

Reform UK's two regional mayors and the two Conservative ones are likely to oppose any levy given criticism from their national parties of the policy.

In a letter to Chancellor John Healey and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner, the Labour metro mayors said 5% represented a "reasonable ceiling" on the tax.

"It provides a balance of ensuring that local levies are not excessive, or vary significantly between regions, while also leaving room for local variation as appropriate," they added.

They added this would still allow for "meaningful investment" in local areas, whilst stressing any future levies in their areas would be "subject to local consultation".

The letter was signed by Labour mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire.

The government had earlier pledged to protect budget holidays "by making sure low-cost accommodation always pays lowest levy" and said the extra cash could be invested in high streets and local transport.

While Labour mayors have backed the new levy, others have expressed caution or signalled they will not bring it in.

Local leaders, including heads of Foundation Strategic Authorities where there is no mayor, will need to clarify by early 2028 how the revenue raised should be reinvested.

They will also be allowed to offer exemptions, such as for campsites.

However, mayors will not be allowed to exempt whole localities within their regions from the tax, to avoid creating confusion for visitors and businesses.

The government said it would introduce a bill to Parliament "in due course" to bring in the levy, which would apply to both Britons and people visiting from abroad.

News.title: I was weeks from marrying a violent serial rapist - my loved ones saved my life
News.content:
This article contains details, including depictions of violence, which some readers may find distressing.

Without the interventions of her family and friends, Amy says she would have married the man who had physically and psychologically abused her for much of their relationship.

Had the wedding gone ahead, she fears he would have eventually killed her.

Christopher Malcolm, a serial rapist who was recently jailed for his crimes, inflicted life-changing injuries on his former fiancÃ©e - on one occasion she said he left her face "black and blue" just before she visited her terminally ill father for Father's Day.

Amy, not her real name, told the BBC that staying in the relationship was often a means to calm the violence and survive. So long as Malcolm was free, she said she did not feel safe enough to report him to police.

Her loved ones, meanwhile, grew increasingly worried. On several occasions they reported their concerns for Amy's welfare to Police Scotland's disclosure scheme for domestic abuse, external (known as Clare's Law in England and Wales), supplying evidence including text messages and photos of her injuries.

This ultimately helped officers build a strong enough case to arrest Malcolm, who was taken into custody in September 2024. Shortly afterwards, Amy gave a full report of the rapes, assaults and abuse she had been subjected to.

She had been due to marry Malcolm four weeks later.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister, Balbir Singh, told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

Asked by Judge Michael Chambers KC if Lashley's body had ever been found, Singh said: "No, because this is 28 years ago and the body was put into the cellar downstairs."

West Midlands Police previously said Lashley, a mother of seven, moved to Dudley in the 1990s and it was understood she and Dunkley knew one another.

Her family made a fresh appeal to trace her in 2017.

Police said she had been known to have links to London, Newcastle, Wales and Scotland, and was known locally as Pat or Jade, and also used the names Vanessa and Tricia, as well as the surname Bradford.

News.title: 'We cannot show our grandson photos of his dad after wildfire destroyed our house'
News.content:
Treasured photos of family members, destroyed forever - those are among the key possessions which Sandy and Uttam Shiralkar say they will never hold again.

They were among the 19 families who lost their homes when two fires started accidentally and tore through dry grass and into their estate in Stourbridge, in the West Midlands, on the hottest day of the year.

"We have lost 20, 30 years of memories. They may be there in the mind but you can't share them with others," Uttam said.

He was working from home on 13 August when he first noticed the smell of smoke, at first thinking someone was having a barbecue.

News.title: Species 'at risk of vanishing' from area of Wales' largest national park
News.content:
Another project which will benefit is Tlysau Mynydd Eryri (Mountain Jewels of Eryri), part of a conservation partnership led by Plantlife Cymru to protect the future of some of the rarest alpine plants in Wales.

Ecological surveys and regular monitoring will map the impact of the restoration work, using species such as the woodcock and otter, and plants including aspen and juniper to give an idea of the health of the valley.

The work will also build on innovative use of GPS livestock collars to manage grazing more precisely.

Cwm Idwal Partnership Officer Rhys Wheldon-Roberts said monitoring was "really important because it allows us to graze in the right areas at the right densities and at the right time".

He added: "The collars on the cattle allow us to move the cattle around the landscape and you can monitor it as you go, and the farmers can see that data live on their apps.

"It can make grazing something much more effective for the cattle and for nature."

As well as local farmers, there will be an emphasis on community involvement and volunteering as part of the work.

"There are opportunities for people to get involved in monitoring, in volunteering, just learning about the landscape in general," said Wheldon-Roberts.

"Here in Cwm Idwal we have lots of school visits every year and they'll be able to see the effects of the project and the effect that the cattle are having in that conservation grazing way, so it's really exciting in that regard as well.

"By bringing people along with us they get a chance to learn and hopefully appreciate, and ultimately try to protect this special landscape that we've got around us."

The project is being funded by nearly Â£1m from the Nature Networks Fund, external, delivered by the Heritage Fund on behalf of the Welsh government and in partnership with Natural Resources Wales.

"What we're trying to do with this project is set a foundation for the future," said Rogers.

"Some things will change in the next three years, but what we're doing is setting ourselves up so that recovery can continue for decades afterwards."

News.title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
News.content:
"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.

Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.

It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.

The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.

Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.

That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.

During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.

Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".

This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.

He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."

Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.

They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.

It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.

Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

News.content:

Remaining with the high-street institution your parents used, or the provider that handed you a student loan for takeaway kebabs, could be needlessly costing you money.

Multiple major UK banks are currently offering £200 or more in cash to persuade consumers to switch current accounts, paired with improved interest rates on savings, and moving accounts has never been simpler.

"Loyalty doesn’t pay, and firms rely on your inertia," agrees Scott Dixon, an Edinburgh-based consumer rights champion who is known as The Complaints Resolver.

Yet as with most things, switching can come with a price. "Everybody wants a frictionless banking experience," says Dixon.

"But you need to ask yourself – is a new bank going to make life easier for me?" If you are planning to switch banks, here is everything you ought to know before taking the plunge…

Why do people tend to feel loyal to banks?

“Often it’s not so much loyalty, but is more about ‘better the devil you know’,” says Dixon. “We all lead busy lives, and our bank account just ticks along in the background.”

open image in gallery Multiple major UK banks are currently offering £200 or more in cash to persuade consumers to switch current accounts, paired with improved interest rates on savings, and moving accounts has never been simpler

Dixon is guilty of that himself. “I’ve been with HSBC since 2009 but I know my branch manager, and if anything goes wrong, I can speak to somebody and get it sorted.

“However, since Covid was treated by banks as a once-in-a lifetime-opportunity to decimate the branch network, forcing everybody to go online, it’s created a multitude of problems for many people.”

What upfront cash incentives could you get from switching?

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

“The biggest benefit of switching is the cash bonus,” says Dixon. “NatWest are currently doing a £200 switch offer, but you can look for the best current deals on Uswitch or MoneySuperMarket.

“People should look at the headline perks and bonuses, and better interest rates, and cash-back and discounts, and customer service is also something to consider.”

But he warns, “It’s easy to get seduced by offers – but make sure that you read the T&Cs to see if you’re eligible before applying and having that credit search logged on your credit file. Some restrictions include things like minimum monthly credits, like your salary or £1k-1.5k a month being paid into the account.”

How easy is it to switch?

The admin involved in switching accounts has been simplified. The Current Account Switch Service (CASS) moves your money, direct debits and standing orders across and closes your old account in seven working days.

“Moving bank accounts is very easy to do now,” says Dixon. “You get in touch with your new bank and they just do everything in one go.”

Are there any drawbacks to switching too often?

If you switch bank accounts frequently, and you need to apply for a mortgage, loan or car finance, credit searches are recorded and frequent searches can work against you.

open image in gallery The Current Account Switch Service (CASS) moves your money, direct debits and standing orders across and closes your old account in seven working days. ( Getty )

Dixon explains, “There are two types of searches – a soft search (which is what Buy Now Pay Later has been doing until recently) and hard searches for products such as mortgages and car loans.

“The problem is you don’t know which one will be carried out. I would take the view that a hard search will be carried out and if you clock up too many searches in a short period of time, it can affect your credit score.”

Some people use ‘burner accounts’ to switch regularly in order to benefit from the cash, but Dixon says, “It’s a lot of ‘faff’, and potentially could cost you time and money monitoring two different accounts with direct debits.”

What other perks might persuade someone to switch?

On top of cash bonuses, some banks offer ongoing 1-2 per cent cashback on spending or household bills, or retail vouchers.

open image in gallery Switching to a new current account could earn you up to £220 in free cash and perks

“One of the best perks is travel insurance,” says Dixon. “But you’ve got to treat it like a proper insurance policy. When it comes to making claims on bank account travel insurance, declaring pre-existing health conditions is a big problem and consumers are coming unstuck.”

Dixon says customer service is an unspoken benefit of switching. “We’re increasingly looking for bank accounts that provide better service. Some banks are better than others – Nationwide, Monzo and First Direct are rated highly.”

What are the benefits of switching to a higher savings interest rate?

Some high street banks are also offering as much as 8 per cent on savings – but these deals are not for long-term lump sum savers. Dixon explains, “If you take out a savings account that sits side by side with the current account, that’s where you’ll find the higher savings interest rates.

“But you need to watch out for banks reducing the introductory interest rate after a length of time.”

Many also charge a monthly maintenance fee that could wipe any interest earned, and usually come with a 12-month rate cliff. They require a monthly deposit of £150-£250 and that headline interest rate is only earned on the rolling amount, so you only bag the 8% rate in the final month.

Emma Bonino, who rose to prominence as a leader of campaigns by the Radical Party that legalized abortion and divorce in the 1970s in heavily Roman Catholic Italy, has died.

Bonino was famed for pushing for change against the objections of the Vatican.

She was 78, her party, +Europa, announced her death.

“Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” the party said.

Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for over five decades. She served as a European commissioner for then premier Silvio Berlusconi and was a co-founder of the death penalty watchdog Hands Off Cain. But her bid in 1999 to become Italy’s first female president failed.

She remained known to younger generations as a sought-after political pundit, appearing frequently on Italian TV with her sharp wit and cutting insights. After her cancer diagnosis in 2015, she invariably appeared in public wearing colorful headscarves.

Born on March 9, 1948, in Bra — not far from the northwestern Italian city of Turin, where carmaker Fiat’s factory drove the economy — she spent her childhood on a farm, where she was often tasked to pasture pigs, a lifestyle she described as “deadly boring” in a 2023 TV interview.

Bonino first got involved in Italian politics because she wanted to change the law. At 26, she became pregnant and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time.

Recalling the experience as one of the most humiliating of her life, in 1975 she was among the founders of the Information Center for Sterilization and Abortion, an organization that provided information and performed abortions before they were legalized.

The following year she was elected to the Italian parliament for the maverick Radical Party, a bastion of anticlericalism, civil libertarianism, feminism, liberalism and radicalism in Italy.

open image in gallery Italy's Emma Bonino, leader of the More Europe party, speaks during a news conference at the Foreign Press Association in Rome, Italy 16 February, 2018 ( Reuters )

The party proposed itself as the strongest opposition to the Italian political establishment, seen as corrupt and conservative, and to the Catholic Church’s extensive influence on Italian society.

In 1978 abortion was legalized. That particular campaign may have been over, but Bonino had found her vocation: Politics was her life, and she became one of the most active leaders of the Radical Party and its successors.

A veteran legislator in Italian politics and an activist for various reform policies, she was elected six times as Lower House lawmaker and two times as senator. In 2017, she became the leader of +Europa, a liberal, European federalist party slate she launched ahead of the 2018 Italian general election.

An explosive presence in politics during her 50-year-long career, Bonino was one of the few Italian political figures who scored important achievements both at home and internationally.

Bonino won European exposure in a role she owed to then center-right Premier Silvio Berlusconi who, in 1995, offered her one of Italy’s two seats in the European Commission.

As a Commissioner she forged the EU’s consumer protection policy and created the European Commission Humanitarian Office, which is now the primary European humanitarian arm. It was this last portfolio, the humanitarian affairs, she felt the most.

She traveled to war zones -- former Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Sudan, Afghanistan -- and convinced Europe that humanitarian assistance couldn’t be an excuse for lack of political or military intervention.

In June 1999 she headed a slate named after her — Lista Bonino — at the European elections. It was an overwhelming success: The party got 8.5% of the votes and became Italy’s fourth political force.

Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian center-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s.

She was one the strongest advocates for a common European foreign and defense policy. “My passion is humanity,” she said in May 2025, when her hometown Bra granted her honorary citizenship. “I’ve got roots, I’ve got a homeland, a family, but precisely all that allows me to be a citizen of the world.”

open image in gallery An electoral manifesto of Italian politician and leader of the Lista + Europa and Radicali Italiani Emma Bonino is displayed on the streets during the electoral vote on March 4, 2018 in Florence, Italy ( Getty )

Getting involved with Arab women’s battle for equity, at the end of 2001 she started spending half her time in Cairo. She became fluent in Arabic — she had graduated in foreign languages at Milan’s Bocconi University — and built a network of intellectuals, politicians and prominent civil society figures.

Never married, she maintained strong bonds with her family in Piedmont. “My father died before I could show him I could accomplish something,” she recalled in a 2020 interview with Vanity Fair. “He never understood my restlessness. He used to tell me: Emma, you are like Japanese poetry: beautiful, but I can’t understand it.”

In January 2015, she announced on Radio Radicale she was suffering from lung cancer and was being treated with chemotherapy but didn’t plan to stop her political activity. In May of the same year, she said her cancer was in complete remission and eight years later appeared on a popular TV interview program announcing she was healed.

Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia.

In November 2024, Francis paid a home visit to Bonino — who had been just released from the hospital after treatment for respiratory problems — bringing her a bouquet of roses and chocolates.

A photo posted by Bonino on social media showed them both sitting in wheelchairs on her sun-drenched terrace in Rome.

Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need.

When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino used to say: “Many, too many. Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research ... Ten lives won’t be enough.”

Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.

Zack Polanski has been selected as the Green Party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by election as he prepares to fight the crucial contest in the historically Labour seat.

The by election was triggered by the resignation of Sir Keir Starmer as an MP, after he was ousted by his party and replaced as prime minister by Andy Burnham.

Speaking as he was confirmed as the party’s candidate in the contest, which will take place next month, the Green Party leader said “everyone knows it's the Green Party against Labour” in what he described as “truly historic” by election.

“The people of Holborn and St. Pancras want better for this place, and I will fight for you, because Greens might be the underdog in this election, but we have the momentum, and we can win,” he said.

He was declared the winner of a local party members’ vote after online hustings on Thursday night, after coming up against local councillor Hamza Chowdhury for the Green nomination.

open image in gallery Zack Polanski has been selected as the Green Party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by election as he prepares to fight the crucial contest in the historically Labour seat ( James Manning/PA Wire )

Green Party MP Hannah Spencer said local party members “overwhelmingly” chose London Assembly member Mr Polanski over Mr Chowdhury for the nomination, after the councillor stated that the constituency does not need "another MP who arrives during an election campaign" and then "disappears once the votes are counted".

The by-election will pose early test for Mr Burnham’s popularity with the public, with the Greens likely to pose the greatest threat to Labour in the contest.

Labour has held the Holborn and St Pancras seat continuously since it was created in 1983, but voters there have moved towards Green and independent candidates in recent years.

Only two Labour MPs have ever represented Holborn and St Pancras: former health secretary Frank Dobson, from 1983 to 2015, then Sir Keir.

But Green Party made gains in the May local elections in the London Borough of Camden, the local authority that covers the constituency.

The contest also poses a challenge for the Green Party leader himself as he takes on Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who has led Camden Council since May this year and been a councillor for Camden Square since 2022, at the October 8 contest.

Support for the Greens surged in his first year as leader but the party’s national polling has dipped since Mr Burnham replaced Sir Keir in Downing Street.

open image in gallery Green Party leader Zack Polanski is not currently an MP (Ben Whitley/PA) ( PA Wire )

“It's clear, everyone knows it's the Green Party against Labour,” Mr Polanski said on Friday. “And before May, we had one councillor here, and now we have 10.”

He added: “In 27 days, voters in Holborn and St Pancras will go to the polls. Between now and then, I'll be on the doorsteps, day in, day out, listening to people about the issues that matter to them, because a Green voice like mine will not waver.”

Labour’s candidate, who is a former child refugee, has faced what has been described as “straightforward racism” from Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf in recent days, after he wrote on X: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia.

"Do you understand what’s happening?”

Mr Polanski called the comments “despicable” and said he would show “unconditional solidarity” with Labour’s candidate.

But he added: “I will stand with any candidate who is facing abusive attacks, and at the same time put forward Green Party policies that are going to make life easier for everyone in this country and in this constituency.”

Mr Polanski, a London Assembly member, has previously said he was “excited” by the prospect of winning the seat and entering the Commons.

He dismissed suggestions from rival Mr Chowdhury that the constituency did not need “another MP who arrives during an election campaign” then “disappears once the votes are counted”.

“I think the local party already knows that doesn’t describe me at all. It’s a place that I know very, very well,” Mr Polanski said on Wednesday.

More follows on this story...
