On normal days, one trader said, “there would be many ships out there,” but “because of the attack of the Huthi there are no ships right now.”

Children played in the Red Sea’s lukewarm waves. Apparently unconcerned about their parents’ worries, they jostled to get into the visiting journalists’ pictures.

But the image that emerges here is of an already war-weary, fragile and poor country being pushed ever closer to a breaking point.

A few miles up the coast, evidence of that is mounting.

The port of Mocha remains closed following a Huthi attack in August that killed 16 people. Ships, boats, equipment and platforms were destroyed in the attack. Michael Pratt/CNN

The port of Mocha, the most northerly government-held city of significance on the Red Sea, is being hit hard. A few weeks ago, more than 25 Huthi rockets slammed into the sprawling harbor as commercial ships were unloading, according to port director Abdel Malek Al-Sharaabi.

In the water, half-sunk ships lie at improbable angles, while the concrete on land is scarred with holes deep enough to hide a large dog. Heaps of scorched motorcycle frames lie beside piles of semi-melted engines.

Sixteen people were killed and 22 injured that day, the port director told CNN, while six commercial ships were sunk and 14,000 motorcycles lost. The Huthis, he said, want to destroy the economy.

“The port had a big role in development and commerce,” Al-Sharaabi said. “This attack aims at hurting this development and stopping services.”

Over the past year, the Huthis have repeatedly fired at targets as far as Israel, more than 1,000 miles away. They claim to possess hypersonic missiles and have an arsenal that includes long-range, sea-skimming anti-ship missiles designed to evade radar. They also possess surface-to-air missiles capable of downing high-altitude US drones and threatening crewed aircraft.

‘Higher price in the future’

On Yemen’s front lines, fighting between Huthi and government forces is intensifying. Government troops are flying new, first-person-view, or FPV, quadcopter drones, attacking concealed Huthi bunkers.

“Our troops have improved due to training and new resources like drones,” Saleh told CNN.

But for every step the government takes, officials say, Iran is trying to keep the Huthis ahead. A journey in a vehicle with blacked-out windows to a heavily guarded warehouse at a secret location offered a glimpse of that challenge – and what the government says is evidence of the scale of Iranian support for the Huthis, including the provision of weapons capable of threatening tanker traffic in the Red Sea.

Abdel Nasser El Mamlouh, the director of Saleh’s military media operation, led CNN through what he said was an Iranian-made weapons shipment captured before smugglers could deliver it to the Huthis.

The National Resistance Forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government say they regularly seize advanced weapons smuggled at sea to their Huthi foes. Michael Pratt/CNN

The cache included enormous, 18-foot-long missiles, complex long-range radar systems, drone engines and optical equipment, even bullets hidden inside a truck battery. Everything, El Mamlouh said, had been disguised as commercial equipment to evade detection.

And what they captured, he readily acknowledged, was only a fraction of what is believed to have made it through. Smugglers “confessed that before this one they had smuggled 11 shipments similar in size and content,” he said, amounting to 750 tons.

If the Huthis seized Perim and gained a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, he warned, they would no longer need long-range weapons to threaten shipping.

“They would mine the strait, just like (Iran) did in Hormuz,” he said.

Along Yemen’s government-held stretch of Red Sea coast, officials have little doubt that their civil war has become part of something much larger.

“(We are) fighting this war on behalf of the Arab world and the international community,” Mamlouh said.

Before hurrying away from his tent on the beach, Saleh was asked what would happen if US support never came.

“We will pay a higher price in the future,” to dislodge the Huthis, he replied. And so, he warned, would “the American army, the international community and international trade.”

CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany contributed to this report.

World.title: ‘Gambling with our lives’: Another AI employee quits over safety concerns
World.content:
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

That blunt admission from former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon made waves Tuesday, as the just-quit 27-year-old AI researcher spilled the beans on his way out the door in a resignation thread on X.

As alarming and serious as Coxon’s revelations sound (“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources”), they’re also not new. Anthropic got its start in exactly this way, as OpenAI employees concerned about the company’s safety protocols left Sam Altman’s startup to launch their own AI company, arguing their approach was more responsible.

The concerns are becoming commonplace. A number of AI employees have loudly quit their companies over safety concerns over the past several months and years. Others have publicly voiced worries that the technology is moving too quickly and will one day outpace humans’ ability to control it.

In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter urging the US government to regulate the technology to rein in Big Tech and slow the pace of AI to ensure its safety. And two days ago, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ ability to reliably monitor and control them.

Now, a relatively junior researcher has become the latest to sound the alarm.

“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon posted.

Coxon’s post gained attention after a more senior Anthropic employee, Evan Hubinger, commented that Coxon was correct.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger posted on X. He said he personally believes the chance is under 10% over the next decade, and despite Anthropic’s good intentions it doesn’t have a plan to avoid so-called superintelligence that could exceed humans’ ability to control AI. Superintelligence, a state at which AI surpasses human capabilities, is a widely debated theoretical milestone with no benchmark that some AI researchers believe has already been achieved and others believe will never come.

Hubinger shortly after clarified his statement in a follow-up post that Anthropic’s own Risk Report acknowledges the concern but says present AI poses little chance of gaining such power.

“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also repeatedly warned that the race to move fast on the technology could unintentionally result in a catastrophic human-caused error that causes a company to lose control of its AI.

“This is a complex engineering problem and I think something will go wrong with someone’s AI system. Hopefully not ours,” Amodei told the New York Times in February.

Regulation stagnation

Despite the constant stream of warnings, regulation seems far off. The Trump administration has actively worked to undermine state AI regulations and Congress has so far been unwilling to rein in the technology. A common refrain: Any effort to regulate AI represents a capitulation to China, which is under no such constraints.

Except China has introduced AI regulation, particularly aimed at risk management and safety. Last year, the government required AI companies to label AI-generated content to make it transparent and traceable. However, China has resisted the kind of stringent regulation that would prevent the kind of problems Silicon Valley researchers have raised.

In the meantime, in the US at least, AI companies are more or less responsible for policing themselves.

The White House has moved toward a voluntary framework to review certain AI models before launch, sources familiar with a meeting last month between the Trump administration and several top AI companies told CNN.

Among the representatives were those from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, according to multiple sources familiar with the situation. The details of the framework will not be released publicly and many of the standards set within it will be classified, according to a June executive order on the framework.

In July, Altman suggested it may be time to slow AI development, saying in the Invest Like The Best podcast that the recent testing incidents involving advanced models were raising “long-term questions” about how AI companies should manage rapid advances in capabilities.

“We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels,” Altman said.

Anthropic, in a statement on Wednesday, concurred with Altman.

“We believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.”

World.title: Netanyahu faces backlash over report he was warned of Hamas attack days before October 7
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faced a fierce political backlash Tuesday over a report that the president of the UAE had warned him of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 2023 attack.

The Prime Minister’s Office dismissed the report as an “absolute lie.” But with Israel’s October elections less than two months away, Netanyahu’s rivals seized on it as the latest evidence of what they say is a growing list of warnings he had ignored.

The four opposition party leaders – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan – issued a rare joint statement calling for “an immediate and thorough investigation” into Netanyahu’s “failures and malfunctioning.”

“The Israeli public is entitled to know: What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn’t update the security establishment, and why he didn’t act to protect Israeli civilians?” the statement said.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said the report is “true,” writing on X that Netanyahu’s alleged disregard for the warnings amounts to “criminal negligence.” Bennett’s political ally, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, said he too had publicly warned of an attack before it happened, as had top Israeli security officials as well as Egyptian officials. “If Netanyahu had fulfilled his role, the massacre would have been prevented,” Lapid said in a statement.

The report, published in the Haaretz newspaper, was based on findings from an upcoming book by Israeli journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruti Yuval. It said UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed called Netanyahu about 10 days before October 7 and, during a 45-minute call, warned him that Hamas’ Gaza leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major move against Israel that could cause bloodshed and destabilize the region. The report cited a message Sinwar conveyed to the UAE and Israel through a Palestinian mediator in mid-September 2023, warning of an upcoming “earthquake.”

Haaretz reported that Netanyahu reacted “relatively calmly” to the information, and assured Bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

The UAE’s Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying that it “does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders” but did not deny the call. “When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities,” the statement said.

An Israeli source familiar with the matter said Netanyahu’s office had tried to get the UAE to deny the Haaretz report, but the UAE only agreed to put out a statement about intelligence sharing.

The Prime Minister’s Office strongly denied the report, stating Netanyahu “did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him.”

Eldar, one of the journalists behind the report, pushed back on Netanyahu’s denial of the report.

“It’s true,” he told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “I worked on this report for almost a year and a half,” he said.

“I have the document, I have records, I have everything that shows that the president of the UAE called Netanyahu a week an a half before October 7 and gave him a warning that Yahya Sinwar is planning a major attack on Israel,” Eldar said.

Accountability as an electoral issue

The report comes as Netanyahu’s rivals work to make accountability for October 7 – the deadliest attack in Israel’s history, during which over 1,200 people were murdered and more than 250 abducted to Gaza – a central campaign issue.

Netanyahu has now outlasted nearly every member of Israel’s top security leadership from that day. Since the attack, the defense minister, the military chief of staff, and the directors of military intelligence, the Mossad and the Shin Bet, have all either resigned, been ousted, or reached the end of their terms.

Gadi Eisenkot, currently polling as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, said the Haaretz report shows Netanyahu “led Israel blindly” toward the October 7 failures and renewed his pledge to establish a state commission of inquiry if elected.

Nearly three years after the attack, Netanyahu has resisted demands from bereaved families and October 7 survivors to establish an independent commission to investigate the security and intelligence failures that enabled Hamas to conduct the operation.

Abandoned and torched vehicles at the site of the October 7 attack on the Nova music festival. Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images

He and his associates have instead promoted a narrative blaming security chiefs for not waking him up the night before the attack despite intelligence indications that a Hamas offensive was imminent.

Last month, his wife, Sara Netanyahu, suggested that Yair Golan – a retired major general and the leader of the left-wing Democrats party who independently rushed to the Gaza border on October 7 to rescue survivors – had advance knowledge of the attack.

In an interview with the pro-government Channel 14, she questioned how Golan was “already dressed and ready” at dawn that day to head south, “while others knew nothing, including the prime minister.”

Golan demanded an apology for what he called a “vile conspiracy theory” and said he would pursue a defamation suit, calling the allegation part of Netanyahu’s attempt to “rewrite” the events of October 7 and deflect responsibility.

Following the Haaretz report, Golan wrote on X that the prime minister’s “they-didn’t-wake-me-up narrative is over. He knew, he was warned.” He called it “not an error in judgment, but a conscious and criminal abandonment.”

Hours later, the Democrats party sharpened its electoral campaign against Netanyahu, erecting a giant billboard over Tel Aviv’s main highway bearing the headline: “The 1,200 murdered file – Causing death by negligence.”

World.title: Video: Large crocodile spotted in Egypt’s Sharqiya drainage canal
World.content:
Residents of Ezbet al-Sidrah in Belbeis Center, Sharqiya Governorate, reported sighting a large crocodile along the banks of a local drainage canal, prompting urgent calls for authority intervention to ensure public safety.

A viral video circulating online shows the crocodile emerging from the canal’s embankment as local residents passed by, before returning to the water seconds later.

Local residents noted that sightings have become increasingly common over recent months, with crocodiles observed both swimming in the canal and basking for minutes at a time.

Recurring sightings

Residents reported witnessing multiple crocodiles simultaneously on previous occasions, both in the water and along the embankments.

Community members emphasized that this is not an isolated event, noting that authorities successfully captured a crocodile in the area last winter, which was subsequently transferred to an authorized facility.

أخبار مصر اليوم الجديدة

Appeals for immediate public safety action

These sustained sightings near canal banks have fueled growing safety concerns, particularly given the proximity of local foot traffic to the water’s edge.

Residents are urging environmental and local authorities to inspect the site immediately, conduct a comprehensive sweep of the canal to clear any remaining crocodiles, and implement strict safety measures to secure populated areas.

World.title: Gold prices rise as US dollar drops
World.content:
Gold prices advanced on Thursday, buoyed by a softer US dollar as investors closely await key inflation data out of the United States.

Spot gold rose zero point three percent to US$4,412.84 per ounce by 02:34 GMT.

Meanwhile, US gold futures for December delivery dipped zero point one percent to $4,457.10 per ounce, according to Reuters market data.

“At present, geopolitical developments in the Persian Gulf are taking a back seat for gold,” said Marex analyst Edward Meir.

“Instead, gold is benefiting from a persistently weak US dollar, which remarkably continues to sag despite the upward trajectory of US interest rates.”

The US dollar remained under modest pressure, making dollar-denominated metals more affordable for buyers holding other currencies.

In a research note, the senior commodities strategist at ANZ Daniel Hynes, highlighted the broader macroeconomic tailwinds: “Gold continues to find support as ongoing US fiscal pressures erode confidence in the long-term value of government debt and the currency used to finance it.”

Overall precious metal market performance

Across other precious metals, spot silver gained zero point two percent to reach $67.42 per ounce.

Conversely, platinum slipped zero point six percent to $1,885.02 per ounce, while palladium edged up zero point two percent to trade at $1,355.50 per ounce.

World.title: Photos: Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reunite for ‘Practical Magic 2’ as sequel hits Egyptian theaters
World.content:
Egyptian and Arab cinemas welcomed “Practical Magic 2” on Thursday, September 10, 2026.

The sequel reunites superstars Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as the witch sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, nearly 28 years after the original film premiered in 1998.

The franchise’s return comes as the first installment has built a massive cult following over the decades, generating intense interest in the announcement—especially with Bullock and Kidman reprising their iconic roles.

European premiere highlights Iconic on-screen sisterhood

Ahead of its release, London served as a major promotional landmark, hosting the European premiere at the Odeon Luxe Leicester Square.

Bullock and Kidman led the star-studded red carpet alongside new and returning cast members. Joey King and Maisie Williams, who join the “Practical Magic” universe in this chapter, were present alongside Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest, who return as Aunts Frances and Jet. Danish director Susanne Bier and members of the creative team also attended.

The premiere was more than a routine press tour stop; it turned into a celebration of one of cinema’s most enduring female relationships.

Bullock and Kidman appeared side-by-side on the red carpet, recapturing the spirit of the 1998 classic and thrusting the characters back into the cultural spotlight.

Kidman and Bullock reflect on legacy, darker themes, and co-producing

During the event, Nicole Kidman highlighted the significance of stepping back into this world after nearly three decades, describing it as an extraordinary moment for both her and Bullock. Kidman noted that if anyone had told them 28 years ago that they would lead a massive studio film together at this stage in their careers, they would not have believed it, adding that it is wonderful to see the film receive such visibility.

She also expressed hope that the new generation of actresses will “carry the torch” and continue the franchise’s legacy.

Kidman reprises her role as Gillian Owens, the freer, more impulsive sister facing a new set of magical and familial challenges, while her bond with Sally remains the emotional core of the story.

Bullock emphasized that the sequel works hard to preserve the original’s DNA, citing essential elements like sisterhood, humor, and the ability to pivot from lighthearted moments to darker, more tragic themes.

Bullock remarked that the film does not shy away from grief or dark spaces, while keeping its warmth and wit intact—stressing that Sally and Gillian’s relationship must remain the foundation if the franchise continues.

Marking her return to acting after a hiatus, Bullock also serves as a producer alongside Kidman, making the project a dual comeback for both stars in front of and behind the camera.

Susanne Bier directs multi-generational ensemble facing new curse

Acclaimed Danish filmmaker Susanne Bier—director of “Brothers”, “Bird Box”, and “The Night Manager”—helms the sequel.

Her appointment aims to preserve the original’s distinct tone while expanding the narrative to encompass a new generation of Owens women.

The story introduces a multi-generational dynamic where the family faces a new magical curse threatening to tear them apart, forcing the women to unite against the danger.

The ensemble cast includes Joey King, Lee Pace, Maisie Williams, Xolo Maridueña, and Solly McLeod, alongside Wiest and Channing. King and Williams portray the younger generation of the Owens family, embodying the passage of power, magic, and legacy across generations.

“Practical Magic 2” follows the Owens women as they confront a generational curse. Sally and Gillian must reclaim their power while joining forces with the younger family members.

More than just a sequel, the film seeks to revive a universe anchored in magic, sisterhood, love, and family ties.

Based on the world created by author Alice Hoffman in her novel “The Book of Magic”, the screenplay was penned by Akiva Goldsman, Georgia Pritchett, and Kelly Marcel. Warner Bros. Pictures is handling worldwide distribution, with United Motion Pictures distributing the film in Egypt.

World.title: Will the Central Bank raise interest rates at its upcoming meeting?
World.content:
Expectations are growing that central banks globally will move to raise interest rates to hedge against an inflationary wave triggered by rising energy prices.

Expert forecasts for the Central Bank of Egypt’s (CBE) upcoming Monetary Policy Committee meeting on September 24 lean heavily toward keeping rates unchanged.

The ECB and Fed prepare policy shifts

The European Central Bank (ECB) is widely expected to hike interest rates, proceeding with caution as the ongoing US-Iranian conflict keeps oil prices elevated and reignites inflationary pressures.

This follows after Brent crude surged over the past month, while European natural gas prices reached their highest levels since early 2023.

Sources told Reuters that the ECB is prepared to raise interest rates again in September, aligning with the minutes of its July meeting.

Traders have priced in a quarter-point move to two point five percent, as the latest data shows Eurozone inflation rising back above three percent in August due to soaring energy costs.

According to the Financial Times, the US August Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation data could serve as the decisive metric for Federal Reserve policymakers during their September 15–16 meeting when deliberating whether to raise interest rates.

Key Drivers Behind Global Tightening

The General Manager of Wathiqah Brokerage, Mohamed Abdel-Hady, expects several central banks worldwide—led by the US Federal Reserve, the ECB, and the Bank of Japan—to raise interest rates.

He attributes this to three primary factors:

Persistent inflation: Inflation rates continuously exceeding central bank target ranges.

Inflation rates continuously exceeding central bank target ranges. Energy price surges: Sustained increases in oil prices threatening further secondary inflation.

Sustained increases in oil prices threatening further secondary inflation. Geopolitical volatility: Ongoing geopolitical tensions increasing overall economic uncertainty and fueling sustained inflation.

Expert perspectives: Global hikes vs. Egypt’s rate freeze

Abdel-Hady told Al-Masry Al-Youm that these combined factors reinforce the case for global central banks to raise interest rates, as each driver fuels inflationary pressures that necessitate monetary tightening.

He noted that while the US might hold rates steady due to underlying economic strength, rate hikes remain highly likely for both the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank.

Regarding the domestic market, Abdel-Hady predicted that the Central Bank of Egypt will opt to keep interest rates unchanged, given that key rates in Egypt are already elevated.

He warned, however, that global rate hikes could negatively impact hot money flows, triggering capital flight from emerging markets toward higher yields elsewhere, alongside driving potential upward pressure on the US dollar against the Egyptian pound locally.

Emerging market risks and CBE outlook

Concurrently, banking expert Sahar al-Damaty emphasized that major central banks leaning toward renewed rate increases stems primarily from fears of resurfacing inflation—particularly as energy and oil prices climb alongside ongoing geopolitical volatility.

She explained that central banks are exercising extreme caution to prevent new price surges from disrupting their longer-term rate-cutting trajectories.

Damaty added to Al-Masry Al-Youm that the CBE is expected to adopt a wait-and-see approach during its upcoming meeting, provided domestic inflation continues its downward trend and foreign exchange pressures remain manageable.

Maintaining interest rates at current levels for an extended period, she noted, offers policymakers valuable room to fully evaluate the impact of previous monetary decisions on the broader economy and local markets.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: A Mystery Vessel, a Prison, and a Warning Nobody Answered
World.content:
MONROVIA — There is a version of this story in which the boat behind the Monrovia Central Prison is nothing more than a stray vessel, pushed toward shore by the tide and forgotten within days.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

But Thursday’s discovery is difficult to view in isolation.

Five weeks ago, the prison’s Deputy Superintendent for Operations, Jackson K. Kolako, publicly warned that he believed a plan was being developed to facilitate a mass jailbreak—potentially freeing foreign nationals detained in connection with Liberia’s largest cocaine investigation.

Now, before dawn on Thursday, a vessel of disputed ownership and unexplained movements was found at the beach behind the same prison.

Coincidence is possible. But the timing has raised questions that authorities have yet to fully answer.

What Kolako Actually Said

Kolako’s account dates to August 1, when, according to him, two men arrived at the prison claiming to be National Security Agency officers. He said the men were dressed in a manner inconsistent with prison security rules and sought access to one of the foreign nationals detained in connection with the drug case.

Kolako said he questioned whether the prison’s chief superintendent and the Assistant Minister of Justice for Corrections had authorized the visit.

He says he was arrested later that day, in front of his officers, on the orders of a senior Justice Ministry official.

According to Kolako, he spent six days in custody without giving a statement and was pressured to surrender his phones and passwords. Following his release, he publicly raised his concerns and appealed to President Joseph Boakai to consider moving detainees connected to the drug investigation to a more secure facility outside Liberia, suggesting Morocco as one possible destination.

Kolako’s account, however, remains contested.

He has not publicly produced evidence establishing that an actual jailbreak plot was underway, while officials he implicated have not publicly addressed all of his allegations. Ministry of Justice records have reportedly presented a different explanation for his suspension, saying he was sanctioned over alleged obstruction of a lawful operation rather than for raising security concerns.

The competing accounts have yet to be reconciled.

On Thursday, Kolako again took to social media, emphasizing the need for heightened coordination among the Liberia National Police, Armed Forces of Liberia and corrections authorities.

Kolako, using the name Gertrude’s Pap on Facebook, said the detention of people connected to sensitive and high-profile cases requires preparedness, coordination and vigilance.

“Security is stronger when institutions work together,” Kolako wrote.

Mystery Vessel Sparks Calls for Independent Probe

The vessel’s appearance has now triggered calls for an independent investigation.

Liberian activist Martin K. N. Kollie, whose network first reported the boat, is calling for an independent inquiry into how the unidentified vessel came to be at the beach behind the Monrovia Central Prison, commonly known as South Beach.

Kollie has described the vessel as a “ghost boat” and questioned conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership, origin and movements.

He has specifically called for an investigation outside the Liberia National Police, including Inspector General Gregory Coleman, arguing that the circumstances require investigators viewed as independent by the public.

The vessel was later moved toward the Miami Beach area, according to accounts surrounding the incident, further raising questions about who controlled it and why it had initially been positioned near the prison.

The Question of the Boat

Kollie has also challenged claims that the vessel found at South Beach belongs to a person identified publicly only as “Charlie,” who reportedly described himself during a radio interview as a Canadian miner.

Kollie maintains that images circulated by people claiming ownership show a different vessel from the one found behind the prison.

That claim has not been independently verified by FrontPage Africa.

The unresolved questions are nevertheless straightforward: Who owns the vessel? Where did it come from? Who was operating it? When did it leave the St. Paul River? How did it reach South Beach? And was anyone aboard at any point during the journey?

Those questions become more consequential because of the vessel’s location.

The beach behind the prison sits within a highly sensitive security environment, particularly as the facility houses detainees linked to Liberia’s ongoing drug-trafficking investigation.

A Country That Has Seen This Boat Before

The episode comes against a backdrop of growing scrutiny over Liberia’s maritime security.

In June, a vessel identified as the IB Atlantic IV remained off the coast of Grand Cape Mount County for several days as Liberian authorities considered how to respond before the vessel eventually moved away and was later intercepted and seized in Ivorian waters.

No drugs were officially reported recovered from the vessel.

The episode nevertheless became another example of the challenges facing Liberia in monitoring and securing its coastline.

The latest vessel presents a different but related set of questions.

Despite competing ownership claims, authorities have not publicly established who owns the boat, how it reached South Beach or whether it was carrying anything when it arrived.

Nor has any official investigation publicly established a connection between the vessel and the ongoing drug-trafficking cases.

What Remains Unanswered

For now, the boat remains less an answer than a question.

There is no publicly established evidence that the vessel was part of a jailbreak attempt. There is also no publicly established evidence that it was connected to the drug investigation.

But the combination of its location, the conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership and movement, and the prison security warnings raised weeks earlier has created a legitimate public-interest question.

An independent investigation could establish the facts without relying on competing narratives—determining the vessel’s ownership, registration, route, occupants, cargo, movements and circumstances surrounding its arrival at South Beach.

Until those questions are answered, the vessel behind the prison wall will remain what it became Thursday morning: a mystery sitting in plain sight.

World.title: Liberia: Expert Warns of Security Risks if Legislature Fails to Approve War Crimes Court Before U.N. Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Summary

Transitional justice expert Aaron Weah warns that failure to approve legislation establishing Liberia’s long-delayed War and Economic Crimes Court could create new security risks, particularly among a young generation raised on memories of the civil wars.

Liberia is preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the U.N. Security Council in December, putting a renewed international spotlight on the country’s unfinished transitional justice process.

Weah says Liberia must address how the wars are remembered and taught, warning that the absence of an agreed historical narrative, public memorials and museums has left younger Liberians exposed to disinformation about the conflict.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Aaron Weah, the leading historian and transitional justice expert, has warned of security risks if the country fails to approve legislation establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court before it assumes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Despite years of advocacy, the push for a long-delayed court to prosecute those accused of “bearing the greatest responsibility” for atrocities committed during Liberia’s two civil wars, which the United Nations estimates left about 250,000 people dead, remains unfinished as the Legislature has so far failed to overcome opposition to the courts among lawmakers.

A recent poll by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives found 89 percent of survey respondents in 11 counties wanted to see the worst perpetrators tried in a war crimes court for atrocities committed during the war.

“You don’t want to raise expectations of people and let them down. I think it has a lot of security risk because we have a youthful population,” Weah, director of the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research, said in a FrontPage Africa/New Narratives interview.

Weah’s warning comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s unfinished transitional justice process. The country is preparing to preside over the Security Council for the first time while lawmakers consider competing proposals for the long-promised court. At the same time, a population dominated by young people who did not directly experience the wars is confronting unresolved questions about justice, reparations and how the conflict should be remembered and taught.

Weah said establishing the court is about more than prosecuting alleged perpetrators. He argued that it could help clarify Liberia’s wartime history and said abandoning the process after years of promises could create new resentment and security concerns.

His warning echoes concerns raised by the Liberian government and the United Nations. In an October 2025, statement to the U.N. General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with international legal issues, the government warned that “the absence of justice perpetuates the cycle of conflict.”

Liberia’s civil wars claimed an estimated 250,000 lives. Credit: Chris Hondros / Getty Images.

The United Nations has also linked the proposed court to preventing recurrence. Christian Mukosa, its top human rights official in Liberia, said that operationalizing a victim-centered court could “contribute to reconciliation and prevent recurrence.”

According to Liberia’s 2022 Population and Housing Census , three in every four of the country’s 5.25 million people were 35 or younger. Forty four percent of the population was born after the civil wars ended in 2003. Weah said many young Liberians have instead grown up with memories of the wars passed down by their parents. After taking the court process this far, he warned, abandoning it could have consequences beyond the justice debate.

Liberia’s official campaign graphic for its successful bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2026–2027. Credit: Government of Liberia

Liberia previously served on the Security Council in 1961, but the December presidency will be its first time chairing the body. The 81st United Nations General Assembly began September 8, with President Joseph Boakai expected to deliver his third address during the General Debate, which begins September 22.

Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, recently urged Boakai to recall lawmakers from their annual constituency break to act on the legislation.

Six proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature. They include proposals from the Liberian National Bar Association and a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; separate proposals from Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah; and two bills from the government’s court office.

Boakai reenergized the process when he renewed the Office’s mandate in May and later submitted its bills to the Legislature. But lawmakers went on their annual constituency break in July without approving legislation.

Before the recess, the Senate Judiciary Committee began consultations aimed at harmonizing the proposals, while more than 40 House members participated in a two-day technical session in Buchanan in June.

Some proposals have raised concerns among justice advocates over issues including the role of international experts and the appeals process. Senator Jallah has suggested international lawyers could serve as “consultants to Liberians” , rather than take direct roles.

“The final bill should include all benchmarks of fair, independent, meaningful and credible trials: crimes and modes of liability in line with international standards,” Michelle Reyes Milk, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, wrote in Just Security, a nonpartisan law and policy journal based at New York University School of Law. She also called for “full guarantees of due process for defendants” and “genuine participation and protection for victims and witnesses.”

Weah said Liberia’s Security Council role could showcase the country’s progress since the wars. He pointed to the success of international peacekeeping and the peaceful resolution of the closely fought 2023 presidential election as signs of the country’s resilience.

But he warned that sustaining that progress requires Liberia to confront how its wars are remembered and taught to younger generations.

“We have no public memorials. We have not agreed on a historical text on the war to teach kids in school,” Weah said. “And so much of what the children learn that’s passed for history is mostly the opinions of history teachers, is the opinions of civic teachers in school, and that’s dangerous.”

Weah said museums, memorials and other forms of public education could give younger Liberians a more structured understanding of the country’s past and help address violent memories transmitted from one generation to another.

Liberia has made some steps up efforts to address memorialization. A high-level government delegation has returned from a United Nations Development Program-supported study mission to Rwanda and South Africa in late August and early September, where it examined approaches to reconciliation, memorialization, peacebuilding and preserving national history. The lessons are expected to inform President Boakai’s proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, envisioned as a national institution to preserve the country’s history, promote reconciliation and strengthen civic education.

TRC’s Controversial Decision to Sanction President Johnson Sirleaf Remains a Point of Debate

But Liberia’s efforts to establish an authoritative account of the wars have themselves generated controversy. More than 15 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued its final report, parts of its findings remain contested.

The commission recommended a 30-year public-office ban for a number of people, including then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, because it said they had been associated with former warring factions. In 2011, Liberia’s Supreme Court struck down the sanction as unconstitutional , finding that it had been imposed without due process.

Liberian civilians flee Paynesville amid fighting between rebel forces and the Armed Forces of Liberia on Aug. 10, 1990, during the country’s first civil war. Credit: Pascal Guyot/AFP via Getty Images.

In testimony to the U.S. Congress in June 1990 , as Taylor’s rebellion was terrorizing people across the country, Sirleaf portrayed Taylor’s uprising as a broad-based struggle, saying people, “many of them children,” had joined what she called a “struggle for freedom,” and describing the rebellion as an opportunity to transform Liberia’s political system. (Taylor’s alleged use of child soldiers was seen as a particularly egregious act that was copied by other warring factions in years to come.)

Weah argued that the commission’s treatment of Sirleaf contributed to her reluctance to champion implementation of its recommendations and questioned whether the report sufficiently established the extent of her involvement in the conflict.

“I think she felt embarrassed. She felt stigmatized,” Weah said. “Before you mention the names of people in report, there has to be a duty of care to make sure that your work is thorough, is rigorous. It can stand up to basic scrutiny.”

John Stewart, a commissioner who chaired the committee that wrote the TRC report, rejected Weah’s criticism. He said Sirleaf was sanctioned because commissioners concluded that her testimony about when she distanced herself from Charles Taylor conflicted with evidence they had obtained.

“We did not do so because we wanted to embarrass Sirleaf,” Stewart said. “We did so because we wanted to be fair to all others. And her being president was no exception to the rule.”

The disagreement underscores the difficulty Liberia still faces in establishing a broadly accepted account of its violent past — the problem Weah says younger generations should not be left to navigate alone.

Against that backdrop, Weah recently co-launched Liberia: Remembering the Future with British journalist Gerry Naughton. The podcast, airing on 10 radio stations across Liberia, examines the country’s history, its transition from war to peace and its election to the Security Council.

Weah said the project aims to provide historical context and clarification for Liberians, particularly younger people, as well as international audiences seeking to understand the country as its global profile rises.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: SpoonTV CEO Details Cooperation With U.S. Investigators That Led to Reduced Sentence and Early Release
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has offered a detailed account of how his decision to cooperate with U.S. federal investigators ultimately helped secure his release from prison after he was convicted in a multimillion-dollar scheme involving fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a motion by federal prosecutors to reduce the sentence to time served, eliminating the supervised-release requirement and dismissing the remaining counts against him.

The reduction was granted under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which allows prosecutors to seek a reduced sentence for a defendant who provides substantial assistance to the government after sentencing.

Witherspoon said Thursday that his cooperation was not simply a strategy to obtain a shorter sentence, but a decision he made after his lawyer and one of his Spoon Talk colleagues advised him that cooperating early could benefit his case and help investigators pursue others involved in the alleged fraud.

‘Cooperate’

Recounting the events on Spoon Talk, Witherspoon said panelist Abdullah Kiatamba advised him in 2023 to consider cooperating with investigators.

According to Witherspoon, Kiatamba told him that he was not making a judgment about his guilt or innocence but was speaking from his understanding of the U.S. legal system.

“He said, no matter what you do, I’m going to talk to you from experience. Cooperate,” Witherspoon recalled.

Witherspoon said he initially questioned the advice.

“I said, what are you talking about? He said, Stanton, I’m not saying you are guilty. I’m not saying you are not guilty. But I know the system. Talk to your lawyer.”

He said he followed the advice and consulted his attorney, who also recommended that he cooperate with investigators at an early stage.

According to Witherspoon, his lawyer warned that delaying cooperation could diminish its value if other defendants cooperated first.

“Every other day, the lawyer would say, Stanton, if you’re the last to cooperate, you are not needed. If you must cooperate, cooperate now,” he recalled.

Witherspoon said his lawyer subsequently explained the cooperation process and its potential implications to him step by step.

What Prosecutors Say He Provided

The government’s court filings indicate that Witherspoon’s cooperation went beyond simply providing information about his own conduct.

According to prosecutors, he was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation contributed to cases against several defendants, including Carleen Noreus, Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon testified against Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Following his testimony, prosecutors said Noreus pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges and is awaiting sentencing.

Witherspoon also signed an affidavit identifying nursing students who received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was provided to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing so state licensing authorities could take remedial action.

‘I Was a Star Witness’

Witherspoon described himself as a key witness for the government, saying investigators needed information and supporting documents that he possessed because of his involvement in the nursing-school business.

He said he had recruited students for multiple schools and therefore had knowledge of people involved in the operation.

“Now they have so many big, big people that were involved in this thing. And a lot of them came to me to recruit students for them,” Witherspoon said.

He said investigators already knew some of the individuals but needed additional evidence.

“The government knew them, but the government needed supporting documents from me.”

According to Witherspoon, one of the principal defendants initially refused to cooperate, leading prosecutors to call him to testify.

“I had to take the stand for the government. For four months, the woman couldn’t break. And the government called a star witness. And I was a star witness.”

Witherspoon said that after he testified, the defendant subsequently agreed to plead guilty.

“After I testified, the next day, the woman begged for the plea. She’s scheduled to be sentenced. It’s a public record.”

The account corresponds with prosecutors’ description of Witherspoon’s cooperation in the case involving Noreus.

A $5.17 Million Fraud

Federal prosecutors said Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC and was also the founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC.

Prosecutors alleged that Witherspoon, working with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves, used NERC to recruit and fraudulently train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fake nursing diplomas and transcripts, which students allegedly used to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, producing a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence.

‘I Wanted This to Stop’

Witherspoon said his decision to cooperate was motivated by more than his own legal circumstances.

He said he wanted to expose the broader operation and help prevent others from being harmed by fraudulent nursing credentials.

“I had to do it not because I was fighting for myself. I had to do it because I wanted this to stop,” he said.

“I had to do it because I want the system to be right.”

Witherspoon said the information he possessed was extensive and involved conversations with professionals and others connected to the business.

He also thanked his attorney for guiding him through the cooperation process.

Prosecutors Backed Sentence Reduction

The government’s motion to reduce Witherspoon’s sentence was supported by prosecutors and investigators from the FBI and HHS-OIG, who cited the scope of his cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the motion on behalf of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Judge Rodney Smith subsequently ordered Witherspoon released on time served and removed the three-year supervised-release component of his original sentence.

The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

For Witherspoon, the sequence of events—from advice to cooperate, through interviews and testimony, to the government’s Rule 35(b) motion—ultimately culminated in his release.

“Yes, indeed, I cooperated with the government. And that’s why I took a plea. And today, the result of the plea is that Stanton is a free man,” he said.

He ended his account by thanking his lawyer and those who supported him during his legal battle.

World.title: Liberia: Ngafuan Highlights Gains in Health, Education and Energy, Admits More Work Remains
World.content:
Monrovia – In an appearance on the state-owned Liberia Broadcasting System, Liberia’s Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, walked Liberians through progress in social delivery, especially in roads, education, health, and energy.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Minister Ngafuan told the audience how the government has been able to make life-touching progress over a little over two years, though he admitted that the government is still confronted with huge challenges amid competing priorities.

US$1.2 Billion Domestic Revenue On Course

He disclosed that, through the collaboration of the MFDP and the Liberia Revenue Authority, the country is nearing a US$1B revenue collection within days.

Health And Education

The Minister asserted that drug supply in public hospitals has improved compared to the past.

“There are more drugs in the hospitals today than there were yesterday. There could be one or two issues, but I am saying that, in comparison with the past, the situation is better,” he stated.

He announced the ongoing total construction of the C.H. Rennie Hospital in Kakata, Margibi County.

It could be recalled that the hospital was gutted by fire during the latter days of the last administration.

As it stands, he revealed that the work has advanced to the roof level.

In the educational sector, Ngafuan announced the ongoing renovations of several public high schools across the country, including the famous Williams V.S. Tubman High, Newport High, Botsweins High, G.W. Gibson, among others, as well as the total renovation of the state-run University of Liberia (UL).

In addition to the rehabilitation works, he disclosed the government’s efforts for the construction and equipping of more than 100 schools for foundational learning across the country.

“Myself, I am a product of public schools, or what we referred to as government schools; I’m a product of Botsweins, BWI and the University of Liberia. We are producing and reproducing our young people through these schools. We are creating excellence in those schools,” he points out.

“Sometimes people make the mistake of trying to grade the government as if it has been in office for five or six years. We have not even reached the halfway point. January 22, 2027, will mark the halfway point of this government. If you grade a two-year and eight-month government as if it has been there for six years, that tells us that we are strong and that we are on course.”

Economy And Budget Procurement

Ngafuan disclosed that President Joseph Boakai will chair an Economic Management Team meeting with the Central Bank governor to review the economy and the new budget.

He indicated that implementation of the US$1.2 billion FY2026 budget is on course and that allocations are increasing for key sectors.

“We are giving more money to Public Works. We are giving more money to education. We are giving more money to almost all the sectors,” the Minister indicated, adding that LBS has also received increased subsidy.

The Minister also announced upcoming procurement reforms.

“We are on an e-procurement platform, but as good as technology is, it has brought some challenges, which we are going to address. In the next week or two, there are going to be some announcements on practical measures that we are going to take to expedite procurement,” he said.

Salary And Pension

Addressing civil servant concerns, Ngafuan asserted that the government is approaching salary increment holistically rather than through individual interventions.

“President Boakai has established a Salary Structure Review Committee chaired by the Civil Service Agency Director General, with MFDP and the Ministry of State as members. The numbers, based on the revenue situation, will determine what will be done at the appropriate time.

He said there have been some top-ups in 2025 for the health sector, where some workers received more than double their salaries, and interventions in the security sector, integrity institutions, and the judiciary.

“With the Supreme Court judges and magistrates, we are almost there,” he added.

On pensions, Ngafuan explained the budget will tackle uncertainty around NASSCORP remittances, stressing that: ” Individuals retiring to some places drag retirement. We intend to change that. We want a situation where people will look forward to retirement.”

Accordingly, touching on minimum wage, the Minister argued Liberia compares favorably regionally.

“A minimum wage, especially in Liberia… Do you know that the minimum wage in Liberia is better than Ghana’s? It is better than Sierra Leone’s. It is better than Nigeria’s. I think we need to do more, but we also have to appreciate where we are as a country.” he

Energy Projects

Speaking further,

Ngafuan narrated that the government, with support from partners including the World Bank and the EU, is funding electrification in several counties.

He named River Gee, Grand Kru and Sinoe, and cited ongoing work in Greenville, River Cess and Gbarnga.

“The Rural Renewable Energy Agency, headed by Samuel Nagbe, is working on that. Lights will soon be available,” declared.

The Minister’s comments come amid public debate over the pace of service delivery and the impact of the $1.2 billion budget.

He urged patience, stating that Boakai’s administration deserves credit for methodical reforms.

“For someone to say that this is not progress and that the minister is just talking is unfair. I don’t talk just because I want to talk. We have been working. I agree that we are not there yet completely. But if we were traveling the road from here to Gbarnga, Bong County, I would say that we are somewhere there in Totota,” added the Finance Ministry boss.

World.title: Liberia: PUL President: Community Radio Critical to Making Fiscal Decentralization Work
World.content:
Monrovia —The Press Union of Liberia (PUL) has warned that the success of Liberia’s fiscal decentralization agenda will depend largely on the strength and independence of community radio journalism, describing local broadcasters as a critical link between government fiscal policies and citizens.

By Patience M. [email protected]

PUL President Julius Kanubah said community radio is more than a channel for disseminating information, stressing that it provides an essential platform for citizens, particularly those in rural and marginalized communities, to understand, question and participate in discussions surrounding public finances.

Kanubah made the remarks Thursday, September 10 at the opening of a four-day training program aimed at strengthening community radio journalism for effective reporting on fiscal decentralization.

The training, organized by the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, brings together 26 journalists and media practitioners from Liberia’s 15 counties.

The program is designed to strengthen journalists’ capacity in budget literacy, public finance reporting and data storytelling, enabling them to translate complex fiscal information into stories that ordinary citizens can understand.

“As Liberia advances toward greater local governance and accountability, it is essential that citizens understand, monitor, and influence how public resources are allocated and used,” Kanubah said.

“In this effort, community radio remains the most trusted and accessible medium, particularly for rural and marginalized communities,” he added.

The PUL President emphasized that effective community radio journalism could help transform fiscal decentralization from a government policy into something that directly impacts the lives of ordinary Liberians.

He said stronger community radio platforms can create inclusive spaces for dialogue, amplify local voices and ensure that citizens are not left out of conversations concerning government budgets, public service delivery and accountability.

However, Kanubah identified several challenges that continue to undermine the effectiveness of community radio journalism, including limited technical capacity to interpret complex fiscal data, inadequate training in investigative and accountability reporting, poor equipment, weak connectivity and financial constraints.

He also cited political and social pressures as threats to the independence and impartiality of community media.

According to the PUL, failure to address these challenges could undermine the transparency and accountability objectives of fiscal decentralization.

Kanubah commended the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning for investing in the capacity of journalists, describing the initiative as an important step toward improving public understanding and reporting on fiscal governance.

“To our colleagues in journalism and media: thank you for dedicating your time to learn, unlearn, and relearn, while exchanging expert perspectives,” he said.

“As journalists, we carry a profound responsibility to our profession and our country. Let us take this training seriously and ensure that the knowledge, skills and networks we gain here are used to advance quality journalism on fiscal decentralization,” Kanubah urged.

Other officials speaking at the training included Deputy Finance Minister for Fiscal Affairs Anthony Myers; Deputy Minister for Local Government and Decentralization Edwin Mulbah; Deputy Minister for Technical Services at the Ministry of Information, Nat Bayjay; and Comptroller and Accountant General of Liberia Elwood Nettey.

Meanwhile, the PUL has reminded journalists and media practitioners to uphold professional standards by adhering to the Code of Ethics and Conduct for Journalists and Media.

The Union stressed the importance of fairness, accuracy, impartiality and responsibility in reporting, particularly as the country advances efforts toward greater fiscal governance, local participation and accountability.

World.title: Editorial: There is a point at which coincidence stops being a credible explanation, and Liberia crossed it this week
World.content:
IN JUNE, THE country watched a vessel — the IB Atlantic IV — sit off Grand Cape Mount County for the better part of a week while officials debated what to do about it, before it slipped away and had to be chased down and seized in Ivorian waters. No drugs were ever officially confirmed aboard. What was confirmed, over and over, was that Liberia’s maritime security moved too slowly to matter.

NOW THERE IS a second mystery vessel — this one not off some distant coastline, but docked directly behind Monrovia Central Prison, the facility currently holding foreign nationals tied to the country’s largest-ever drug case. Authorities have offered no explanation for how it got there, or why.

WE DO NOT know yet what this boat is carrying, or who it belongs to. But we know this: five weeks ago, the prison’s own deputy superintendent for operations, Jackson K. Kolako, stood up publicly and warned that someone was laying the groundwork for a breakout to free exactly these detainees. He was suspended days later, under circumstances that remain disputed. His warning was never confirmed — but it was never disproven, either. It was simply left hanging, the way too much in this case has been left hanging.

TWO VESSELS, TWO separate months, two moments of confusion about who is watching Liberia’s waters and its walls. If this were happening to any other country’s highest-value prisoners in the middle of a half-billion-dollar drug scandal, the response would not be a quiet search at 2 a.m. It would be a visible, immediate hardening of security around the facility holding them.

WE ARE CALLING on the Government of Liberia — specifically the Ministry of Justice, the Armed Forces of Liberia, and the Liberia National Police — to do the following, without delay:

• DEPLOY A DEDICATED, round-the-clock security detail at Monrovia Central Prison for the duration of the drug case proceedings, separate from routine prison staffing.

• ORDER AN INDEPENDENT review of Kolako’s allegations, rather than allowing them to sit unanswered while new incidents pile up around the same facility.

• EXTEND COASTAL AND riverine patrols around Monrovia’s port-adjacent areas, given that two vessels have now surfaced in proximity to major elements of this case within a matter of weeks.

• PUBLICLY CLARIFY THE status and security arrangements of every foreign national currently detained in connection with the case, so that public confidence does not continue to erode by default.

LIBERIA HAS ALREADY lost credibility once this year over how slowly it responded to a ship it could see. It cannot afford to lose it twice over one it apparently didn’t see coming until it was already at the back door of the prison itself.

THE GOVERNMENT DOES not need to have all the answers about this boat by tomorrow. But it needs to show, starting today, that it takes the question seriously.

World.title: Liberia: Acting Justice Minister Blamo  Pledges to Lead With Integrity, Fairness and Impartiality As She Officially Assumes Office
World.content:
Former Justice Minister and Attorney General of Liberia Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh formally presenting the handover notes and official documents to the Acting Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Liberia, Cllr. Betty M. Lamin Blamo during the elaborate transition ceremony held at the Ministry of Justice.

Monrovia — Acting Justice Minister and Attorney General of Liberia, Cllr. Betty M. Lamin Blamo, has officially taken charge of the Ministry of Justice, pledging to lead with integrity, fairness and impartiality.

By Augustus D. R [email protected]

Cllr. Blamo made the commitment Thursday, September 10 during an elaborate transition ceremony held in the 6th Floor Conference Room of the Ministry of Justice, where she officially assumed her new responsibilities before senior officials, employees and stakeholders within the justice sector.

She expressed gratitude to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai for the confidence reposed in her among many distinguished legal professionals, describing the appointment as both an honor and a call to greater service.

Cllr. Blamo also commended former Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh for his distinguished leadership and the significant contributions made during his tenure, noting that his service left a strong foundation for the Ministry.

The Acting Minister also emphasized that advancing the work of the Ministry of Justice will require collective commitment and collaboration among all justice and security institutions.

She specifically acknowledged the vital roles of prosecutors, the Liberia National Police, Liberia Immigration Service, the Bureau of Corrections and Rehabilitation and other partners, stressing that their cooperation will be essential in achieving the Ministry’s mandate.

Giving the welcome remarks, the Deputy Minister for Administration and Public Safety, Cllr. Cora N. Hare Konuwa, said, ‘‘We are gathered here today for a significant institutional milestone—the official handover ceremony at the Ministry of Justice. This transition marks a seamless continuation of our collective duty to uphold the rule of law, protect constitutional integrity, and ensure the impartial administration of justice across the Republic of Liberia.’’

Deputy Minister Konuwa extended the Ministry’s deepest appreciation to the former Minister of Justice and Attorney General, Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh and the former Solicitor General, Cllr. Augustine C. Fayiah.

‘‘During your respective tenures, you led this Ministry and the department of public prosecution with a steadfast commitment to legal excellence. You worked tirelessly to guide our justice and security sectors through complex national landscapes, leaving behind an impactful legacy of diligence. As you both prepare for your next national reassignments, we thank you for your patriotic service to the state and wish you continued success,’’ Deputy Minister Konuwa stated.

She said it is a tremendous honor to officially welcome the incoming Minister of Justice and Attorney General, Cllr. Betty M. Lamin Blamo, and the incoming Solicitor General, Cllr. Abraham Boimah Sillah, Sr.

‘‘Madam Minister, your return to the Ministry of Justice is greeted with immense confidence. Your distinguished legal career, notably including your prior exceptional service as the Solicitor General of Liberia, brings invaluable institutional memory back to the forefront of our justice system,’’ she intimated.

‘‘Mr. Acting Solicitor General Cllr. Sillah, we welcome you with equal optimism. Your extensive legal background, your scholarly contributions and your leadership within the Liberia National Bar Association equip you remarkably well to head the government’s litigation and public prosecution efforts. The leadership, prosecutors, security forces, and administrative staff stand fully prepared to align with your shared vision and support your execution of the law with absolute integrity,’’ the Ministry of Justice official pointed out.

According to her, the transitions of this magnitude reinforce the strength of our democratic institutions.

She stressed that they remind them that while leaders change, the foundational mission of the state—to provide transparent, evidence-based justice for every Liberian citizen—remains absolute.

‘‘On behalf of the entire Ministry of Justice family, I welcome everyone to this symbolic ceremony. Thank you, and may God bless the Republic of Liberia,’’ she added.

For his part, the former Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh expressed confidence in the ability of Cllr. Blamo and Acting Solicitor General, Cllr. Sillah to provide effective leadership and leave a lasting impact at the Ministry of Justice.

Cllr. Tweh encouraged officials and employees of the Ministry to extend their fullest cooperation and support to the new leadership, emphasizing the importance of unity and professionalism in advancing the institution’s mandate.

Meanwhile, the ceremony was attended by senior management officials, representatives from justice and security institutions, and other stakeholders who gathered to witness the formal transition of leadership at the Ministry of Justice.

World.title: Liberia: Deputy MFDP Minister Myers Challenges Media to Join Fight Against Misuse of Public Resources Amid Power Shift
World.content:
Buchanan, Grand Bassa County – After nearly 200 years of total centralization, Liberia is now moving into a new direction of decentralization; hence, the Deputy Minister for Fiscal Affairs at the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP), Anthony G. Myers, wants journalists’ involvement in the process.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Deputy Minister Myers challenged journalists to take the lead in tracking public spending and exposing misuse of county resources as the government shifts power, money and decision-making to Liberia’s 15 counties.

The top MFDP official spoke Thursday, September 10 at the start of a training program for journalists titled: “Strengthening Community Radio Journalism for Effective Reporting on Fiscal Decentralization in Liberia”.

The training program is taking place in the port city of Buchanan, Grand Bassa County.

“For over 170 years or 200 years, if we go back to 1822, everything about our national institutions has been concentrated in Monrovia,” Deputy Minister Myers told journalists.

“This is not only restricted to services provided by government, businesses and international institutions, even the media has been unwittingly a party to the culture of over centralization.”

According to Deputy Minister Myers, the history has produced ” two parallel Liberia,” a one in Monrovia with greater access to information about government and national affairs and another in the counties with little.

He pointed out that fiscal decentralization provides an opportunity to bridge that gap, but only if journalists move beyond Monrovia-centered reporting.

He urged the media to pay greater attention to county budgets, public contracts, development projects, service delivery and local government operations.

To make that work, Deputy Minister Myers called for stronger partnerships between community radio and national media outlets. He also asked government to formally recognize citizen journalism on the heel of new media – the social media.

“There is now the emergence of the informal or citizen journalism on Facebook and other forms of social media. These people need to be recognized that they also have their own audience who don’t have time for television or radio neither newspaper.’’

“In that way, those issues that are in hard-to-reach place or places that appear to be not too familiar to us in Monrovia, issues from there can quickly be lifted up at the level of national decision makers,” he added.

In an effort to achieve total fiscal decentralization, the MFDP official put the responsibility on MFDP to ensure transparency.

He called for wider dissemination of County Development Agendas so citizens and journalists can monitor priorities in all 15 counties.

“The onus is on us at the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning to ensure that there is sufficient public dissemination of both hard and soft copies of the content development agenda for the 15 counties,” he said.

Comptroller and Accountant General Elwood T. Nettey backed the call by Deputy Minister Myers as he also urged journalists to follow the money.

This, he believes, is only possible by understanding budgeting and procurement. “We said we have built 10 clinics this month, there must be a question of: “Where are those clinics? Somebody has to answer where the resources went,” CG Nettey told the gathering.

In remarks, PUL President Julius Kullie Kanubah asserted that community radio is a bridge between national fiscal policies and local realities” but cited poor equipment, weak connectivity and lack of budget literacy as key challenges.

Deputy Information Minister for Technical Services Nat Bayjay and Deputy Local Government Minister Edward Mulbah also spoke at the occasion.

A Reminder To The Media

Deputy Minister Bajay, who spoke on behalf of his boss, Information Minister Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, indicated that the media serves as the critical bridge between policy formulation and public ownership in implementing Liberia’s National Policy on Decentralization and Local Governance.

“As Liberia accelerates its fiscal decentralization program, the role of journalists, especially locally based ones, is very important. The thought of carrying the media along in this process goes beyond just being participants. This is a reminder that the media serves as the critical bridge between policy formulation and public ownership in implementing Liberia’s National Policy on Decentralization and Local Governance.”

The ongoing four-day training workshop is organized by the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, in collaboration with the Ministry of Local Government.

For his part, Deputy Minister Mulbah warned that without media oversight, decentralization risks reality.

Without media overnight, he claimed this would just be moving civil servants from Monrovia without real power or resources.

World.title: Henry Shula Kasolo Sentenced to 7 Years Imprisonment With Hard Labour
World.content:
The Lusaka Magistrates’ Court has sentenced 54-year-old Henry Shula Kasolo to seven years imprisonment with hard labour for trafficking in high-grade cannabis.

Kasolo was arrested in June 2025 in Lusaka District of Lusaka Province after being found trafficking in 117 packs of compressed high-grade cannabis weighing a combined 73.9 kilogrammes.

According to a statement issued by Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) Public Relations Officer Allan Tamba, Kasolo concealed the cannabis in four suitcases.

Mr Tamba said the DEC also seized 10,200 United States dollars and 6,000 Kwacha in cash, which was reasonably believed to be proceeds of crime.

He said a Toyota Hilux motor vehicle used in the commission of the illicit activity was also seized.

Mr Tamba said the landmark court outcome demonstrates the dedication, discipline and professionalism of DEC officers, which culminated in meticulous intelligence gathering, strengthened inter-agency investigations that crossed borders and effective prosecution by the National Prosecution Authority (NPA).

He said in order to ensure that crime does not pay, the Commission has instituted investigations into assets linked to Kasolo’s illicit activities.
