Mike Rogers said of his opponent. "Abdul El-Sayed may be comfortable with that crowd. I certainly am not. He's a con man. I'm a law man."

Wednesday, Trump said that America "has beaten communism before and we will beat it again."

"In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals," Trump said. "They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually they're communists. They're not socialists. They're long beyond socialists."

What war?

Trump campaigned on a promise of "no new wars," but the war in Iran is still ongoing with no resolution in sight.

The conflict has led to higher gas prices, with diesel topping $6 a gallon and the price of crude oil shooting to near-record highs.

toggle caption Alex Wong/Getty Images

But speakers barely acknowledged the war or the military, save for a plea from Vice President Vance that people who disagree with the administration's policy "not throw the baby out with the bathwater" by voting for Democrats.

"Don't give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there," he said. "Look, I'm not asking anybody to agree with me on every single issue. I'm not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration. What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months."

2028 looms over everything

Speaking of Vance, he and some other potential 2028 Republican presidential contenders spoke at the convention, though there was not a clear passing of the torch moment.

Sponsor Message

Convention attendee Meredith Smith said she wishes she could vote for Trump again.

"Trump is kind of a one time thing," she told NPR's Tamara Keith. "I really think God picked him personally for such a time as this."

Like many Republicans NPR spoke to, Smith mentioned Vance as the party's likely heir apparent. Her friend Sherri Hopson is also looking to the president's cabinet for what comes next.

"[Trump's] built this Republican Party and the bench is deep," Hopson said. "I have a lot of faith in JD Vance and Marco Rubio and I really hope they run as a ticket."

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Donald Trump Jr., possible 2028 hopefuls, also spoke.

It may be too late to turn the tide

The midterm convention comes after Labor Day, which is widely considered the kickoff to the general election season. Current polling averages show Republicans at risk of losing the majority in both the House and the Senate.

In many key races, Democratic candidates have outraised and outspent their Republican opponents and have dominated the airwaves. But official Republican Party committees and Trump's MAGA, Inc. super PAC are sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars that they could deploy to blitz voters with their messaging in the closing weeks of the campaign.

Still, those polls illustrate a fundamental disconnect between the issues voters want candidates to address and what they feel the Republican Party is focused on. Last-minute ad spending may not be enough to persuade people to change their support — or show up to vote at all.

Mail ballots are already being returned in states like North Carolina, in-person early voting will begin soon and many television ad reservations have already been booked out by candidates and outside groups.

World.title: The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers
World.content:
The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers

toggle caption Cole Burston/AFP via Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The U.S. and Canadian auto industries have been tightly woven together for decades. But the latest tariff flareup between the two countries may complicate that.

Think of that sticker on the windows of new cars breaking down how much of the vehicle's content comes from the U.S. and Canada. From a manufacturing point of view, content from both places has long been considered deeply intertwined.

But the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a new trade deal this summer, and the trade war between them has escalated quickly. In August, the U.S. enacted new tariffs on aluminum and steel, and President Trump has also threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel effective on Jan. 1. On Tuesday, Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs on a variety of U.S. goods — including on American steel and aluminum.

Sponsor Message

All of this puts the auto manufacturing industry in a jam.

For major U.S. carmakers, analysts say, the tariffs introduce uncertainty as companies determine whether to adjust their supply chains in the long run, or to absorb new costs in the short term. But for the smaller businesses that supply those big companies with thousands of parts — think bolts, or the steel rods for steering wheels — the tariffs could spell bigger, more expensive trouble.

" It's really, really damaging to the industry and to the financials of the industry. It makes planning for things very difficult," says Dan Hearsch, global co-leader of automotive and industrial at the consulting firm AlixPartners.

For these companies, he says, the new tariffs follow years of chaos — the aftermath of Covid supply chain shortages, the start-and-stop ramp up to making more electric vehicles, the need to grapple with pre-existing tariffs.

"It's one more thing, on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing," Hearsch says.

The U.S. and Canada's auto relationship

The U.S. and Canada started weaving their auto supply chains together in 1965, when they signed a pact with a goal of consolidating their auto industries and expanding their combined market. The pact removed duties on auto products or equipment crossing the border when they are made of at least 50% of U.S. or Canadian content.

Sponsor Message

Their trade relationship deepened with the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement, which included Mexico and removed many duties between the three countries, as long as they contained a certain proportion of North American parts. The 2020 United States Mexico Canada Agreement, which revised that deal, included a requirement that auto content be 75% North American to be able to pass borders without any tariff.

For the auto industry, the free flow of many goods meant that components could be assembled in plants in each country, and ultimately combined in another. The auto supply chain grew into a single ecosystem.

"I've often described it like an omelet" with ingredients from all three countries, says Jim Jarrell, president and CEO of Linamar Corporation, a Canadian manufacturing company that handles both auto and agricultural products.

"Think about a casting that starts in Mexico and that gets sent into the U.S. to get processed. That part then jumps over to Canada to get further processed," says Jarrell, referring to a molded piece of metal. "Then we ship it back into the U.S. sub-assembly, to get it finished and assembled," Jarrell says.

"And that story is, quite frankly, not unusual," he continues. "That is actually how the industry works."

Linamar Corporation has a roughly equal number of plants in the U.S. and in Canada, but they also have plants in Mexico and in Asia, Jarrell says. And each of them make slightly different things, Jarrell says, making it potentially difficult to alter those supply chains in response to new tariffs — or the threat of additional tariffs in January.

To alter where or how parts are made would mean re-evaluating entire supply chains, Jarrell says. "So it's a lot of cost and time."

Aisin Corporation, one of the world's largest transmission makers and suppliers, is based in Japan, but does about 20% of its business in North America, and often moves materials back and forth as their supply chain warrants it. " We've always looked at North America as totally North America, not Canada-specific or U.S.- specific," says Chuck Sanders, the executive vice president for the company's North American division. " When there's rapid changes or new tariffs that are introduced suddenly," he continues, "that kind of creates chaos on the business."

Sponsor Message

Shifting production means moving jobs around. That's a problem both the company and its workers would like to avoid. "We want to continue the business so they have a long-term future with us," Sanders says.

The effect on the auto-part supply chain

Cars are made with tons — literal tons — of steel and aluminum, and with thousands of parts. How many? It depends on when you stop counting.

For instance, take a steering wheel. There's a metal rod, often padded in leather or vinyl. Then there are sensors, an airbag, an instrument cluster with "lots of dials and things that move," Hearsch from AlixPartners says. In that steering wheel system, he says, "There's probably 50 to 100 different parts coming from all over the world."

Manufacturers occupy different tiers within the automotive supply chain. "Tier one is a supplier that delivers a part or a system to the automaker," Hearsch says. Think of a headlamp, for example. " A tier two is a company who makes something that goes to a tier one" — the smaller pieces that make up a headlamp, he says. And then a tier three company feeds parts to tier two.

Any of these components might be made from raw metals like steel and aluminum, which could have been subject to tariffs when they were first imported to North America. Now, those components could be subject to additional tariffs as they repeatedly move across the border.

For now, many auto suppliers are taking a watch-and-wait stance. Bosch and Magna, two of the biggest suppliers to North American companies, emailed NPR statements saying that they are monitoring the situation and its potential effects, particularly on customers.

The Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association trade group also wrote in an emailed statement that it's "concerned by the continued escalation of trade actions between the United States and Canada."

"The vehicle supplier industry has built deeply interconnected North American supply chains over decades, and policies that increase costs or create barriers ultimately weaken the competitiveness of the entire region as we face challenging global competition," the statement continued.

Sponsor Message

That global competition comes from the makers of Chinese electric vehicles, which are becoming increasingly popular, says economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University.

Like Hearsch, she says the uncertainties of the post-Covid supply chain and the transition to EVs, as well as potential disruptions from AI, make it hard for automakers to decide when to make changes to their supply chains, so they "don't make the wrong investment and don't jump too soon or too late," she says. "So it's a really difficult time. It's always a tough business, but it's particularly tough right now."

"The challenge is that the automotive industry does not move at the speed of politics," says Sean Tucker, an editor at Cox Automotive, an automotive services and technology provider. It takes time for automakers to reconfigure their supply chains — or decide whether they should, since tariff policy could change under a future presidential administration.

If Canada and the U.S. do manage to disentangle their supply chains, Jarrell of Linamar says, it could cost years — and a lot of money for auto-parts makers. "The more uncertainty there is, obviously the harder it becomes to invest and grow in a confident way," he says.

World.title: Trump administration allows TPS to continue for Salvadorans – for now
World.content:
Trump administration allows TPS to continue for Salvadorans – for now

toggle caption Alex Wong/Getty Images North America

Roughly 170,000 immigrants from El Salvador covered by Temporary Protected Status can still legally work and live in the U.S. – for now.

The Trump administration declined this week to terminate TPS for Salvadorans, even though it has done so for people from other countries like Haiti and Syria. But it also hasn't said whether it will extend the protection in the future.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said it will make an announcement on Salvadoran TPS, "at the appropriate time."

The lack of action means that TPS recipients still have legal status, but their lives remain in limbo.

Sponsor Message

'I feel numb'

"I feel numb … the physical and emotional damage of the last month, it's so frustrating that it feels like we suffered that all for nothing," TPS recipient Daysi Gonzalez said in an Instagram post .

Gonzalez has been chronicling on social media what it has been like to live under the weight of uncertainty.

Gonzalez, who is now 31, arrived in the U.S. with her parents and older sister when she was six years old. They were visiting family in California and she was promised a trip to Disneyland. But a month and a day into their six month tourist visa, a 7.7 magnitude earthquake devastated El Salvador, and TPS was extended to Salvadorans who were in the country at that time.

She's never been back to El Salvador. She's now a partner at the political consulting firm where she started off as an intern. She and her older sister own a home together. Those accomplishments have turned into a painful checklist of things she has to figure out how to dismantle, if her TPS is ultimately revoked and she has to leave the country.

"I've tried to adjust status in different ways, but there are very limited legal options to adjust your status and there is no pathway to citizenship for TPS," she told NPR.

Sponsor Message

The start of TPS

Congress created TPS in 1990 to allow eligible migrants to live and work legally in the U.S. if they can't return safely to their home countries because of things like natural disasters and armed conflicts.

It was granted to Salvadorans in 2001, after earthquakes devastated the country. Since then, more than 150,000 Salvadoran TPS holders contribute an estimated $5.4 billion to the U.S. economy each year as part of the work force, paying about $1.5 billion in federal and state taxes, according to immigrant advocacy group fwd.us . And over the last 25 years, they've given birth to approximately 150,000 American children.

A legislative solution

In his second term, Trump has ended TPS for more than 10 countries. And in June, the Supreme Court ruled the president has virtually unrestrained power to end the program.

Groups like the National TPS Alliance are advocating for Congress to step in.

"There are legislations in Congress that would provide a pathway for permanent residency," said Jose Palma, a TPS recipient and the national coordinator for the National TPS Alliance.

Palma said one of those bills is one Republican vote away from reaching the House floor.

The National Salvadoran American Association is trying to convince Republicans to pass a more short term solution that would extend TPS for another 18 months.

"Let's not think about this as solving an immigration issue as make this like the next humanitarian extension for people that just can't all of a sudden be told, you can't be here anymore and you only have 60 days or 6 months to leave," said Francisco Semiao, chairman of the association. "But people need more time than that if they need to sell their homes, sell their businesses, other arrangements."

That would at least give Salvadoran families more time to make plans on how to proceed.

World.title: From DOGE to space lasers, Alex Gibney peels back the many layers of Elon Musk
World.content:
From DOGE to space lasers, Alex Gibney peels back the many layers of Elon Musk

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard remembers having dinner with Elon Musk in the early 2000s, when the billionaire became a key investor in the fledgling electric car company. Musk uttered words that Eberhard would never forget: "One thing that nobody can take away from you is that you're the founder of Tesla."

It left a real mark on Eberhard's mind, since Musk would later take unconditional credit for Tesla's runaway success and anoint himself its sole founder, setting off litigation and an eventual settlement that allowed Eberhard and Musk, along with three others, to all claim the title of co-founders of Tesla Motors.

Sponsor Message

Director Alex Gibney believes those remarks provide a glimpse into who Musk really is: A confidence man who will deceive, gaslight and fabricate to get what he wants.

Eberhard is one of many people who fell in and out of Musk's world who are featured in Gibney's new documentary, Musk, which never drags despite its three hour and 45 minute runtime (which includes a 10-minute intermission). It opens in theaters on October 16.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The film traces Musk's path from his early days as a dot-com-era entrepreneur in Silicon Valley to the present, as one of the world's wealthiest people, exerting extraordinary influence over politics and culture around the world. While many people may be familiar with the general outlines of Musk's story, Gibney taps pivotal characters at crucial moments for the tech mogul to infuse this biography with new life.

Along the way, the Oscar-winning filmmaker, whose past documentaries have taken on corporate greed and government malfeasance, explores Musk's many bitter feuds and contradictions. Gibney attempts to explain how Musk is seen as both a once-in-generational business genius and an impulsive and deranged chaos agent.

I've covered Musk for years, and have been the target of his attacks, so I was initially interested in whether Gibney would dredge up any new revelations, or connect the dots in ways obscured by the steady stream of news about Musk and his many ventures.

Sponsor Message

While there were very few nuggets of new information, the sheer breadth of the film makes for a stunningly comprehensive accounting of a man Gibney considers a danger to society. We hear from Musk's father, Errol, reflecting on how his son was bullied as a child, there are interviews with Musk's scorned exes, including his first wife, Justine Musk, prying journalists and former business associates who once occupied his orbit.

Early in the film, a far younger Musk is seen on a television program declaring his three animating principles as developing the internet, transitioning the economy to sustainable energy and exploring space. That trio of objectives has remained remarkably consistent for someone whose views and business goals seem to be in a perpetual state of flux.

Gibney first began the project in 2023, thinking it would be a tighter and more focused look at the tech titan. But then Musk barreled his way into Donald Trump's sphere during the 2024 campaign and soon entered the White House, taking a wrecking ball to swaths of the federal government through his cost-cutting effort, DOGE. It led to some observers describing Musk as the "shadow vice president." So Gibney retooled the film as a more ambitious and much longer project to convey just how many facets of modern life are being influenced by one man.

"Particuarly in this bewildering world of inputs that we all live in," Gibney said at a news conference at the Venice Film Festival, where the documentary premiered on Tuesday, "a lot of incidents happen, and there are so many trees, but sometimes it's useful to stitch together a narrative that shows the forest."

Gibney saw parallels between Musk and his past film subjects, including his documentary on the Enron scandal, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, and the downfall of the Silicon Valley blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.

Sponsor Message

"The story of Musk was not in a way a new tech story," Gibney said in Venice. "His story is the story of old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper, his wealth and power comes from inflated stock."

toggle caption Andreas Rentz/Getty Images

Musk did not agree to be interviewed by Gibney, so the filmmaker dove into the archives. (Musk's lawyer claimed in a letter to the film's production company that Gibney "refused" to fact-check the documentary with Musk's team, saying Gibney defamed the billionaire. Musk accused Gibney on X of "fabricating a false film.")

Without Musk's participation, Gibney made a risky choice when it came time to address the many claims and allegations leveled by the billionaire's former exes and business partners: He uses a creepy AI-generated avatar of Musk talking directly to the camera. It's impossible to get used to it.

Appearing svelte and wearing a black leather jacket, AI Musk sits in a gaming chair in front of red and blue lights and echoes words actually spoken by him in podcast appearances and speeches.

Gibney has described his use of AI as "intentionally ironic," but for a project that tackles all the big weighty subjects of our time, the deepfake Musk only serves to cheapen and distract an otherwise serious film.

I felt similarly about other stunts that Gibney deploys. Near the end of the film, Gibney decides to ask Musk's AI tool, Grok, whether robots will save us, an avoidable ask-the-chatbot cliché that doesn't add much.

There are also scenes that transform the film into a first-person- shooter-style video game, including one with a chainsaw-wielding Musk slicing up federal agencies, a far too on-the-nose reference to DOGE that takes the film's narrative off course.

In defending these choices, Gibney wrote in a director's statement handed out to press at a recent screening in Los Angeles that his aim was to subvert "Musk's favorite tropes of video gaming and simulations," in an effort to showcase "the dangers of becoming like the 'Game Master' in Ready Player One."

Sponsor Message

Yet the moments that are the most damning of Musk's character are when Gibney lays bare the gulf between Musk's words and reality.

In a section of the film about the safety of Tesla's full self-driving software, Gibney shows footage from a deposition in which a company engineer reveals that a promotional video claiming to show a Tesla driving fully autonomously was staged. The engineer said when the car was filmed trying to park itself, it crashed into a fence.

Even as Musk has repeatedly celebrated the self-driving technology, 65 deaths have been linked to car crashes where Tesla's software was a contributing factor, according to a public database that tracks National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports, court records and news reports. (Tesla says its "Autopilot and Full Self-Driving Capability are intended for use with a fully attentive driver, who has their hands on the wheel and is prepared to take over at any moment.")

In February 2025, Musk bragged on X that DOGE had fed the United States Agency for International Development "into the wood chipper." Gibney speaks to the agency's former administrator, Samantha Power, who gets choked up with emotion as she explains how the closure of USAID is projected to result in more than 14 million preventable deaths. The film then cuts to heart-wrenching footage of families and children in Africa who have learned nutritional aid was being cut off.

As the repercussions of Musk's actions are tallied, Gibney keeps coming back to the same question: How does his wealth keep growing despite it all?

Lawrence Fossi, a longtime critic of Musk and Tesla, appears on screen to offer an explanation: investing in Musk's companies is not a bet on corporate America, "it's investing in a religion."

This observation gets to the heart of Gibney's central argument about Musk: that he is a hype artist whose highest skill is making financiers and the public believe in him.

"His motives may have been pure at the beginning. But over time, in an attempt to get his companies to succeed, he ruthlessly broke the rules many of us live by. Musk is just the latest example of what I call noble cause corruption. Essentially, it's a belief that you're justified in breaking the rules because you think you are a force for good. Over time, as you begin to imagine you can get away with anything, the corruption becomes as total as the zealotry," Gibney said in promotional materials provided to the press.

Sponsor Message

Ashley St. Clair, formerly a pro-Trump influencer who has turned against the MAGA movement, plays a major role in the film. She's Musk's ex and the mother of one of his children.

In the film, St. Clair says one of the more outlandish and confounding claims Musk made to her was that he would "unleash the anomaly in the matrix" ahead of the 2024 presidential election to ensure Donald Trump would win. She said Musk texted her that he has "over 10 thousand lasers in space." (NPR obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair.)

toggle caption Tiziana Fabi/AFP via Getty Images

Gibney asked St. Clair if she understood this to be a reference to Musk's SpaceX. St. Clair replied, "I don't know where else he has lasers," before dwelling on the moment, as if to force the viewer to think hard about Musk's sci-fi gibberish.

Election officials repeatedly debunked the false narrative purporting to show a connection between SpaceX's Starlink satellites and the November vote count. Nonetheless, the theory ricocheted online in the days after the 2024 election.

Musk's legal threat to Gibney seized on that moment with St. Clair, saying the film elevating a disproven theory is problematic. Musk's lawyer wrote that "the insinuation is false" and "the material refuting it is public."

While most of Gibney's film is rooted in solid facts, he does dabble in conspiratorial thinking in the scene about the "lasers in space," and later in the film when he raises the specter of Musk using DOGE data to somehow interfere in the November midterms, another idea without any evidence.

Throughout the film, other Musk texts emerge.

After The Wall Street Journal published an article detailing Musk's alleged recreational drug use, which was raising concerns among leaders at SpaceX, St. Claire said Musk personally called News Corp. owner Rupert Murdoch in hopes he would intervene to stop the reporting. He did not.

Sponsor Message

Musk then texted St. Clair that the Journal's articles were "saying that I'm high all the time."

Musk added in a separate text: "I mean, I'm high a little … sure," punctuating the message with a shrugging emoji.

World.title: These Michigan swing voters are bracing for higher prices from trade war with Canada
World.content:
These Michigan swing voters are bracing for higher prices from trade war with Canada

toggle caption Paul Sancya/AP

President Trump's tariff standoff with Canada is rankling some key voters ahead of this year's midterm elections.

NPR observed two online focus groups Wednesday night with 13 people in Michigan who voted for Joe Biden in 2020 and then Trump in 2024. Eleven of these swing voters said the trade war with Canada, which borders Michigan, would be bad for the state. Not a single person said they felt there was something positive to gain from this tension with their northern neighbor.

A majority of the participants said they are most worried higher tariffs could worsen an affordability crisis — a central issue in this year's midterms. Nine said they were concerned Trump's tariffs would affect what they personally pay for some products.

Sponsor Message

"Prices are going to go up," said P.J., a 45-year-old self-described Democrat. (Participants took part in these sessions under the condition their last names would not be used.) "The more we put tariffs on stuff, the more they put tariffs on stuff. I mean, prices are just ultimately going to go up for all of us."

While focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, these sessions do provide insight into what this politically powerful sliver of the electorate is thinking and feeling. This year, Michigan voters will weigh in on a closely watched Senate race that could be key in deciding whether Democrats regain control of the chamber.

These focus groups with swing voters in battleground states are held by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting. NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project.

Rich Thau, the president of Engagious, moderates these discussions. He said because Michigan borders Canada, voters there are particularly nervous about financial blowback from Trump's tariff policies.

"It's real for them," Thau told NPR. "It's proximate and they're concerned that this is going to be damaging to them personally and to the state overall."

Some of these voters said they personally witness a lot of commerce between the two countries. Tanya, a 61-year-old independent, said she often sees trucks coming back and forth over the border.

Sponsor Message

"It's going to decrease the border crossings because we have two bridges now," she said. "We just opened the Gordie Howe Bridge. It's going to affect the amount of traffic and the business that those bridges are going to see in the future."

High prices aren't coming down

Barbara, a 77-year-old independent voter, said she's worried items that do make it across the border are going to get significantly more expensive.

"I just went into the store and I looked at my shampoo and I said, 'OK, this is going to go up 50%,'" she said. "I mean, because my shampoo is made in Canada."

Sylvia, a 62-year-old Democrat, said she might put off buying some products from Canada.

"I like to buy certain alcohol and other types of products [from Canada]," she said. "And if it's going to go up, it's going to cost me more. So I probably wouldn't be able to pick it up right away or would have to wait a little while and hope that maybe this will slow down and quiet down and they could get a better resolution from all of this."

Month after month, frustration over high prices has remained a sticking point for swing voters who have participated in these focus groups. In Michigan, eight of the 13 said they feel more economically anxious now than they did before Trump took office again.

"They complained bitterly about the high prices of an endless number of goods, groceries, gasoline … go down the list," Thau said. "So they are not in a happy mood when it comes to the cost of everyday goods. So the tariffs just add more fuel to the fire."

Samantha, a 31-year-old independent voter, said she finds the whole situation angering because she voted for Trump because of his promises to bring down prices.

Sponsor Message

"I feel like my only reason for voting for him was in the hopes of fixing the economy," she told Thau. "And right now from where I am — I would consider myself middle class — things are more expensive such as food, gas."

Many of these voters said they also thought Trump's ego motivated his decision to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, in response to Canada's retaliatory tariffs.

"It is a little bit of his ego," Sylvia said. "But I just don't understand why he is focusing on that. Like what Samantha had said, he needs to focus on our country and get it back running good and inflation down like he keeps saying, but I haven't seen it yet."

"He's just trying to get a rise out of the opposition in Canada and … get a reaction," said David, a 67-year-old independent voter who identifies with the MAGA movement. "And I think that's the only reason he's doing it, and his ego, too. 'OK. I can do it, and what are you going to do about it?'"

World.title: Inside the New York lab using genetic genealogy to identify 9/11 victims’ remains
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

25 years after the September 11 attacks, a team of forensic experts continues the monumental task of identifying remains from the World Trade Center debris. CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault goes inside the lab using cutting-edge DNA science to bring closure to families — and explores the difficult reality that not everyone wants to know.

This lab is still trying to identify 9/11 victims. Not everyone wants to know

Inside a lab in Manhattan, forensic scientists in white lab coats are still diligently working to keep a promise made 25 years ago.

They're extracting DNA from thousands of pieces of human remains recovered following the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, trying to match them to samples from toothbrushes, razors and other sources provided by family members of victims.

What has changed is the science they're using to draw out the DNA from the remains, and the evolving forensic investigative techniques that didn't exist in 2001.

"When … after years of pushing that science, you're finally able to figure out who it is and return that loved one to their family … that's powerful," said Mark Desire, assistant director of forensic biology at the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

Forty per cent of the 2,753 people who died at Ground Zero have not had their remains identified, including approximately 10 of the 24 Canadian victims.

Last month, the lab announced it made its first identification of previously unknown remains using a breakthrough technique.

The woman's family chose to keep her name private. It's the first identification the lab has made in a year.

WATCH | Special live coverage from New York City on the 25th anniversary of 9/11: 9/11: 25 years later | Live from Ground Zero COMING UP The CBC's Adrienne Arsenault and Paul Hunter host special coverage from New York City of the 25th anniversary for the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Victims' families and former U.S. presidents are expected to attend a memorial ceremony at Ground Zero.

The technique combines DNA testing with genetic genealogy — which uses family tree research conducted by members of the New York City Police Department.

"I think it is sort of a new frontier," said Dr. Jason Graham, New York's Chief Medical Examiner.

"We had really found a breakthrough innovation that's going to open the door, I hope and I believe, likely to many other identifications."

For Monica Iken-Murphy, whose husband Michael Iken died in the collapse of the south tower where he worked as a bond trader, this development brings renewed hope.

"I didn't get a ring, I didn't get an ID. People got cards. They found papers with their names on it," she said. But for her, "it's like he went to work and that's it. Nothing."

Monica Iken-Murphy had only been married to her husband Michael Iken for 11 months when he died in the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center. (Submitted by Monica Iken-Murphy)

Challenges of excavating, preserving remains

Desire was a rookie scientist in the New York crime lab back on Sept. 11, 2001, and was sent to the scene to preserve evidence soon after the second tower was hit. He had never worked on a mass fatality before.

"One of the … first victims I saw die that day landed right in front of us."

Soon after Desire and his colleague arrived, he heard a sound he described as a "crack," and he realized they were far too close to the south tower as it began to collapse.

He sprinted toward a nearby building to take cover and barely made it in time. Debris fell on him just as he was escaping into the building through a broken window.

"It just fell across my legs, shattered my foot — the most violent moment of my life."

He survived, and made it his mission to keep the promise made by then-chief medical examiner Dr. Charles Hirsch to preserve and identify the remains of all the victims.

Mark Desire, right, the assistant director at the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in New York City, observers a lab technician at work on April 15, 2014. Desire has been working to identify victims of the attack on the World Trade Center since day one. (Bebeto Matthews/The Associated Press)

The World Trade Center was reduced to a 21-metre hill of debris that for visual reference, if spread out, could cover approximately eight city blocks.

Plans were made to excavate debris from the site and move it for sifting and sorting at a landfill site on Staten Island in hopes of preserving whatever remains they could.

"Everything that destroys DNA was present at Ground Zero: the fire, the water to put out the fire, the jet fuel, the diesel fuel, the chemicals in the building, the chemicals on the ground, sunlight, mold, bacteria," said Desire.

Excavation work officially ended in 2002, but scientists continued to search for DNA in the remains they had.

Four years later, more debris was found on the roof of a nearby Deutsche Bank building, where more than 700 bone fragments were recovered.

That led to reopening searches in the area that lasted until 2014, leading to approximately 2,000 additional bone fragments being recovered.

Firefighters and emergency personnel remove debris from the site of the World Trade Center towers' collapse in New York on Sept. 13, 2001. The debris was later moved from Ground Zero to a landfill on Staten Island where workers sifted through it searching for human remains. (Stephen Chernin/The Associated Press)

At first, the remains were preserved by freezing them.

Later, as best practices for handling remains for forensic purposes changed, they began drying the bone fragments out to preserve them longer.

Nearly 22,000 pieces of human remains have been recovered since 2001.

The science behind identifying remains

During the early years, victims were identified using fingerprints, dental records and what was then considered cutting-edge DNA technology.

Since then, science has advanced such that more DNA can be extracted from bone fragments. But it still hasn't advanced far enough.

Bone, Desire says, is the toughest material to get DNA from.

"Blood and hair and skin cells — easy. Bone … you have to pulverize it."

He says thousands of samples that still need to be identified haven't even had DNA extracted because they're so badly burned.

WATCH | How scientists are keeping a promise to families of victims: Inside the lab working to identify 9/11 victims | Duration 2:15 CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault visits a New York City lab still working to identify the remains of the people that died in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, 25 years later.

One of the challenges scientists face is whether to keep testing a sample. Each time remains are tested, some of the material is consumed and can't be re-tested. Doing too many tests on one sample risks losing it altogether before a match can be made.

"It's very stressful, because we have remains today that we've tried 10, 15 times over the years," said Desire.

That's why this new technique brings so much hope.

The process involves sending DNA from unidentified remains to an outside lab that can generate a whole genomic sequence.

Then, similar to genealogical methods that have been used to generate new leads in cold cases, New York police conduct family tree searches. If a prospective match is found, it would come back to the medical examiner's office to confirm a relation through DNA testing.

Desire noted that there were 47 sets of remains for which they have full DNA profiles that don't match any of the 17,000 reference samples provided by family members.

So the individuals may have relatives that never contacted the lab or provided samples.

"Using genealogy to help identify them, that was an excellent next step."

The chief medical examiner's office is renewing its call to families to provide samples — in hopes it can help make more matches.

Families face tough decisions

Despite the lab's ongoing work, many families of victims whose remains have never been found don't want to know if a match is made.

"That can be very traumatic," said Jennifer Odein, the World Trade Center anthropologist at the New York City Medical Examiner's Office.

She is the direct line between families and the lab, and says some families are contacted multiple times because their loved one has been matched multiple times to their remains.

"And if they've already had phone calls in the past they might have said, 'OK, we've had enough, we've had our ceremony … we're OK with not getting the notification.'

Long ago, Abigail Carter, a Canadian expat whose husband Arron Dack died while attending a trade show at Windows on the World in the north tower, decided she didn't need to know if his remains were ever found.

"I know he was there," said Carter. "He called me and that was good enough for me."

She has found her own way to honour him.

Abigail Carter's husband, Arron Dack, was born in the U.K., but raised in Canada. He was 39 and left behind two children when he died after the north tower was struck. (Marc Aderghal/CBC)

At their daughter's wedding this past summer in France, where Carter now owns a chateau, they placed a framed photo of Dack on a chair, and later added a martini — shaken, not stirred, just as he liked it — to make sure his presence was felt.

"He was very funny and very charismatic. He had different personas a little bit. He had a very, very silly, silly side," she said.

Iken-Murphy understands that complexity of grief. She hopes that one day, her husband Michael's remains will be matched to samples provided to the lab, but says she wouldn't want to keep them herself.

"I want to remember Michael as a whole human. With his beautiful face and his blue eyes and his smile."

Instead, she says they'll stay at the repository in the 9/11 Memorial and Museum at Ground Zero where all the unidentified remains are stored by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

World.title: Why Trump likely won't have to fulfill his $5,000 'dividend' promise
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The long-standing trend of the incumbent U.S. president's party getting thumped in the midterms strongly suggests Donald Trump won't need to make good on his new promise to send every American citizen a $5,000 US cheque.

The president is pledging what he calls the "Trump dividend," but says the money will come only if the Republican Party wins control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

While the Democrats face a tough challenge to take the Senate away from Trump's party, the House is well within reach. The Republicans currently hold the slimmest possible majority in the House, with 218 of its 435 seats.

Michele Swers, professor of American Government at Georgetown University, told CBC News it will be very difficult for the Republicans to hang on to such a small majority.

"As a practical matter it's probably unlikely that they maintain control of the House, so it's not likely that this comes about," she said of the promised dividend.

The incumbent president's party has lost House seats in all but three of the 41 midterm elections dating back to the Civil War.

WATCH | Critics slam Trump's promised dividend: Trump's $5K dividend promise slammed as desperate attempt to buy votes | Duration 2:34 Critics slammed U.S. President Donald Trump's promise to give out $5,000 cheques for voting Republican in the upcoming midterm elections as a desperate attempt to bribe voters. But some lawyers say that while the move is probably unethical, it may not be illegal.

Since the 1960s, when a president's approval rating has been below 50 per cent, his party has lost an average of 32 House seats and has never lost fewer than nine, according to an analysis by North Star Opinion Research, a U.S. polling and strategy firm.

Trump's approval rating is currently averaging 38.5 per cent, according to the Silver Bulletin polling aggregator.

Republicans lost 40 seats in Trump's first midterm

In the 2018 midterms, during Trump's first stint in office, his approval rating sat at 44 per cent heading into election day and his party lost 40 seats in the House.

This all makes Trump's promise a little bit like a Canadian party leader vowing to send every adult $5,000 if the Toronto Blue Jays win the World Series this year: contingent on an outcome that is not within his control, possible in theory, yet in reality pretty unlikely.

If the Republicans somehow overcome Trump's low approval ratings, buck the historical trend and hang on to both chambers of Congress, the question will quickly turn to how the Treasury pays for Trump's promised dividend.

Sending $5,000 to every adult American citizen would cost more than $1.2 trillion US, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a non-partisan advocacy group in Washington, D.C.

WATCH | Trump all but ignores Canada during lengthy midterm convention speech: Trump mostly avoids trade war with Canada at GOP convention | Duration 3:51 U.S. President Trump mostly avoided the Canada-U.S. trade war during his speech at the Republican convention, in a possible sign that he's aware how unpopular it's becoming before the midterms, even among Republicans.

"This proposal is fiscally dangerous, economically backwards, and fundamentally unserious," said the group's president Maya MacGuineas in a news release.

"It’s hard to understand how anyone could look at our current fiscal and economic situation and think we need to borrow another $1.2 trillion to send everyone cash," MacGuineas said.

The total is approximately nine times the net revenue from Trump's tariffs since they began in March 2025.

Yet Trump is saying tariffs will pay for the dividend, and that's part of his rationale for making it contingent on Republican control of Congress.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000," Trump said in his speech at the GOP convention in Dallas on Wednesday night.

"The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs," he said.

Also far from clear is how the government could possibly enforce the caveat that Trump added about how people can spend the $5,000.

"The dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," he said. "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money. We don't want you going to China, to Germany."

'Socialist vote-buying scheme'

The reaction from Democrats was unsurprisingly scathing, but even some Republicans were skeptical of Trump's floated $5,000 dividend.

"Some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," said Texas Republican Congressman Chip Roy in a post on X.

Bob Good, a Republican who served two terms in the House representing Virginia, slammed it as a "socialist vote-buying scheme."

Trump's promise is "pathetic and sad at the same time," said California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat.

"Pathetic because it's just bullshit, and sad that he had to go in front of people and basically bribe them," Newsom told The Associated Press.

The political strategy behind Trump's promise appears to be aimed at giving his supporters some motivation to get out and vote in the midterms.

WATCH | Why tariffs on Canada could be a factor in some U.S. midterm races: Could Canadian tariffs swing votes in U.S. midterm elections? | Duration 7:48 While Democratic governors warn of the 'catastrophic' economic impacts of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada, Trump promises each voting-age American a $5,000 US 'dividend' if Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections. Power & Politics hears from Chuck Todd, former host of NBC's Meet the Press and current host of the Chuck ToddCast, on what it could all mean as Americans head to the polls in November.

Trump said in his convention speech that his supporters should "pretend that I'm on the ballot" in the upcoming midterms.

His message suggested that he believes he can be the exception to the historical rule that midterms are not kind to the president's party.

"For some reason, even if he's really a good president or a great president — there aren't too many of them — they don't win the midterms, and nobody quite knows why," Trump said.

"We're going to change that."

Trump is battling a tough political environment heading into the midterms.

Poll after poll suggests the cost of living is the top concern among voters right now, whether it's from the war against Iran pushing up the price of gas or Trump's tariffs boosting the cost of consumer goods.

While Trump didn't admit it in his speech, his offer to send U.S. citizens $5,000 implicitly acknowledges that voters are feeling the economic pinch.

World.title: Why isn't Canada blocking the Welland Canal? Other trade war questions answered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Can Canada actually win a trade war with the U.S.? | About That

Reading through the emails that readers send to CBC News, one gets the impression they don't want just "elbows up" in the Canada-U.S. trade war, but also sticks, knees, skates and whatever else might be lying around.

One of the most common questions is some variation of, "Why isn't Canada doing X?" — where X is a tactic or tariff the reader supposes will hit the U.S. where it hurts.

Here's a look at some of those suggestions and what key players or observers have had to say about them.

Why doesn't Canada put export duties on energy as the cost is borne by Americans not Canadians?

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, told CBC News late last month that export taxes are an option. Former prime minister Jean Chrétien said this week that an export tax on oil, gas, electricity and potash might be needed.

In 2025 , Canadian commodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81 per cent of imported electricity, 99 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

However, Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa, warned that the long-term effects of such a move could be severe for Canada, both through lost revenue and damage to the relationship with its biggest customer. The U.S. could respond much as Canada has to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs: by trying to diversify away from a partner it can no longer count on and finding new suppliers.

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe and Christopher Ragan, founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy, made the same point separately: targeting U.S. energy could play into the hands of the U.S. administration and unite Americans against Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in July he doesn't "see the value" in using energy exports as a bargaining chip. Carney said being a reliable supplier is important.

"Canadians are reliable. Canadians can be trusted," he said.

Why not ban sales of certain goods in Canada?

This has mostly already happened at a provincial level with alcohol, in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan this week added a retaliatory levy on U.S. alcohol.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has shown no interest in that sort of approach, stressing that Canada's response will be proportionate, strategic and targeted.

The U.S. may, of course, reply in kind to any ban, as it has with alcohol: Most imports of Canadian-made alcohol will be banned from the United States on Sept. 29.

Tombe, discussing tariffs, told CBC News late last month that Canada has to be careful when selecting products to target because they need to be items Canadians can replace relatively easily but Americans cannot.

If tariffs are applied to harder-to-replace items — "a particular type of circuit board, say, or piece of machinery," that merely complicates life and increases costs for the Canadian importer, Tombe said.

WATCH | CBC's Linda Ward answers a reader question about toilet paper: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

Can Canada stop U.S. ships using the Welland Canal?

The Welland Canal is on the western half of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which connects the St. Lawrence River to the Great Lakes. The canal links Lake Ontario to Lake Erie using eight locks, all in Ontario, that can be filled with water or drained to move vessels between different water levels.

But the seaway is overseen by both the U.S. and Canada.

The Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation administers the seaway on the American side as a federal agency within the U.S. Department of Transportation.

Boats sit idle in Lake Ontario close to the Welland Canal on Oct. 26, 2023. (Tara Walton/The Canadian Press)

In Canada, the federal government owns the Canadian portion of the seaway, but it is managed by the non-profit St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation.

The U.S. also controls several important locks, including ones in New York state between Lake Ontario and Montreal and others in Michigan that connect Lake Superior and Lake Huron.

John Boscariol, a Toronto-based co-head of international trade and investment law at the Canadian law firm McCarthy Tétrault, told CHCH News in Hamilton that closing the canal would be "shooting ourselves in the foot" and would hurt Canadian businesses just as much as U.S. businesses.

Trump critic Jennifer Hillman, formerly general counsel at the Office of the United States Trade Representative under then-president Bill Clinton, told CBC News Network it would "absolutely be a total violation of international law, and I think not really a good idea because you're blocking both sides' goods.

"I would hope that's not a road anybody would go down."

What questions do you have about the latest tariffs? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

World.title: Wildfires, permafrost melt in Canada causing even more climate change, new study shows
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

We know that global warming has made wildfires worse, and melted permafrost that's been frozen for years.

Now, a new study is detailing how the fires, permafrost thaw and other changes are adding even more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, and speeding up climate change at a scale not currently reflected in global estimates.

These climate "feedback loops," where climate change triggers more carbon emissions that in turn feed into even more climate change, could add 20 to 30 per cent more warming over current estimates for this century, according to a new study by researchers at U.S. institutions, including Stanford University and the non-profits Environmental Defense Fund and Spark Climate Solutions.

"Our remaining carbon budget is most likely ... much smaller than what we think it is," said Ben Poulter, program director with Spark Climate Solutions and co-author of the paper.

“If you don't include these additional feedbacks, we're going to have a disconnect between the policy targets and how the Earth system is responding to climate change.”

The paper, published on Thursday in the journal Environmental Research Letters, is one of the most comprehensive reviews to date of these warming-induced emissions and their impact on global temperature rise. Current climate models mostly track emissions from anthropogenic sources — the burning of fossil fuels for energy, food production and cattle rearing, decomposing waste and other human activities that release greenhouse gases.

The findings have particular significance for Canada, which is home to a large chunk of these warming-induced emissions.

Wetlands in northern Ontario. Ecosystems like these are emitting more carbon because of climate change, which in turn feeds into even more global warming. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Happening here

As a northern country, Canada is already warming faster than the rest of the world.

This September, the federal government released its landmark Canada’s Changing Climate assessment, which said that the country could be heading to a whopping five degrees of warming in this century, bringing with it profound changes to people, ecosystems and landscapes.

The new paper brings into view how the changes in Canada won’t just be felt locally, but feed into climate change globally. It draws on previous research already highlighting the impacts of specific extreme weather events.

For example, during Canada's worst wildfire season on record in 2023, the flames released one billion tonnes of carbon. If they were a country, the wildfires would have been the eighth highest emitter in the world.

“Canada is a large northern country, so these feedbacks is going to occur within Canada to a large degree,” said David Olefeldt, professor at the University of Alberta and a leading permafrost researcher.

“Therefore we have a responsibility to make sure we have studies that are focusing on it.”

Why is the permafrost melting?

Rising temperatures from global warming are heating up the Arctic at two or three times the global average, and that’s leading to the permafrost thawing. But while previously permafrost thaw was seen as a gradual process happening throughout the region, Poulter said the new paper included emissions from the process of "abrupt" thawing.

The abrupt thawing, also triggered by warming as well as extreme weather like wildfires and rain, happens much more locally and causes the land to cave or slump suddenly. Olefeldt said that while these abrupt thaws happen over smaller areas, usually at the edges of wetlands and lakes, they have the potential to release much more carbon.

A slump caused by abrupt permafrost thaw in the Northwest Territories. (David Olefeldt)

The abrupt thaw exposes the soil, and the ancient organic material that was previously locked up in it, to microbes that feed on that soil and produce methane and carbon dioxide.

“You're creating new lakes or new wetlands, for example, or warming the soil quite a lot faster in those locations,” he said.

But coming up with exact estimates of how much carbon is being released is tough.

“We have very sparse measurement networks in the high latitudes just because of the remoteness of the sites, the challenges for doing research in these areas,” Poulter said, pointing to a need, especially in Canada, for more field studies to monitor this process.

The wetland methane puzzle

Another major source of warming-induced emissions are wetlands, which cover large parts of Canada.

Scientists have grown increasingly worried about methane emissions from wetlands because of a major spike in the growth of methane in the atmosphere starting around 2020, Poulter said. The emissions growth could not be fully explained by direct human activities like oil and gas production and agriculture, which produce methane, and attention turned toward wetlands.

Lisa Stein, a professor and microbiologist at the University of Alberta, said she hopes the new paper will push institutions to include freshwater wetlands in their climate models.

When microbes break down organic matter in wetlands, methane is created as a byproduct of that biological process and emitted into the atmosphere. Warmer temperatures increase that microbial metabolism and therefore create more methane, Stein said.

“When scientists have looked at methane increase in the atmosphere over the last five years, they've noted that almost all of it has the signature of biology,” Stein said, meaning that rising methane emissions can't fully be explained by human activities and are also being driven by this rise in microbial activity.

Warmer winters, where lakes don't freeze as long, matter too, Poulter said.

“As we see the frozen season get shorter and shorter, we're seeing sort of an increasing duration of these persistent methane emissions coming out of Canada's wetlands,” he said.

World.title: Canadian teens score well on OECD tests, but sharp drops in reading, math raise concerns
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian teens have good knowledge of science, reading and math, according to a major international assessment, but the latest PISA results also indicate a long-term slide in scores for all three subjects, with a steep and worrisome drop in the latter two over the past few editions.

That downward trend — amid an overall decline for teens worldwide — raises concerns for some educators and researchers, who hope the latest results propel policymakers toward more consideration and action to improve student learning.

The joint body comprising all Canadian ministers of education and higher education noted as much in a statement earlier this week, saying, "comparative results over time emphasize the imperative for ongoing attention to educational outcomes."

Held every three years, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)'s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) tests 15-year-olds in about 90 countries and economies worldwide on three subjects, with a heavier, rotating focus on one subject each edition.

For the 2025 edition, about 24,600 students across Canada participated (Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut did not participate and are not represented in the results). Additional data about student attitudes, behaviours and school atmosphere was gathered from student and school principal questionnaires.

WATCH | Canadian students continue slide as PISA 2025 results released: Experts blame AI, screens for slipping Canadian student test scores | Duration 2:05 While Canadian students still perform well globally in math, science and reading, scores have dipped significantly in recent years. Some educational experts blame the rising overuse of AI and too much screen time.

The latest results show Canadian students rank above the OECD average and among the upper tier of top-performing PISA participants globally.

Canadian students scored 510 points in science, 490 in reading and 485 in math. Students from China and Singapore were the highest performers.

Yet comparing Canadians' performance to past editions shows a notable decline over two decades. Canada has slipped gradually in science (24 points since 2006) and fallen sharply in reading and math (declining 37 and 42 points respectively since 2006, with a drop of 30 and 27 points alone since 2018).

Though small variations in scores are expected, the OECD considers changes greater than 20 points (which represent a school year's worth of learning) statistically significant.

"If a country’s score falls by 20 points between two PISA assessments, it is as if students were performing at the level expected of 14-year-olds in the previous cycle," it says.

"The steepness of these declines post-pandemic is ... what some would call shocking. I would call it very concerning," said Louis Volante, a professor at Brock University who researches international achievement testing, educational governance and policy.

Volante points to factors that researchers think are impacting student achievement: more digital distractions, increased use of artificial intelligence since the last edition and teacher shortages worldwide.

"When you put those three together, they are being attributed to really having a negative impact on overall rating scores," he said from Oakville, Ont.

Prof. Louis Volante, seen at the Brock University campus in St. Catharines, Ont., says the sharp decline in PISA reading and math scores since the international assessment's last edition is concerning. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

The 2025 edition had the lowest OECD-average performance observed so far, the organization said. After an unprecedented drop in performance in 2022 — the first edition reflecting the disruptions of COVID-19 — learning outcomes across all participants stagnated or continued to fall in 2025, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann wrote in a report detailing the latest results.

He singled out an overall steep drop in reading scores as particularly of note "because reading skills underpin learning across the curriculum and are essential for finding, evaluating, interpreting and reflecting on information in an increasingly digital world."

Countries with the largest reading declines also tended to see the largest drops in science and math, he said.

Secondary and post-secondary teacher Tasha Ausman has noticed a decline in student reading comprehension and ability to identify key information. (Brian Morris/CBC)

It's something seen in classrooms, as well. Both with her students in the West Quebec School Board and the University of Ottawa, Tasha Ausman has noticed a decline in student reading comprehension and ability to identify key information.

During a test for an advanced math class this week, "students were asking me things that were directly written in the question," the high school teacher and university educator shared as an example.

Meanwhile, her post-secondary students regularly email questions easily answered at the start of her syllabus — like which textbook to buy or where to buy it.

She praises students today as empathetic as they team up with classmates, eager to learn and connect and excited by hands-on learning. Yet she's also found them much more stressed by tests and struggling with some basics.

"It's not a lack of willingness. I think it's an actual literacy challenge."

Ausman says she's seen students in both high school and university struggle with reading comprehension. 'It's not a lack of willingness. I think it's an actual literacy challenge,' she said. (Jean-François Fort/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)

Canada slow to change, says consultant

In the past, Canada was a top 10 PISA participant, but our school systems have since weakened and we've been slow to respond, says education consultant Paul Bennett, director of Schoolhouse Institute.

The PISA results are "a cause for alarm, especially given the dramatic declines since 2015. The trends that were visible in 2022 after the pandemic are proving to be more permanent than we ever imagined," he said from Halifax.

"We've lost ground to the countries in Asia who have focused much more on test preparation. They're much more in favour of direct instruction. They've had great success in teaching that way."

Education consultant Paul Bennett thinks the latest results are 'a cause for alarm, especially given the dramatic declines since 2015.' (Schoolhouse Consulting)

Given that education is a provincial rather than federal responsibility in Canada, as well as the different socioeconomic and other challenges in each jurisdiction, Bennett feels Canada has been inconsistent with education policy updates and changes.

He noted, for instance, that in provinces with higher PISA scores — Alberta, Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec — "there's much more of a focus on the science of learning," he noted. "They were early onto it. They've begun to match their teaching methodologies with what works in the classroom."

Bennett thinks a host of practices require fresh consideration, from screen learning and technology use to a comeback for physical textbooks.

"I don't want to turn back the clock," he said, "but we need to readjust our focus."

An indicator for the future

What's behind sliding student performance is a billion-dollar question for everyone, says Darryl Hunter, a recently retired education professor at the University of Alberta.

PISA, national tests like the Pan-Canadian Assessment Program and provincial assessments are designed to serve as periodic status checks, Hunter explained — to inspire deeper conversation, thorough investigation and new research to guide educational policymakers.

"If Canada is going to be a dynamic country in the future, we have to attend to the performance of our students."

Darryl Hunter, a recently retired professor of educational policy studies at the University of Alberta, has worked as a high school teacher, administrator and with ministries of education in three provinces. (Laura Sou/University of Alberta)

While PISA results are a high-profile measure, Volante at Brock University cautions it should be taken in perspective and that comparing test scores shouldn't be the sole focus.

The student and principal questionnaires dive into what Volante called "non-cognitive" aspects, things like whether students are curious, seek help or believe in their own ability to achieve, as well as school attendance, if they read for pleasure, feel they belong and whether they receive family support.

Those indicators contribute to a more holistic picture of how schools are doing, he said, noting that faring well in these areas is linked to stronger student outcomes.

"Success in the future will not solely be dictated by how well [students] do in reading, math and science," Volante said.

"We hear a lot of rhetoric around, 'We need our reading and math and our science scores to go up so that we can improve our economy.' But I would argue 'Yes, we do, but we also need all these other things as well.'"

World.title: Man flees road rage incident near Vancouver that ended with him being chased with a knife
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robin Nuber was in Los Angeles on the weekend, but it was after he returned home to British Columbia that he found himself in a scene he likened to an "action movie," speeding in reverse to escape a man with a knife who was chasing a frightened victim clinging to the outside of Nuber's Tesla.

"I just got back, so I literally felt like I was at Universal Studios where they do the staged remakes of movies, and everything's kind of like an action movie," the Surrey, B.C., photographer said on Thursday

"It felt like I was at an actual movie set, but nope, it was not — it was very real."

Nuber had been heading to a photo shoot in Redwood Park in Surrey on Wednesday when he encountered the scene of a man with a knife clambering over a pickup truck in pursuit of another man, who ran toward Nuber's Tesla.

A video captured by Nuber's vehicle shows the assailant chasing the car as it reverses away, the other man hanging onto an open back door as Nuber tries to put distance between them and the pursuer.

Nuber can be heard telling the victim to "hold on" before the vehicle stops and the man climbs inside when they are far enough away from the attacker.

WATCH | B.C. road rage incident leads to knife chase: Man is chased with a knife after driving altercation near Vancouver | Duration 0:35

He said the victim suffered multiple injuries, including a bloody mouth, gouged right eye and cuts on an arm.

Surrey police said a 37-year-old man was facing multiple charges, including assault with a weapon, criminal harassment and uttering threats and he remained in custody.

He was due in Surrey Provincial Court on Thursday to set a next appearance date.

"The victim attempted to drive away in his Ford pickup truck when the suspect drove his Jeep Wrangler into it," Surrey police said in a statement on Thursday.

"The victim then ran from the truck as the suspect allegedly brandished a knife and chased after him. Fortunately, a nearby witness driving a Telsa provided the victim safety until SPS officers arrived.

The statement said several police officers were called to the scene at about 4:44 p.m. and took the suspect into custody without incident.

Nuber said he had turned up at a parking lot when he saw a pickup truck and a Jeep had collided, with both cars' airbags deployed.

"I thought that it might be a road rage incident. So, I slowed my car down, and then I took my phone out and started to film what started to happen," said Nuber.

Then he heard someone yelling "he's got a knife.'

The chase ensued after a man with no shoes ran toward him, shouting for help.

"The guy basically ended up hanging onto my car and then being kind of dangled underneath the door for about 100 feet. I think I dragged him just to get him away from the guy," Nuber said.

"And then eventually he kind of begged me to stop the car so he could get inside because he was obviously getting road rash."

Nuber said the suspect gave up the chase, walked to the woods and threw the knife into the forest, before police arrived minutes later.

He said the incident was a test of his survival instincts.

"I think if you ever face a situation, you might be impressed with yourself, with what your instincts do," said Nuber.

World.title: Carney says he's regularly speaking with Trump and still believes there's a deal to be had
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's still in regular contact with U.S. President Donald Trump despite the ongoing trade rift and some unsavoury remarks from administration officials.

The prime minister suggested that his recent conversations with Trump have been focused on global events, including how the wars in Ukraine and Iran are impacting international energy and grain markets.

"In terms of playing that [international] role, we continue to work with the United States. We can compartmentalize," he said during a news conference alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary on Thursday.

"I spoke to [Trump] recently in the last few days, a couple of times, related to issues [in Ukraine], related to issues in Iran, other global developments. Because that's part of our responsibility."

WATCH | Carney gives examples of topics of discussion with Trump: Canada ready to support Russia-Ukraine ceasefire where U.S. can play 'decisive role': Carney | Duration 2:17 Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said a cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine offers a possible 'shorter-term solution' to global issues around access to energy and agricultural goods.

Tariff negotiations between Canada and the U.S. fell apart last month, with both sides hurling blame at the other.

The U.S. immediately slapped 50 per cent levies on hundreds of Canadian goods, and Canada countered with new tariffs on roughly an equivalent value of U.S. imports on Monday. The Trump administration responded on Wednesday by announcing it would place further tariffs on some Canadian imports and outright ban others later this month.

Carney didn't say whether his government would respond with more counter-tariffs on U.S. goods.

"We're looking closely at the measures the Americans just recently announced," he told reporters later on Thursday.

Carney said that even though talks have stalled, he believes there's still a deal to be had with the U.S.

"Canada's always ready to strike a fair deal. We believe there's still a mutually beneficial deal for Canada and the United States," he said at the news conference with Zelenskyy.

WATCH | Carney says government is reviewing Trump's latest trade actions: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Trump and some of his key cabinet members have disparaged Canada in the media and online in recent weeks.

The president notably decided his government would refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have both derided the Canadian Armed Forces. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told the Financial Times that it's "unhinged" for Canadian leaders to characterize the administration's tariffs as a trade war.

Carney has pushed back when asked about some of the Trump administration's more unsavoury remarks, saying they're "beneath their office."

WATCH | More about the trade war: Is toilet paper an unlikely pressure point in the Canada–U.S. trade war? | Duration 2:28 U.S. President Donald Trump dropped tariffs on certain Canadian products, including toilet paper, cement and salt. In 2024, Canada exported approximately $328 million worth of the product, making it the largest international provider of toilet paper to the U.S.

When asked about why he thinks Trump has continued to disparage Canada since talks fell apart, Carney wouldn't speculate.

"I can't look deeply into the souls of other people and see their emotions. This isn't a question of emotion, it's a question of sovereignty for Canada," he said.

World.title: Man accused in Mexican condo scheme claims he was a victim, too
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC's Mexico team traveled to Harry Robinson's real estate office to discuss the accusations he faces in a Mexican court, including arrest warrants issued for him and his former business partner, Jacqueline Herrera Herrera. Robinson is a suspect in a fraud case involving an Ontario couple, Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown, who invested $280,000 in a plan to flip condos in Playa del Carmen, but never received the property or their money back. Robinson and his lawyer, Blanca Figueroa Ornelas, agreed to an interview for this report.

Accused in Mexican scam of Canadian couple tells his side of the story

A U.K. man facing accusations he took part in a scheme that wiped out a Canadian couple's retirement savings says he's provided proof to Mexican authorities probing the case that he never touched a dime of the vanished funds, and that he's also a victim of his co-accused.

Harry Robinson, 66, is accused of working with a Mexican national named Jacqueline Herrera Herrera to defraud Cindy Thompson and Glenn Brown of Curve Lake, Ont., of $280,000 by offering them a fake deal to buy and flip seven condos.

Robinson provided CBC News with a memo and HSBC bank records, both filed with the state attorney general's office of Quintana Roo, that he says proves Herrera redirected Thompson and Brown's money — sent over three installments — through cashier's cheques and transfers to other, unknown accounts.
