Later in his article, Grillo wrote that in his “subjective judgement,” about “a third of Mexican states have a severe cartel presence and high levels of violence; another third have a medium (but still important) level of cartel problems and bloodshed; and a last third have levels of violence compared with regular U.S. cities, and less serious problems from gangsters.”

Since that article was published in late January 2024 — around nine months before Sheinbaum took office — homicides and other high-impact crimes have declined, according to official statistics, suggesting that Mexico’s overall security situation has improved. Nevertheless, cartels continue to operate, fight turf wars and pose major challenges to authorities in various parts of the country.

World.title: Mexico gears up for Independence Day with a military parade, concerts and of course the Grito — all set for Sept. 15-16
World.content:
More than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are preparing to march, fly and roll out new equipment in Mexico City next week as the country marks the 216th anniversary of its independence.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo reviewed the logistics for the capital’s Sept. 16 Independence Day parade.

In Mexico, Día de la Independencia commemorates the start of the rebellion against Spanish rule in 1810, although the nation’s War of Independence didn’t end until 1821.

The parade will include Army, Navy, Air Force and National Guard personnel, cadets, pilots, military engineers, medical workers, communications specialists, military police and special forces. It also will include horses, dogs and even eagles, according to El Heraldo de México.

Contingents will be designated “Justice and Peace,” “Sentinels of the Nation,” “Crucible of Patriots” and “Roots of Honor,” among other names, Trevilla Trejo said during his briefing on a military base in Naucalpan, México state.

The roughly 5-kilometer parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Sept. 16 with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central plaza — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes, continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

The capital’s celebrations begin the night before, when President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the traditional Grito de Independencia (“Shout” or “Cry” of Independence) from the National Palace balcony.

In conjunction, the Grammy-winning Texas-based band Intocable, whose Norteño-Tejano sound has landed them 21 No. 1 songs on Billboard’s Regional Mexican Airplay chart, will headline a free concert in the Zócalo.

Free concerts, food fairs and municipal Grito ceremonies are also planned across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs. The musical lineup includes norteño-banda group Calibre 50 (a record 27 No. 1 hits on Billboard’s regional Mexican chart) and Sinaloan balladeer Pancho Barraza (a headliner since the 1990s).

The observances will reach beyond the capital, as well, as the Grito tradition is replicated by governors and mayors nationwide.

In present-day Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato — then known simply as Dolores, where priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla called on residents to rise against Spanish rule in the early hours of Sept. 16, 1810 — Independence Day festivities are running nearly all month.

In nearby San Miguel de Allende, Sept. 16 observances include a reenactment of the start of the independence movement in 1810.

This year, the Sept. 16 national holiday falls on a Wednesday, meaning there will be no three-day weekend. Public schools and banks will close, as will many government offices and private workplaces, as it is a mandatory day of rest under federal labor law. Employees required to work are entitled to premium holiday pay. Sept. 15 remains a regular work and school day.

With reports from Milenio, Infobae, El Informador, El Heraldo de México, N+, El Sol de Bajío and ADN Noticias

World.title: Education Ministry blames screen use for Mexican students’ falling scores
World.content:
Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students in the latest international PISA evaluation test by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Speaking in Mexico City during the opening of National Days of Traditional Games, Delgado expressed doubt that the results amount to a comprehensive evaluation of the Mexican educational system, though he did concede that the sample was “statistically representative.”

“The low reading comprehension scores can be explained by the fact that screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images, and teenagers find it difficult to read more complex and longer texts,” he said.

Mexico ranked 64th out of 91 countries evaluated, with a drop in math and reading scores to the lowest levels since 2009.

Before promoting team games as a partial remedy, Delgado defended the New Mexican School — the official public education model implemented under the previous presidential administration — though without providing specific pedagogical strategies.

Delgado said the Education Ministry (SEP) simultaneously implemented formative assessment programs under the New Mexican School scheme, including 7 million integrative learning exercises during the past year.

Still, officials sought to put Mexico’s poor scores in a global perspective, insisting that international reading and math scores declined by 27 points and 22 points, respectively. Such emphasis ignores the fact that the lower scores are equivalent to losing a year of learning.

Although President Claudia Sheinbaum has often criticized what she calls “the structural limitations of the PISA test (saying “it applies the same exam across countries with vastly different local characteristics”), she initiated a public debate about the excessive use of screens and the early access of children and adolescents to digital platforms. This led to new national guidelines restricting cell phone use in schools.

Delgado said that with cell phone regulation in place, new activities — such as team games — can be used to effectively get the attention of students and build cooperative learning skills.

Unlike mobile phones, which promote isolation and limit social skills, Delgado said games like yo-yo, marbles, spinning top, and cup-and-ball encourage teamwork, shared fun and the formation of new friendships.

The aim is to encourage students to spend more time playing and socializing, Delgado said, insisting that being in front of a phone limits opportunities to connect with other people.

With reports from Vanguardia, Animal Político and El Universal

World.title: Mexico’s inflation rate rises to 3.26% in August, ending 4-month decline
World.content:
Mexico’s annual inflation rate rose slightly in August compared to July, ending a four-month streak of declines.

The national statistics agency INEGI reported Wednesday that the annual headline inflation rate was 3.26% in August, up from 3.12% in July.

Month-over-month inflation was 0.20% in August, while the annual core rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 3.88%, down from 3.95% in July.

Both the annual headline rate and the core rate came in just below the median estimates of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.

The increase in Mexico’s annual headline rate came after inflation slowed on a month-over-month basis in each of April, May, June and July. The headline rate thus fell from 4.59% in March to 3.12% in July, a decline of 1.47 percentage points. During the same period, the Bank of Mexico (Banxico) cut its key interest rate by 25 basis points on two occasions, lowering it to 6.75% in March and 6.50% in May.

The central bank, which targets 3% inflation, appears unlikely to make any additional cuts to its key rate this year. Banxico is currently forecasting that inflation will be 3.5% at the end of 2026. It anticipates that the headline rate will gradually decline in 2027 to converge to its 3% target in the final quarter of next year.

Services inflation remains above 4%

Of the four broad categories monitored by INEGI, services recorded the largest year-over-year increase in prices in August. Annual services inflation was 4.33%, down slightly from a 4.36% reading in July. Education fees, one of the services sub-categories, rose 6.04% annually in August, the month in which students across Mexico returned to school.

Annual inflation for goods was 3.41% in August. Within that category, inflation was 4.68% for processed food, beverages and tobacco, and 2.32% for non-food goods.

Energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline, rose 3.33% annually in August, while prices for agricultural products fell 1.53% year-over-year. The overall deflation for the agricultural products category was the product of a 5.22% decrease in meat prices and a 4.1% increase in fruit and vegetable prices.

World.title: While Mexico’s northern border states deal with a heat alert, monsoon conditions drench the Pacific Coast
World.content:
Low-pressure troughs and Tropical Wave 37 were baking large swaths of Mexico on Thursday, even as the Mexican monsoon was dumping heavy amounts of rain over much of the rest of the country.

The Pacific Coast states received the brunt of the storm system, although the Gulf-side municipality of Coatzacoalcos suffered extensive flooding after being pounded by an intense storm on Wednesday.

Cooler temperatures are expected on Friday, but for Thursday the National Meteorological Service (SMN) issued a heat alert for residents in north and northwestern Mexico. Temperatures above 45 C (113 F) were forecast for parts of Baja California and Sonora, with temperatures between 40-45 C (104-113 F) in parts of Sinaloa, Coahuila, Tamaulipas and Nuevo León.

“Stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun and take precautions against the heat,” the SMN advised in a social media post.

The heat wave extended south to Guanajuato and Guerrero, while some regions along the Gulf Coast saw temperatures hitting 38 C (100 F) on Wednesday.

At the same time, the rainfall map showed persistent heavy rains across the length and breadth of the country, accompanied by lightning and hail in some instances.

While Sinaloa was projected to get the most rainfall through Friday, the SMN said Guanajuato could expect to see the most intense midweek rains.

The SMN said rainfall produced by the Mexican monsoon could reach 150 millimeters in Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco and Colima through Thursday. Very heavy and locally intense downpours were also forecast for Baja California Sur, Sonora and Sinaloa.

The Friday forecast also calls for continued heavy rain storms in central Sinaloa, with heavy to very heavy rainfall in Baja California Sur, Sonora, Durango and Nayarit.

The SMN said Tropical Wave 37 has been met by the arrival of Tropical Wave 38, which has crossed into the Yucatán Peninsula and southeastern Mexico from the east, increasing the likelihood of heavy rain in those regions through Sunday.

The SMN said the states of Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo will register heavy to very heavy rainfall with electrical activity during the initial approach of the new weather system.

Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero will also experience an increased probability of heavy rains with electrical discharges as the system moves west, while Michoacán, Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit will be affected by the passage of the phenomenon throughout the weekend.

With reports from El País, El Financiero, Milenio, Diario del Istmo and El Sol del Chilpancingo

World.title: Cancún airport’s international traffic drops 15% in August
World.content:
In August, Cancún International Airport (CUN) recorded a 15% year-over-year drop in international passenger traffic, handling 1.19 million international passengers.

The drop doesn’t come as a surprise.

In July, an analysis by the Center for Advanced Research in Sustainable Tourism (STARC) of the Anáhuac University of Cancún, anticipated that U.S. airlines would offer nearly a million fewer seats to Mexican beach destinations in July and August, a trend industry experts attributed to rising jet fuel prices, sargassum-covered beaches and safety concerns, among other issues. Cancún, Cozumel and Tulum alone were expected to lose over half a million seats.

A more recent report by STARC revealed that CUN’s decline began early this year after losing 845,714 international passengers between January and August, falling from 13.7 million to 12.9 million passengers — down 6.1% compared to the same period last year.

Although the decline was greater in the international market, the domestic market also fell 4.8% in the same period, from 6.6 million passengers to 6.3 million.

In total, Cancún International Airport served 19.2 million domestic and international passengers so far this year — 5.7% less than the 20.4 million passengers CUN mobilized during the same period last year.

STARC’s figures show that Cancún has now seen six consecutive months of decline, with the steepest drops being registered in May (down 11.1% compared to 2025), June (down 13%), July (down 12.7%) and August (down 15%).

Including national and international travelers, CUN handled 2.1 million passengers in August, compared to 2.3 million the previous year — a 9.3% total drop.

CUN’s Director Carlos Trueba Coll told El Economista that the drop in international traffic is partly due to the bankruptcy of U.S. airline Spirit.

However, he noted that the lost seat capacity has been gradually recovered through airlines such as JetBlue, and expressed confidence that the resumption of seasonal flights in December would help reverse the negative figures recorded between May and August.

Other airports across Mexico saw more moderate declines: Southeast Airport Group (ASUR), which operates Cancún’s airport, said in a statement that on average, its airports in Mexico reported a 13.6% year-on-year decrease in international traffic. One exception to the trend: Mérida, ASUR’s second-busiest airport in Mexico, reported a 4.5% increase in international traffic, serving just over 280,000 international travelers so far this year.

World.title: MND Local: Earthquake drills, K-pop and El Grito in CDMX
World.content:
Mexico News Daily is officially launching MND Local CDMX, a weekly roundup of the news, events and cultural moments that capture the beating heart of the nation’s capital.

Coming up: South Korean culture takes over the capital, the city pauses for a national earthquake drill, coveted tickets for the NFL Mexico City Series 2026 go on sale, and President Claudia Sheinbaum leads the country in its annual Independence Day celebration.

K-EXPO takes over Mexico City, Sept. 25-27

From bibimbap to gamja hot dogs, and BTS to “Squid Game,” South Korean culture shows no sign of slowing its march across Mexico. Now, the South Korean government and one of the country’s leading creative-content agencies are bringing K-mania to Mexico City with K-EXPO 2026, a three-day celebration of Korean food, music, entertainment and lifestyle.

The free public events run Sept. 25-27 at the Centro Internacional de Exposiciones y Convenciones (CIEC) WTC in Colonia Nápoles, roughly 15 minutes driving from Chapultepec Park. Visitors can meet some of Korea’s leading tastemakers in food, content creation and lifestyle, while taking in a K-Pop All-Star cover-dance performance, a live cooking show and an idol makeup workshop.

Then comes the main event — and this one isn’t free. On Sept. 26, K-Pop acts Winner, Dayoung, Soyou, Touched and Alpha Drive One will perform at Pepsi Center WTC. Ticket details are expected to be announced soon.

For the latest updates, check K-EXPO Mexico City’s official website or Instagram page.

What: K-EXPO Exhibition and Events

Where: CIEC WTC, Filadelfia s/n, Nápoles, Benito Juárez, CDMX

When: Sept. 25-27

Price: Free

What: K-EXPO Concert

Where: Pepsi Center WTC, Dakota s/n, Nápoles, Benito Juárez, CDMX

When: Sept. 26

Price: To be announced

Don’t be alarmed — this is only a test

It may not be the most exciting item on the calendar, but anyone in Mexico City on Sept. 19 — especially visitors — should know what’s coming.

At noon, the city’s loudspeakers, cellphones, radio and television broadcasts will erupt with an earthquake alarm, marking the start of Mexico’s second national earthquake drill of the year. The simulated scenario: a magnitude 7.7 quake.

According to the National Coordinator of Civil Protection, the exercise is designed to strengthen government preparedness and coordination while encouraging the public to play an active role in reducing disaster risk.

If you live here, consider it a good excuse to finally put together that go-bag. If you’re visiting, take a deep breath, remember it’s a drill and don’t freak out.

The date itself carries some serious significance. Several of Mexico City’s most devastating earthquakes have struck on Sept. 19, including the disasters of 1985 and 2017. To mark the solemn occasion, President Claudia Sheinbaum will raise the national flag in the Zócalo at 7:19 a.m. in honor of the victims.

NFL tickets are coming. Good luck.

Football fans, get your clicking fingers ready.

The NFL is bringing the 2026 Mexico City Series to Estadio Banorte on Nov. 22, when the Minnesota Vikings face off against the San Francisco 49ers.

The game is still more than two months away, but if previous NFL games in Mexico City are any indication, waiting until the last minute for tickets is probably not the move. When the league last played here, in 2022, presale tickets reportedly disappeared within an hour, while general-sale tickets are also said to have sold out almost immediately.

Here’s the schedule for the 2026 ticket rush, with sales taking place through Ticketmaster:

American Express Presale: Sept. 14 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 6 tickets per person

Banorte Presale: Sept. 17 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 4 tickets per person

General Sale: Sept. 22 at 10 a.m. CST — limit of 4 tickets per person

And, of course, El Grito

MND Local CDMX will always aim to point you toward the things happening below the radar. But considering our inaugural edition lands just ahead of El Grito, we’d be remiss not to give you the quick-and-dirty guide to one of the biggest nights on Mexico’s calendar.

The official celebration of Mexican Independence is held Sept. 15 and draws enormous crowds to Mexico City’s Plaza de la Constitución — better known as the Zócalo — in the historic center.

The festivities begin well before the main event, with people arriving hours in advance to stake out a spot with a view of the Palacio Nacional. Then, at 11 p.m., President Claudia Sheinbaum steps onto the main balcony and delivers the iconic Grito de Dolores, or Grito de la Independencia, officially kicking off the celebrations.

What follows is exactly what you’d expect from Mexico City on one of its biggest nights: street food, music, fireworks, flags, an abundance of green, white and red, and a whole lot of people. This year’s musical lineup is headlined by Tejano superstars Grupo Intocable.

If you don’t shy away from crowds, we highly recommend experiencing the spectacle at least once. It’s loud, chaotic, deeply patriotic and very, very Mexico City.

If, on the other hand, the prospect of being packed into a square with millions of people sounds less than appealing, fear not. Hundreds of smaller celebrations will be happening across the city, offering plenty of Grito energy, with plenty more breathing room.

Welcome to MND Local CDMX. We’ll see you next week.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Argentina Inflation Falls to 1.7 Percent, Lowest in 14 Months
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts —The headline. Argentina’s consumer prices rose 1.7% in August, the statistics agency INDEC reported on September 10 — the lowest monthly reading since June 2025 and the lowest for an August since 2017. —The big picture. Annual inflation eased to 33.5%, and prices are up 21.3% so far this year. Core inflation, which strips out seasonal and regulated items, ran at 1.8%. —On forecast. The print matched exactly the 1.7% median projection in the central bank’s REM survey of analysts. —What rose most. Housing and utilities led with a 2.8% increase, followed by education at 2.5% and health at 2.4%. Food and non-alcoholic drinks rose 1.7% and contributed most to the monthly index. —The celebration. The Economy Ministry declared it “the lowest inflation of the last 14 months,” and President Javier Milei cheered his economy minister: “¡Vamooo Toto!”

Argentina’s August inflation came in at 1.7% — a 14-month low that landed exactly on analysts’ forecast. The government is celebrating; skeptics are watching the peso, the reserves, and a year-end forecast still near 30%.

Inside a supermarket in Buenos Aires. Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose 1.7% in August and were the largest contributor to the monthly index. (Photo: MewMeowth, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Numbers Behind the Slowdown

The 1.7% monthly increase extends one of the most abrupt disinflations anywhere in the world. When Javier Milei took office in December 2023, monthly inflation was running above 25%. It has now spent most of 2026 between 1.5% and 2.5%, and August’s reading is the lowest since the 1.6% recorded in June 2025, according to INDEC data reported by La Nación and TN.

The composition matters as much as the headline. Seasonal goods actually fell 0.9% in the month, while regulated prices — utility and transport tariffs still adjusting to the removal of subsidies — rose 2.2%, Economy Minister Luis Caputo noted in a social media post. That leaves core inflation at 1.8%, slightly above the headline, a sign that the remaining pressure is concentrated in administered prices rather than in the broader economy.

By division, housing, water, electricity and fuels rose 2.8%, the fastest of any category, reflecting ongoing tariff catch-up. Education climbed 2.5% and health 2.4%. Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose 1.7%, in line with the general index — and, because food weighs heavily in Argentine household budgets, it was the largest single contributor to the monthly figure.

August was also the softest reading for that month since 2017 — before the currency crises of the Macri era and the triple-digit inflation that peaked under the previous government in early 2024.

A Government Victory Lap

The government moved within hours to claim the number. The Economy Ministry posted on X, in capital letters, that August delivered “LA INFLACIÓN MÁS BAJA DE LOS ÚLTIMOS 14 MESES” — the lowest inflation of the last 14 months. Milei amplified the message with a personal jab at his critics and praise for his economy minister: “¡Vamooo Toto!” he wrote, using Caputo’s nickname, Minutouno reported.

The print also landed on the consensus. The central bank’s REM survey had projected exactly 1.7% for August, so the figure surprised no one — which, in a country accustomed to inflation shocks, is itself news. The same survey’s median forecast sees inflation ending 2026 near 30% annually; the Top-10 group of forecasters puts it at 30.2%, while the Facimex consultancy projects 28.7%.

Markets had already been drifting in the government’s favor. Country risk, measured by the JPMorgan EMBI spread, fell below 500 basis points earlier this week to around 403 — its lowest since April 2018, Infobae reported — extending a rally in Argentine bonds.

What the Skeptics Are Watching

The critique of the disinflation is not about the index but about how it is being achieved. The peso’s official rate has crawled far more slowly than prices, and the outlet La Política Online warned this week that “el atraso cambiario se profundiza” — the exchange-rate lag is deepening — a gap many private economists believe will eventually force a sharper devaluation. The wholesale dollar traded near 1,510 pesos per dollar around the release, with Banco Nación quoting 1,485 to buy and 1,535 to sell.

Reserves are the second pressure point. The central bank managed net purchases of about US$127 million over the five sessions through mid-week — a welcome streak — but gross reserves stand near US$50.8 billion while net reserves, after deducting liabilities, are estimated around US$12 billion. Rebuilding that cushion while keeping the peso steady is the central bank’s defining challenge for the rest of the year.

The third is the exit from the current regime. With year-end inflation still projected near 30%, the disinflation is real but unfinished: tariffs continue to adjust, wage negotiations are reopening, and every month of exchange-rate lag raises the stakes of the eventual correction. August’s 1.7% shows the strategy is still delivering. The question that will define the coming quarters is what it costs to keep it going.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Argentina’s inflation rate in August 2026?

Consumer prices rose 1.7% month over month, INDEC reported on September 10 — the lowest monthly reading since June 2025 (1.6%) and the lowest for an August since 2017. Annual inflation eased to 33.5%.

Which prices rose the most in August?

Housing and utilities led with 2.8%, followed by education (2.5%) and health (2.4%). Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose 1.7% and, given their weight in the index, contributed most to the monthly increase.

What do analysts expect for the rest of 2026?

The central bank’s REM survey projects annual inflation near 30% for 2026, with the Top-10 forecasters at 30.2% and Facimex at 28.7%. Analysts are watching the peso’s exchange-rate lag and the central bank’s thin net reserves as the main risks.

World.title: Ecopetrol Purge Reaches the Subsidiaries as Colombia’s Oil Giant Heads for a Full Board Vote
World.content:
COLOMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts — The sweep Ecopetrol has replaced its CEO, five vice presidents and two more top executives since late July, in what Colombian media openly call a purge of the Petro era.

— The latest This week the changes reached subsidiary Essentia, where Carlos González left and Juan Carlos Álvarez took over as acting president.

— The next step On 15 September, an extraordinary shareholders assembly will elect all nine members of a new board of directors.

— The rationale Board chairman Luis Felipe Henao says Ecopetrol must stop being “governed by ideology” and has ordered a forensic audit with all internal evidence frozen.

— The backdrop The state owns 88.49 percent of Ecopetrol; the company just posted a net profit of 6.1 trillion pesos (about US$1.9 billion) for the second quarter.

— The interim Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra has been acting CEO since 31 July, while a headhunter searches for a permanent chief executive.

Six weeks after the board changed hands, the broom is still moving through Ecopetrol’s executive floors. The new government calls it depoliticization. The departing names tell the story.

Ecopetrol’s Barrancabermeja refinery on the Magdalena river, with the Cristo Petrolero monument. The state oil giant is replacing most of its executive layer. (Photo: Yesid Ferney Patiño, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Ecopetrol purge is no longer a plan — it is a personnel ledger. Since the end of July, Colombia’s state-controlled oil company has lost its chief executive, five vice presidents and at least two further top executives, almost all of them appointees of the Gustavo Petro years, and this week the turnover reached into the subsidiaries: gas retailer Essentia confirmed that Carlos González is out and Juan Carlos Álvarez takes over as acting president, Valora Analitik reported.

It is the first visible purge inside the company since the board of directors changed hands under President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government — and it is not finished. On Monday, 15 September, an extraordinary shareholders assembly convenes at 11:00 a.m. at Ecopetrol’s Bogotá headquarters to elect all nine members of the board for the remainder of the 2025–2029 term, and to vote on a statutory reform of how the board is renewed.

Who Has Left So Far

The cascade began at the top. Ricardo Roa Barragán, the Petro-appointed CEO whose tenure was marked by scandal coverage, formally ended his presidency on 30 July. Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra, the company’s upstream vice president, has served as acting president since 31 July while an executive search firm hunts for a permanent successor.

In late August, the new board — chaired since early August by Luis Felipe Henao, an independent member backed by the new government — authorized five senior-management changes effective from September. La República named the departing vice presidents: Sandra Lucía Rodríguez Rojas (territorial transformation and HSE), Jaime Andrés García Cuello (administrative and services), Julián Fernando Lemos Valero (strategy and new business) and Felipe Trujillo López (refining and industrial processes), along with the head of institutional relations. Days later, as The Rio Times reported on 1 September, the science, technology and innovation vice presidency under Sergio Andrés Moreno Acevedo and the executive vice presidency for transition energies followed, both filled by internal acting appointees.

The pattern is consistent: Petro-era hires out, interim insiders in, permanent decisions deferred until after the new board is elected. On the board itself, the Petro-aligned members Ángela María Robledo and Tatiana Roa resigned in July; Infobae has reported that directors Alberto Merlano, Hildebrando Vélez and Carolina Arias could follow when shareholders vote on Monday.

The ‘No Ideology’ Doctrine

Henao has been unusually explicit about the philosophy behind the sweep. “We have to remove the idea that Ecopetrol should be governed by ideology,” he told Caracol on 25 August. “An oil company has to produce oil. You cannot put it to producing bread or cars.”

His first decisions went beyond personnel. On 9 August, Pulzo reported, Henao ordered a protocol to freeze internal evidence — documents and institutional chat logs — ahead of a forensic audit of the company’s recent governance. “So that they don’t destroy documents on us, being able to freeze all the institutional chats that have taken place,” he said. The audit framing signals that the Ecopetrol purge is meant to produce a paper trail, not just new business cards.

What Ecopetrol does. Ecopetrol S.A. operates as an integrated energy company. It operates through four segments: Exploration and Production; Transport and Logistics; Refining and Petrochemicals; and Energy transmission and Toll Roads Concessions. The Exploration and Production segment engages in the exploration and production of oil and gas. The Transport and Logistics segment is involved in…

A Profitable Patient

The company being restructured is not in crisis — which is precisely the new board’s argument. Ecopetrol posted second-quarter revenue of 40.2 trillion pesos (about US$12.8 billion), EBITDA of 17.7 trillion pesos (about US$5.6 billion), up 59 percent year on year at a 44 percent margin, and net profit of 6.1 trillion pesos (about US$1.9 billion), up 235 percent. Peso figures are converted at roughly 3,145 pesos per dollar, the rate Reuters used on 10 September.

Beneath the headline numbers, gas sales fell 23 percent on lower contracted volumes from the Cusiana and Cupiagua fields — the supply crunch The Rio Times has tracked in Colombia’s run-up to the board vote. Henao’s case is that operational focus, not political programming, closes that gap.

What Monday Decides

The state holds 88.49 percent of Ecopetrol’s shares, so Monday’s assembly is, in practice, the government’s decision. The electoral quotient system reserves space for minority shareholders, but the majority slate will carry. Once the nine-member board is seated, the interim structure — acting CEO, acting vice presidents — can be converted into permanent appointments.

Three questions hang over the vote. First, whether the new board keeps Henao and fellow independent Ricardo Rodríguez Yee, the two members the government publicly wants to retain. Second, whether the permanent CEO search produces an oil-industry name or a political one — the market will read that appointment as the true test of the “no ideology” doctrine. And third, whether the forensic audit produces findings that outlast the news cycle.

For foreign investors, the signal so far is double-edged: a government asserting control over its largest company, and a management layer being rebuilt in public. Monday turns the interim into a structure. What that structure does with a 17.7-trillion-peso (about US$5.6 billion) EBITDA machine is the story of the next quarter.

World.title: Guyana Signs Mineral Agreement With Mako Mining for Eagle Mountain Gold
World.content:
GUYANA · MINING

Key Facts — The deal Guyana signed a mineral agreement with Mako Mining Corp on 10 September 2026, locking in a 10-year legal and fiscal framework for the Eagle Mountain gold project.

— The signatories Natural Resources Minister Vickram Bharrat signed for the government, with Mako CEO Akiba Leisman and President Steve Parsons, alongside the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission.

— The project Eagle Mountain, about 8 kilometres from Mahdia in Region 8 (Potaro-Siparuni), holds 1.18 million ounces of indicated gold resources plus 582,000 ounces inferred.

— The timeline Construction is expected to begin by the third quarter of 2027, with first gold production by the end of 2028, subject to regulatory and environmental approvals.

— The terms Guyana’s standard mining fiscal regime applies — an 8 percent net smelter royalty and 25 percent corporate tax — which company filings estimate could mean US$146.7 million in royalties over the mine’s life.

Guyana’s oil boom gets the headlines, but the country just signed its most important gold deal of the decade — a decade-long framework that could put a new industrial mine into production by the end of 2028.

Guyana’s government signed a mineral agreement with Canada’s Mako Mining Corp on Thursday 10 September 2026, advancing the Eagle Mountain gold project toward construction, the Department of Public Information announced.

The agreement was signed by Minister of Natural Resources Vickram Bharrat, Mako Mining Chief Executive Officer Akiba Leisman and Mako President Steve Parsons, in the presence of representatives of the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission (GGMC). It establishes the legal, fiscal and operating framework for developing Eagle Mountain, held through Mako’s wholly owned subsidiary Stronghold Guyana Inc.

What the Agreement Locks In

Mineral agreements are the top tier of mining contract in Guyana, negotiated under the Mining Act with individual companies. This one gives Mako a 10-year stability framework covering its mining and prospecting licences, authorizations and fiscal terms. After the initial term, the parties can renegotiate in good faith or renew on the same conditions.

The fiscal architecture follows Guyana’s standard mining regime rather than the bespoke terms that made the country’s ExxonMobil oil contract so controversial. Company technical documentation describes an 8 percent net smelter royalty on gold payable to the government — deductible against the 25 percent corporate tax on chargeable income — and estimates the royalty alone would deliver US$146.7 million to the state over the life of the mine, with after-tax free cash flow of roughly US$38 million a year.

The agreement also carries social obligations: annual funding for community development and social programs, starting no later than 24 months after the mining licence is granted or 12 months after production begins, whichever comes first, plus an annual contribution to the Ministry of Natural Resources’ Training Centre for skills development.

The Project: Gold Near Mahdia

Eagle Mountain sits in west-central Guyana, roughly 200 kilometres south-southwest of Georgetown and about 8 kilometres from Mahdia, the hub town of Region 8 (Potaro-Siparuni). The area has been mined for over a century, and Mahdia remains the center of Guyana’s small and medium-scale gold sector.

The project’s resource base, from an April 2022 estimate prepared under prior ownership, stands at 1.18 million ounces of gold in the indicated category (31.1 million tonnes at 1.18 grams per tonne) plus 582,000 ounces inferred. Preparatory work has already started, DPI said, with construction targeted for the third quarter of 2027 and first production by end-2028, subject to environmental and regulatory approvals.

Mako is no newcomer. The Vancouver-based company, listed on the TSX Venture Exchange and Nasdaq with a market value of about C$1.2 billion (roughly US$0.9 billion), operates the high-grade San Albino gold mine in Nicaragua, bought the permitted Mt Hamilton project in Nevada in March 2026, and has worked in Guyana for more than a decade.

Why Gold Still Matters in an Oil Economy

Gold was Guyana’s biggest export before oil, and it remains the anchor of the non-oil economy. Declarations rose by about 50,000 ounces in 2025, and the sector earned close to US$1 billion in 2024 as large-scale producers restarted and expanded. The Rio Times reported this year that gold declarations reached about US$955 million in the first half of 2026 alone.

Eagle Mountain would join a short list of industrial-scale projects in a sector dominated by small miners — alongside G Mining Ventures’ Oko West, whose US$2.2 billion takeover by a Canadian major was approved by shareholders in June. For a government eager to show its economy is more than oil, a second world-class gold build carries symbolic and fiscal weight.

Region One Investment Adds Context

The same week illustrated the government’s broader interior push: on 9 September, Agriculture Minister Zulfikar Mustapha commissioned 230 million Guyana dollars (about US$1.1 million at 209 Guyana dollars per US dollar) in agriculture and waterway equipment for Region One (Barima-Waini), including a pontoon and two excavators, the Guyana Chronicle reported. The works target farm access and drainage in a region where rivers double as roads.

For foreign investors and expatriates watching Guyana, the pattern is the point: oil revenue is being parlayed into hard infrastructure and resource contracts across the interior, and the state is signing long-dated stability agreements to pull projects forward. Eagle Mountain’s approvals process — especially its environmental permit — is the next checkpoint to watch.

World.title: Milei Suspends London Trip as Falklands Confrontation Deepens
World.content:
Argentina · Diplomacy

Key Facts —The decision. President Javier Milei has suspended his planned trip to London on October 23–24, presidency sources confirmed to Clarín and TN on Thursday, September 10. —The agenda. The visit was to include a lecture at the University of Oxford and meetings with business leaders. —No official reason. Officials who confirmed the suspension did not give a reason; Argentine outlets uniformly place the decision in the context of the escalating confrontation with Britain over the Falklands/Malvinas. —The escalation. In one week, Argentina opened sanction proceedings against 45 entities over oil work near the islands, expanded the list to 60, and extended criminal complaints to name company executives personally. —London’s line. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament his government would be “relentless” in defending the islanders’ choice to remain British; his defence secretary called the commitment “absolute and unshakeable.”

Javier Milei has suspended his planned late-October trip to London — an Oxford lecture and meetings with business leaders — in the first concrete diplomatic cost of Argentina’s escalating confrontation with Britain over the Falklands/Malvinas.

President Javier Milei received with military honors at Quito’s Government Palace during an official visit to Ecuador on August 6. His planned late-October trip to London has been suspended. (Photo: Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Was Cancelled

The trip was set for October 23 and 24, according to Canal 26 and La Gaceta: a public lecture at the University of Oxford — a stage Milei favors for his free-market evangelism — and meetings with business leaders in London. It would have been the libertarian president’s most high-profile visit to Europe this semester.

The suspension became public on Thursday afternoon, when presidency sources confirmed to the newspaper Clarín and the news channel Todo Noticias that the visit was off, Infobae reported. The confirmation was notably thin: officials did not explain the decision, and the news agency EFE reported that its government sources gave no reasons.

The groundwork for retreat had been laid two days earlier. Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier told reporters on Tuesday: “I don’t have dates and I don’t have confirmation of the president’s trip to London, but I do know that it is a possibility” — language that, in hindsight, signalled the visit was already in doubt.

The Week That Sank the Trip

No Argentine official has said on record that the Falklands escalation caused the cancellation. But the sequence is hard to miss. Last Friday, the government announced sanction proceedings against 45 companies and individuals linked to hydrocarbon exploration around the islands, a list expanded to 60 within days. On Monday, it filed criminal complaints against companies holding UK-granted licenses in the North Malvinas Basin, including Navitas Petroleum and JHI Associates. On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said the complaints would name directors, managers and auditors personally.

Britain answered in kind, rhetorically. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons his government would be “relentless” in defending the Falkland Islanders’ right to choose to be British, Mercopress reported. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting posted that “the Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” calling the UK commitment “absolute and unshakeable.”

Against that backdrop, an Argentine president shaking hands in London while his government criminally charges British-linked executives had become untenable optics — in both capitals.

Milei’s New Malvinas Doctrine

The suspension caps a rhetorical transformation. Milei, who during his 2023 campaign praised Margaret Thatcher — the victor of the 1982 war — has this month made the sovereignty claim a centerpiece of his nationalism. In a prime-time address he declared the islands “indisputably” Argentine “by history and by right,” described the islanders as an “implanted population” without a right to self-determination, and warned that any further advance on the islands would be treated as a national security issue.

At the same time, he has kept one door open. “We will not renounce our sovereignty, nor will we seek a conflict with the United Kingdom,” he said — a formula that lets him escalate economic and legal pressure while ruling out confrontation. The cancelled London trip fits that pattern: pressure without rupture.

What the Suspension Signals

For foreign readers, the cancellation matters less as a scheduling change than as a measurement. Until now, the Milei-era thaw with Britain — trade talks, warmer rhetoric, a president openly aligned with Washington and its allies — had survived even his sovereignty speeches. The Oxford visit was to be its symbol. Its suspension is the first tangible diplomatic price either side has paid in the current round.

Neither London nor Oxford commented publicly on the cancellation as of Thursday night. Whether the trip is rescheduled — or quietly buried until after the oil-sanctions battle plays out — will indicate how far Milei intends to push the confrontation, and how much of the bilateral relationship he is willing to spend on it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Milei cancel his London trip?

No official reason was given. Presidency sources confirmed the suspension to Clarín and TN on September 10; Argentine media uniformly link it to the escalating confrontation with Britain over the Falklands/Malvinas, including new sanctions and criminal complaints against oil companies operating near the islands.

What was Milei going to do in London?

He was scheduled to travel on October 23–24 to give a lecture at the University of Oxford and meet business leaders, according to Argentine outlets Canal 26 and La Gaceta.

How has Britain responded to Argentina’s campaign?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament his government would be “relentless” in defending the islanders’ right to remain British, and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the UK commitment to the Falklands “absolute and unshakeable.”

World.title: Vinko Fodich: Chile Ex-Prosecutor Detained in Kidnapping Ring Probe
World.content:
CHILE · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The arrest Former prosecutor Vinko Fodich was detained on September 9, 2026, with three active PDI detectives and three others, in a kidnapping-for-ransom and money-laundering investigation.

— The accusation Criminal association, extortive kidnapping, extortion, breaches of the police’s organic law and asset laundering — investigated by the Fiscalía Supraterritorial, Chile’s organized-crime unit.

— The method A fake police facility and forged arrest warrants were allegedly used to abduct victims — especially Chinese nationals — and extort cash payments for their release.

— The assets Ex-Ante traced four properties with a combined fiscal valuation of 1 billion Chilean pesos (about US$1.08 million), including a Las Condes house valued at 641 million pesos (about US$692,000).

— The money trail Prosecutors suspect a currency-exchange house co-owned by Fodich laundered billions of pesos; courts authorized phone taps and bank-account reviews.

— The context Second blow to Chile’s prosecution service in 2026: former regional prosecutor Manuel Guerra has been in pretrial detention since March over the Caso Audios bribery scandal.

He spent nearly a decade putting criminals behind bars as one of Chile’s emblematic prosecutors. This week Vinko Fodich sat in a cell himself — accused of running with a kidnapping ring.

Vinko Fodich, one of the best-known prosecutors of his generation in Chile, was detained on Wednesday, September 9, in a case that reads like the plot of the crime dramas he once prosecuted: a criminal ring accused of kidnapping-for-ransom, with active police detectives among the seven people now under arrest.

What Happened This Week

The operation was run by the Fiscalía Supraterritorial, the Ministerio Público’s specialized unit for organized crime, together with the Policía de Investigaciones (PDI). Seven people were detained across the Santiago metropolitan region. Alongside Fodich, officers arrested three active PDI detectives — two of them assigned to the BICRIM robbery unit in La Pintana — plus Ángelo Stevens Aguilera, José Pinto Insunza, Exequiel Calderón Flores and Luis Moraga Parisi, a cousin of television economist and political commentator Franco Parisi.

The charges under investigation, as summarized by the prosecutor’s office and Chilean media: criminal association, secuestro extorsivo — kidnapping to extort ransom — extortion, breaches of the PDI’s organic law and money laundering. A court extended the detentions while the Fiscalía prepares the formalization hearing, at which charges will be formally presented.

According to reporting by The Clinic, the ring allegedly operated a fake police facility, complete with forged arrest warrants. Victims — especially Chinese citizens with businesses in Chile — were picked up in what looked like lawful operations, then held until cash payments bought their release or the supposed suspension of judicial action against them.

From Emblem Prosecutor to Suspect

Fodich, 47, spent almost ten years in the Ministerio Público and rose to head the local prosecutor’s office of Ñuñoa, Providencia and La Reina, covering Santiago’s affluent eastern districts. Chilean media profiled him for years as a “fiscal emblema” — an emblematic prosecutor associated with high-profile investigations. After leaving the institution he reinvented himself as a criminal defense lawyer and businessman.

It is that second career that now interests investigators. Fodich is a partner in a casa de cambio — a currency-exchange house — which prosecutors suspect was used to launder billions of pesos, in a scheme linked to Chinese business figures, according to T13 and Biobío Chile. Courts authorized interception of his phone calls and a review of his bank accounts months ago; the kidnapping investigation grew out of that money-laundering probe, which itself began inside the PDI, where investigators stumbled on detectives moonlighting for the ring.

The Property Web

Parallel reporting by Ex-Ante mapped Fodich’s asset structure: four properties with a combined fiscal valuation of about 1 billion Chilean pesos (about US$1.08 million), headlined by a house in Las Condes fiscally valued at 641 million pesos (about US$692,000). The same reporting documented outstanding debts of 108 million pesos (about US$117,000). Companies and corporate links are still being untangled by the Fiscalía, which suspects the exchange house sat at the center of the laundering operation. Conversions use the Banco Central’s dólar observado of 926 pesos per dollar on September 10, 2026.

Investigators emphasize that the map is not finished. The probe now runs on two tracks — the kidnapping ring and the laundering scheme — and prosecutors say both are still expanding.

A Prosecution Service in Crisis

The case lands on an institution already reeling. In March, former regional prosecutor Manuel Guerra was placed in pretrial detention over the Caso Audios, the influence-peddling scandal centered on lawyer Luis Hermosilla; Guerra faces charges of aggravated bribery, breach of secrecy and administrative prevarication. Two emblem prosecutors falling within six months has produced what Chilean television called a “strong tremor” in the justice system — and fresh questions about vetting, oversight and the revolving door between the prosecutor’s office and private defense work.

What It Means for Foreigners in Chile

For expats and foreign business owners, the uncomfortable detail is the victim profile: the ring allegedly targeted foreign nationals — chiefly Chinese merchants — precisely because newcomers are least equipped to tell a real arrest from a staged one. Chile remains one of Latin America’s safest countries by regional standards, but the case is a reminder that official-looking procedure is not proof of legality: real Chilean police identify themselves, warrants can be verified, and no legitimate authority collects cash for release.

The next milestone is the formalization hearing, expected in the coming days once the extended detention expires. If the Fiscalía’s account holds, Chile will be trying a man who once embodied its prosecution service — for the crimes he was meant to fight.

World.title: Uruguay Risks US Assistance over Cuba Medical Missions
World.content:
URUGUAY · POLITICS

Key Facts — The warning Washington has formally warned Montevideo over the Cuban medical brigade working in Uruguay since 2005; the weekly Búsqueda reports that Uruguay risks losing U.S. State Department “international assistance” if nothing changes.

— The brigade Twenty-one Cuban health professionals work at the Hospital de Ojos José Martí, the eye hospital in the former Saint Bois building, under a contract between Uruguay and Havana.

— The accusation The U.S. classifies Cuba’s overseas medical missions as state-sponsored forced labor and human trafficking — a designation Havana and host countries reject.

— The mechanism Uruguay now appears in U.S. trafficking-in-persons documentation over the brigade; a Tier 3 rating in the annual TIP report would let Washington suspend non-humanitarian assistance.

— The stakes U.S. aid to Uruguay is modest — roughly US$1.5 million a year, mostly military training — but the diplomatic cost for a small democracy could be far larger.

— The response Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin says no formal U.S. communication on this specific issue has arrived, while confirming Montevideo is in dialogue with Washington.

Twenty-one Cuban eye doctors in Montevideo have put South America’s most stable democracy on a collision course with Washington’s campaign against Havana’s medical diplomacy.

Cuba medical missions have operated in Uruguay without controversy for two decades. That ended this week: the weekly Búsqueda reported on September 10 that the United States has formally warned Uruguay that it risks losing State Department “international assistance” if it keeps hosting the Cuban medical brigade — the most direct pressure Washington has applied to Montevideo in years.

What Washington Told Montevideo

According to Búsqueda’s report by journalist Gabriel Pereyra, the U.S. warning was delivered in writing to Uruguay’s foreign ministry and defense ministry: if Uruguay does not end the contract with the Cuban brigade at the Hospital de Ojos — the eye hospital housed in the former Saint Bois hospital — the country will be treated as part of a group of states that facilitate forced labor, with consequences including the loss of State Department international assistance.

The U.S. embassy in Montevideo confirmed to local media that the letter was a warning, and that Uruguay has been included in State Department reporting on human-trafficking cases linked to Cuba’s medical missions. Búsqueda’s diplomatic sources were specific about the trigger: if nothing changes and Uruguay appears in the next edition of the annual Trafficking in Persons report in that context, the country would no longer be eligible for that assistance.

Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin publicly played down the letter. His ministry, he said, has received “no official communication from the United States” specifically on this issue — but he confirmed the matter is being discussed with Washington, and signaled Uruguay wants to preserve what it sees as the program’s positive results within a negotiated framework.

A Small Brigade with a Long History

The program at the center of the dispute is modest. Twenty-one Cuban medical professionals currently work in Uruguay, according to a State Department country table published on August 21, 2026 — a number matched by independent monitoring of Cuban brigades. They staff the ophthalmology program at the Hospital de Ojos José Martí, which has provided free eye surgery to Uruguayans since 2005 and marked its 50,000th free operation in recent years, according to the Uruguayan presidency.

Under the arrangement, Uruguay contracts the brigade with the Cuban state rather than hiring the doctors individually — precisely the structure Washington condemns. The U.S. argues that Cuba’s medical export program amounts to forced labor: the government in Havana pockets most of the payment, doctors’ passports and movements are controlled, and defectors face retaliation. Cuba and the host governments call it South-South cooperation that delivers care to people who would otherwise go without.

Cuba Medical Missions Under U.S. Pressure

Uruguay is the latest stop in a systematic U.S. campaign against Cuba medical missions. On February 25, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio expanded visa restrictions to target foreign officials involved in Cuba’s “labor export program,” explicitly including overseas medical missions. Restrictions on Central American officials followed in June 2025, and on officials from African states, Cuba and Grenada in August 2025.

The campaign is working on the numbers Washington cares about. The State Department’s August 2026 report on the “coerced and trafficked labor” of Cuban medical professionals counts 15,000 to 18,000 Cuban medical workers in 51 countries in 2026 — down from 24,000 in more than 58 countries at the start of 2025, a decline the department attributes to its own diplomacy. The same document lists Uruguay, with its 21 doctors, among the remaining holdouts.

What Is Actually at Stake

The financial exposure is small but real. U.S. foreign assistance to Uruguay runs to roughly US$1.5 million a year, concentrated in military training and security cooperation rather than development aid. The Trafficking Victims Protection Act allows Washington to suspend non-humanitarian, non-trade assistance to countries rated Tier 3 in the TIP report — a rating Uruguay, currently Tier 2, does not hold. Between here and there lie intermediate steps: a watch-list downgrade, the Cuba-missions listing Uruguay already carries, and the suspension of military advice, training and equipment that Uruguayan media describe as the letter’s concrete threat.

For President Yamandú Orsi’s left-of-center government, the dilemma is political more than financial. Ending a twenty-year program that provides free cataract surgery to poor Uruguayans — under open U.S. pressure — is domestically costly. Keeping it carries a different price: a formal trafficking stigma from Uruguay’s most powerful partner.

What It Means for Foreigners in Uruguay

For the expat community, nothing practical changes this week: the eye hospital keeps operating, and no U.S. program affecting residents or travelers is in question. What the dispute signals is structural. Uruguay has built its brand — and much of its appeal to foreign residents — on being the region’s rule-of-law outlier. A trafficking-report downgrade would strike directly at that reputation, and at the visa, investment and security relationships that rest on it.

Montevideo is simultaneously investing in the opposite kind of headline: as The Rio Times reported this week, Uruguay is paying airlines US$20 for every additional tourist they bring in. The next milestone in the Cuba medical missions dispute is the 2027 edition of the TIP report, typically published mid-year. Until then, expect quiet negotiation rather than public rupture: Montevideo has every incentive to restructure the program rather than cancel it — and Washington has already shown it counts partial withdrawals as victories.

World.content:

LIFE & CULTURE · RIO DE JANEIRO, 11 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —Date — Réveillon Copacabana 2027 happens on the night of 31 December 2026 into 1 January 2027, along four kilometres of Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. —Scale — Around two million people attend in a typical year; Guinness World Records recognizes Copacabana as the world’s biggest New Year’s Eve party. —Fireworks — A display of more than ten minutes is launched from barges anchored offshore at midnight, synchronized with music along the beach. —Music — Multiple stages with free concerts run from early evening until after midnight, mixing Brazilian headliners across samba, pop and gospel. —Tradition — Dress in white for good luck; at midnight many wade into the surf to offer flowers to Iemanjá, the sea goddess. —Cost — The beach party, concerts and fireworks are entirely free; paid alternatives are hotel rooftop parties and boat cruises. —Logistics — The Metro runs a special all-night operation with pre-bought cards; road closures around Copacabana begin in the afternoon of the 31st.

Réveillon Copacabana 2027, on the night of December 31, 2026, is the biggest New Year’s Eve party on Earth — two million people in white on four kilometres of sand, free concerts on multiple stages, and fireworks fired from barges over the Atlantic. This guide covers the program, the traditions, transport, safety and where to watch if you want to skip the deepest crowds.

Réveillon Copacabana 2027: how the night works

The celebration builds through the evening of 31 December. Concert stages along the beach — traditionally near the Copacabana Palace hotel and further toward Leme — start live music around 20:00, with the biggest acts playing the countdown slot.

At midnight, fireworks launch from barges anchored offshore for a display of more than ten minutes, reflected across the bay and synchronized to music. The crowd count in typical years reaches around two million people, a scale recognized by Guinness World Records as the world’s biggest New Year’s Eve party.

Everything on the sand is free — entry, concerts and fireworks. The night’s full line-up is announced by the city in December; expect a mix of samba, Brazilian pop and gospel across the stages, continuing Rio’s evolution of the event into a city-sized countdown machine.

The traditions: white clothes, flowers and the sea

Wearing white is the near-universal dress code, a tradition rooted in Afro-Brazilian religiosidade and believed to bring peace for the year ahead. Accents carry meanings: yellow for money, red for love, green for health.

At midnight, thousands wade into the surf to jump seven waves and toss white flowers to Iemanjá, the goddess of the sea, making wishes for the new year. Small candles and flower boats line the waterline — a ritual that predates the modern mega-party by generations.

Vendors sell flowers, candles and sparkling wine along the promenade, but prices inflate as midnight approaches; locals buy earlier in the day from supermarkets and street markets away from the beachfront.

Getting there: metro, road closures and the way home

Rio’s Metro runs a special Réveillon operation: trains run through the night, but entry requires a pre-purchased special card, sold in the days before the 31st. Stations closest to the beach — Cardeal Arcoverde, Siqueira Campos and Cantagalo — are the main gateways.

Road closures around Copacabana begin in the afternoon, and ride-hailing is heavily restricted near the beach after midnight — the established pattern of New Year’s Eve vehicle restrictions gets stricter every year. Walking back toward Botafogo or Ipanema before hailing a ride saves an hour or more.

Security is massive and layered: thousands of police, checkpoints on the access streets, drone patrols and observation towers along the waterfront, an operation Rio has refined over years of drone patrols and waterfront checkpoints. Bags are checked at entry points; glass bottles are banned on the sand.

Where to watch: from the deep crowd to a rooftop

The densest crowd packs the stretch between Posto 3 and Posto 5 near the main stage. For more space, head toward Leme at the beach’s eastern end or Posto 6 toward Ipanema, where the fireworks are equally visible and the crush far thinner.

Paid alternatives sell out months ahead: rooftop parties at the Copacabana Palace and neighboring hotels, and boat cruises that watch the fireworks from the water at a fraction of the stress. Expect prices from several hundred reais for simple cruises to several thousand for premium hotel packages.

Copacabana is not the only option — Flamengo, Ipanema and Barra da Tijuca stage smaller fireworks and parties — but the main event remains the world’s reference. Follow our Brazil coverage through December for the confirmed line-up and transport plan.

Practical tips: weather, money and what to bring

Late December is full Rio summer: expect 28-35°C with high humidity and possible tropical showers. Bring water, sunscreen for the afternoon, and a light cover for the sea breeze after midnight; the sand stays crowded until roughly 02:00.

Carry minimal valuables — a phone, one card and small cash in a front pocket or money belt. ATMs near the beach run dry or face long lines; vendors accept cards and PIX widely, but connectivity can buckle under two million devices.

Agree on a meeting point with your group before the countdown — mobile networks often saturate at midnight. The promenade’s numbered lifeguard posts (postos) are the easiest landmarks for regrouping.

Réveillon Copacabana 2027 — Night at a Glance When: Night of 31 December 2026 into 1 January 2027, Copacabana Beach, Rio de Janeiro. Program: Free concerts on multiple stages from ~20:00; fireworks from offshore barges at midnight, 10+ minutes. Crowd: Around two million expected — the world’s biggest New Year’s Eve party per Guinness. Dress code: White for luck; flowers for Iemanjá at the waterline. Transport: Special all-night Metro operation with pre-bought cards; road closures from the afternoon; no glass bottles on the sand. Line-up and transport details are confirmed by the city in December; verify before travel.

This is reporting, not travel or safety advice. Conditions vary by year and individual circumstance. Confirm current arrangements with official sources before making plans.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Réveillon Copacabana 2027? Réveillon Copacabana 2027 takes place on the night of 31 December 2026 into 1 January 2027, along four kilometres of Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. Free concerts start around 20:00, and fireworks launch from barges offshore at midnight.

Is Réveillon Copacabana free? Yes — entry to the beach, the concerts and the fireworks is completely free. Paid alternatives include hotel rooftop parties and boat cruises that watch the display from the water; these sell out months in advance.

Why does everyone wear white on New Year’s Eve in Rio? White is a tradition rooted in Afro-Brazilian spirituality, believed to bring peace for the coming year. Color accents carry wishes — yellow for money, red for love, green for health. At midnight, many jump seven waves and offer white flowers to Iemanjá, goddess of the sea.

How do I get to Copacabana on New Year’s Eve? The Metro runs a special all-night service, but entry requires a pre-purchased special card sold in the days before December 31. The nearest stations are Cardeal Arcoverde, Siqueira Campos and Cantagalo. Roads around Copacabana close in the afternoon and ride-hailing is restricted after midnight.

Is Réveillon Copacabana safe? The city deploys thousands of police, bag checkpoints, drone patrols and towers along the waterfront, and the event is generally orderly for its size. Standard big-crowd rules apply: carry minimal valuables, agree on a meeting point before midnight, and use the numbered lifeguard posts as landmarks.

World.title: Los Tiguerones Designated Terrorists as Ecuador Escalates Security Buildup
World.content:
Ecuador · Security

Key Facts —The designation. The United States designated the Ecuadorian gang Los Tiguerones as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and Specially Designated Global Terrorist on September 9, announced by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Quito. —The money. Rubio said he will seek US$45 million in security funding for Ecuador, as the designation tightens the financial and legal encirclement of the gang. —The council. President Daniel Noboa chaired a meeting of the Public and State Security Council (Cosepe) at Carondelet Palace on September 10; its decisions are classified, but the government says new security actions are being activated nationwide. —The police upgrade. The anti-kidnapping unit Unase has become the Dinae, a full investigations directorate with more staff and budget; in its first week it reported 25 operations, 60 arrests and US$610,018 kept out of kidnappers’ hands.

Ecuador’s security escalation now runs on three tracks at once: a US terrorist designation that tightens the legal and financial noose around Los Tiguerones, a classified security council chaired by President Noboa, and a rebuilt anti-kidnapping police directorate that is already producing numbers.
