Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The candidate of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), one of Poland’s main political groups, has been disqualified from Kraków’s mayoral election after over 2,000 of the signatures from local residents collected in support of his candidacy were found to be invalid. One of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, admitted that the situation was an “embarrassment” and “catastrophe”. He responded by dismissing the candidate, Bartosz Bocheńczak, as head of his party’s local structures in Kraków and launching an investigation into how the blunder occurred. Podobnie jak i wielu naszych działaczy, wolontariuszy, sympatyków i wyborców, czuję się bardzo zawiedziony brakiem rejestracji kandydatury Bartosza Bocheńczaka w Krakowie. Przyczyną braku rejestracji było to, że spośród około 5000 zebranych podpisów, ponad 2000 były błędnych.… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) September 7, 2026 Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, is holding a mayoral election this month after the previous incumbent, Aleksander Miszalski, was removed mid-term in a rare recall referendum earlier this year. Over a dozen potential candidates announced plans to stand. But, in order to be registered, they had to collect at least 3,000 signatures from residents of the city supporting their candidacy, then submit them to the municipal electoral commission by 3 September. Twelve candidates made such submissions, after which the commission began assessing all signatures to ensure that each candidate had at least 3,000 that were valid. On Monday, reports began to emerge that, although Bocheńczak had submitted just over 4,600 signatures, the commission had found that fewer than 3,000 of them were valid. That evening, the candidate himself confirmed the news. Mentzen, who is leader of the far-right libertarian New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one half of Confederation, revealed that over 2,000 signatories had listed their address as their place of residence rather than where they are officially registered as living. In Poland, it is common for people to live somewhere different from where they are officially registered. That is particularly the case for young people, who are often registered at their parents’ address while residing elsewhere. Confederation is particularly popular among young people, and Kraków has a large student population. Moja kandydatura na Prezydenta Krakowa nie została zarejestrowana. Zabrakło ważnych podpisów. Nie będę snuł teorii spiskowych, szukał winnych ani przerzucał odpowiedzialności na kogokolwiek. Uważałem, że złożenie niemal 5000 podpisów zapewni nam wystarczający margines… — Bartosz Bocheńczak (@BBochenczak) September 7, 2026 Mentzen said that the regulations regarding collecting signatures for candidates are “absurd”, yet admitted that Bocheńczak’s campaign should have done a better job of complying with the rules. There must now be “consequences from this embarrassment”, said Mentzen, who announced that Bocheńczak had been dismissed as New Hope’s local leader in Kraków and that a party commission would “determine responsibility for this disaster”. Confederation also faced scrutiny last year when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected its financial report for the 2024 European elections after it found irregularities. The party also failed to submit the required documents on time. As a result, it lost access to state subsidies. The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by the far-right Confederation against the electoral commission's decision to reject its financial report for last year's European elections due to irregularities. The group will now lose access to state subsidies https://t.co/hNGu2Zvzii — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Bocheńczak is not the only candidate who has struggled with collecting signatures. Last week, just days before the deadline, it emerged that over 3,000 signatures collected in support of the favourite in the elections, Łukasz Gibała, an independent, were invalid because the word “Kraków” was missing from the form. Gibała – a perennial candidate in mayoral elections who finished runner-up to Miszalski in 2024 – quickly scrambled to collect more signatures, and his team managed to gather an additional 9,000 in three days. On Monday this week, it also emerged that three other independent candidates, Marian Banaś, Stanisław Kułach and Marta Ratuszyńska, had failed to gather enough signatures. All three have taken up their right to appeal against the commission’s decision to reject their candidacies. Dziś złożymy dodatkowe podpisy do komisji wyborczej – ponad 9 tysięcy (oprócz wcześniejszych 5,5 tys.). Skala Waszego zaangażowania i pomocy była bezprecedensowa – w 3 dni zebraliśmy więcej podpisów niż którykolwiek z naszych rywali przez 3 tygodnie 💪 Bardzo Wam dziękuję i… — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) September 3, 2026 Six candidates have so far been accepted, including Gibała; Monika Piątkowska, who is supported by the centrist Civil Coalition (KO) and Polish People’s Party (PSL); Michał Drewnicki of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS); Aleksandra Owca of the left-wing Together (Razem); and Michał Klimek of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Two candidates, Daria Gosek-Popiołek of The Left (Lewica) and Sławomir Pietrzyk of Social Democracy of Poland (Socjaldemokracja Polska), are still awaiting confirmation from the electoral commission that they submitted enough valid signatures. A decision is due to be announced today. The first round of the election will take place on Sunday 27 September. If any candidate receives over 50% of the vote, they will become mayor. If not, a run-off between the top two candidates will take place on 11 October. There has been little polling on support for candidates, but one survey by the Opinia24 agency for Polityka Insight two weeks ago showed Gibała with 25.2%, ahead of Piątkowska (15.3%) and Gosek-Popiołek (8.7%). Bocheńczak was in sixth with just 3.2%. Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland urges EU to deny asylum to migrants who violently cross its borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: September 28 Holiday in Czechia: What Will Be Open and Closed
World.content:
Czech Statehood Day falls on Monday, September 28, giving people across Czechia a three-day weekend. But anyone planning to shop should be aware that many large stores will be required to close.

The public holiday commemorates Saint Wenceslas, the patron saint of the Czech lands and one of the most important figures in Czech history. September 28 has been observed as Czech Statehood Day since 2000 and is a statutory day off.



For shoppers, however, the key issue is the country’s restrictions on retail opening hours.

Which shops will be closed on September 28

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square metres must close on September 28.

This means most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centres will not be able to operate as normal.

The restriction does not apply to all businesses. Smaller shops with a sales area of up to 200 square metres can remain open, although individual owners decide whether to operate during the holiday.

Some types of businesses are also exempt from the restrictions. These include pharmacies, petrol stations and shops located at airports and major railway stations.

Restaurants, cafés and most other services are not covered by the retail law and can therefore open according to their normal schedules or the decision of their operators.

People planning to use smaller independent shops should still check opening hours in advance. Many owners choose to close during public holidays, particularly when the holiday creates a long weekend.

Why is September 28 a public holiday

Czech Statehood Day is linked to Saint Wenceslas, the medieval ruler who became the patron saint of the Czech lands.

Wenceslas was the son of Duke Vratislav I and Drahomíra. His grandmother, Ludmila, who was later canonised, played a major role in his upbringing and is traditionally credited with influencing his Christian education.

Wenceslas is believed to have been killed in Stará Boleslav on September 28, either in 929 or 935, depending on the historical source.

His death turned him into a martyr and helped establish his lasting importance in Czech religious and national traditions.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague by Saffa Maso Bistro
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can can buy a basic ticket or a ticket with a braai package, which includes traditional South African boerewors sausage (500g) and a portion of biltong (150g).

On-site you’ll also find original Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices, and more for sale.

World.title: Dominik Szoboszlai interview with Steven Gerrard: leadership, new head coach, and preferred position on the pitch
World.content:
Liverpool and Hungary midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai has opened up about his new five-year contract, his preferred position, growing leadership role and first impressions of new head coach Andoni Iraola in an exclusive interview with club legend Steven Gerrard for TNT Sports.

Szoboszlai wants to keep improving

The Hungarian captain has committed his long-term future to Liverpool, saying he wanted to make clear how much the club means to him. “I always want to be better than I was in the previous season,” Szoboszlai said. Despite scoring and assisting in double figures last season, he insists there is still room for improvement.

“I want to be even better,” he added, although he declined to reveal any specific targets for goals or assists.

His favourite position is in midfield

Szoboszlai has played in several positions since arriving at Anfield, including right-back, but made it clear where he feels most comfortable.

“Eight or ten,” he said when Gerrard asked where he would place him to cause the most danger. The midfielder particularly enjoys the box-to-box role, where he can help build attacks, play long passes, arrive in the penalty area and shoot from distance. He also revealed that Iraola has already told him he will not be used as a regular right-back.

“If he needs me in that position, of course I am available,” Szoboszlai said, while admitting that the right-sided number seven role is the position he likes least. That led to a humorous exchange with Gerrard. Asked whether the two could have played together, Szoboszlai jokingly said he would take the number 10 role, while Gerrard would have to play at number two – right-back. Ironically, the Liverpool legend started his first team career as a right-back, then moved to the centre of the midfield.

Growing into a Liverpool leader

Now entering his fourth season at Liverpool, Szoboszlai has become one of the squad’s more experienced players and has taken on a greater leadership role. He explained that he does not necessarily see himself as the loudest voice in the dressing room, with players such as Virgil van Dijk, Joe Gomez and Alisson Becker more naturally suited to that role. Instead, Szoboszlai wants to lead through his performances.

“I try to give my best every day, in every match and every training session,” he said.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Szoboszlai welcomes Iraola’s intensity

The Hungarian is also enthusiastic about Iraola’s football philosophy, describing the new manager’s approach as direct and intense. Szoboszlai had spoken to fellow Hungarian Milos Kerkez, who worked with Iraola at Bournemouth, about what to expect.

“I want us not to be afraid of anyone,” Szoboszlai said. “They should be paying much more attention to what we are doing.” He also highlighted his appreciation for combination football and praised the quality and versatility of Liverpool’s midfielders, singling out Alexis Mac Allister as the player who performs most consistently in training.

Tricky questions at the end

Finally, Gerrard tested Szoboszlai’s confidence by asking whether he would beat Van Dijk in a one-on-one duel. “Yes,” came the immediate answer, but Gerrard was unconvinced. Szoboszlai simply replied: “He is sure of it too…”

For the Hungarian midfielder, however, the message behind the jokes is serious: he believes Liverpool have the quality, intensity and ambition to achieve something special.

World.title: Shocking warning by demographer: Hungary could have just 5 million people by 2100
World.content:
Hungary’s population could fall to just 5.2 million by the end of the century, with the country facing an increasingly ageing population that may be unable to reverse the decades-long decline, according to demographer Pál Péter Tóth.

Hungary’s population could shrink to around 5.2 million by 2100, according to a demographic forecast presented at the 64th Hungarian Economic Association’s Annual Meeting in Eger.

Demographer Pál Péter Tóth said the projected population would also be considerably older and less economically active than today. He argued that Hungary’s population decline, which has been ongoing since 1980, has reached a point where simply increasing the number of births would not be enough to reverse the trend.

Tóth made the comments during a session examining Hungary’s demographic challenges.

Population decline could become irreversible

According to the demographer, Hungary could face a demographic crisis by 2100 from which it would be extremely difficult to recover. He said the projected population of 5.2 million would be predominantly elderly, with relatively few people of working age and fewer women able to have children.

Such an age structure would make it increasingly difficult for Hungary to maintain its population naturally, Tóth argued.

He also cited estimates suggesting that the number of Roma people in Hungary could rise from around 800,000 today to approximately 1.5 million by 2100, meaning that a significant share of the country’s much smaller future population could belong to the Roma community.

Tóth argued that stopping population decline should be the most important task of any Hungarian government, with policies aimed both at encouraging people to have children and at reducing mortality.

He also criticised the exclusion of migration from what he described as the three main components of population change: births, deaths and migration.

Migration, he said, has been part of Hungarian history throughout the centuries and should not simply be left out of the demographic equation. Tóth concluded his presentation with a blunt assessment of Hungary’s family policies:

“They thought that if they gave families money, there would be children. But they gave families money, and there were no children.”

Are family policies actually increasing births?

Sociologist József Benda focused on what he called the “demographic paradox”, arguing that families and the economy are effectively competing for the same resources. In his view, modern societies have increasingly prioritised immediate production and consumption over investing in raising the next generation.

Benda pointed to a relationship between women’s participation in the labour market and falling birth rates. He noted that periods when female employment rose significantly — including the 1970s and the past decade — also coincided with declines in the number of children being born.

At the same time, he stressed that Hungary’s falling fertility rate fits into a broader trend seen across Eastern Europe.

Benda called for a change in approach. While the previous Hungarian government placed strong emphasis on supporting families over the past decade, he argued that many of its measures were primarily designed to facilitate women’s participation in the labour market rather than directly increase the number of children being born.

He identified measures such as childcare support and the Babaváró loan, a state-backed family loan, as examples of policies more directly linked to encouraging childbearing.

If you missed it: Hungary population decline continues: country loses tens of thousands of people in 6 months

Hungary’s society is becoming less child-friendly

Journalist Anita Élő, a board member of the Hungarian Economic Association’s Demographic Section, argued that Hungary is increasingly not a family-friendly society. She pointed to the growing number of child-free services and businesses, including travel agencies targeting people who do not want to travel with children, as well as childfree hotels and restaurants.

According to Élő, social attitudes towards having children are changing rapidly, and neither governments nor demographers can reverse this trend on their own. She also highlighted the growing number of young people who consciously decide not to have children, arguing that ultimately only they can change that decision.

Élő was also the only speaker during the session to mention climate anxiety as a factor that could discourage people from having children.

The generation at the centre of the issue was missing

The discussion itself came under criticism for being somewhat “old-fashioned”, as the generation currently making decisions about whether to have children was largely absent from the panel, 444.hu writes.

The role of men in family life, having children and raising them was also not discussed in detail.

Instead, the session included examples of foreign workers being brought into Hungary to work as nannies.

World.title: Has one of the weakest candidates been installed at the helm of the all-but-omnipotent National Asset Recovery and Protection Office?
World.content:
Ákos Hadházy has received the applications for the presidency of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) and believes that Anna Unger, the candidate elected to the post, would not have placed even in the top 60 under a genuine scoring system. Meanwhile, one of the Tisza Party’s deputy speakers has said there was indeed a scoring process – just not as one would expect in a serious job competition.

She should not have been called for interview

Ákos Hadházy has disclosed further details on the selection of the leadership of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH). The former MP claims he obtained the full list of applications for the posts of president and deputy president, together with the applicants’ professional CV data, and on this basis finds it hard to explain how Anna Unger reached the second round of the selection process.

According to Hadházy, the field included numerous candidates with substantial professional backgrounds, appropriate qualifications and managerial experience. In his view, under an objective evaluation system based on these criteria, Ms Unger “would not have made it into the top three – not even into the top 60”. He concludes from this that the selection committee cannot have properly reviewed a significant proportion of the applications.

Contorted scoring for one of the most important offices

At the heart of the dispute lies the much-discussed points system. The parliamentary call for applications stated that the three candidates with the highest scores were to be invited for personal interviews. Anikó Hallerné Nagy, a deputy speaker of parliament, later said, however, that no detailed, quantifiable objective system had existed. According to 444, the decision on who would be called for interview was ultimately taken by a simple committee vote on a 1–3 scale. Those who received a “yes” were awarded three points – and, as it happens, there were exactly three such candidates.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Hadházy regards this as particularly problematic because, in his view, such a procedure fundamentally undermines confidence in the independence of the NVVH’s leadership. If the office takes action against a politician, the person concerned can cry political motivation; if it does not open or closes a case, the public may suspect a political deal behind it.

Hadházy Ákos, running as an independent candidate, received 16.12% (10,207 votes) in Budapest’s 6th constituency, finishing third behind Velkey György László (TISZA) and Radics Béla (Fidesz–KDNP). Photo: Facebook / Hadházy Ákos

Politically unsuitable candidates?

The politician also argues that creating the appearance of an open competition could backfire: in his view it would have been cleaner had the prime minister simply named a candidate, rather than presenting what looks like a preordained selection as a public contest.

According to Anikó Hallerné Nagy, it was not possible to express in points the political risks that would have arisen had someone been appointed to head the office who was later found to have ties to the NER.

If you missed: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes

Hadházy also raised objections to the applications for the deputy presidency. He claims that 39 people applied for the public-finance post, yet no decision was taken – for which, he says, it is hard to find any explanation other than that no politically suitable candidate could be found. He added, however, that he considers it possible that Anna Unger will prove a good president and independent of the government.

The NVVH’s remit will be, on the one hand, the protection of public assets and, on the other, the conduct of investigations into circumstances in which public assets have passed into private ownership in ways giving rise to suspicion of abuse. In practice, the NVVH will function as a detached prosecutorial body, with wide-ranging powers to carry out investigations (including with the involvement of other authorities), freeze assets, and even propose the appointment of state supervisors to private companies in matters involving public assets.

World.title: Budapest Airport air cargo traffic plunges on EU tariffs – and further difficulties may lie ahead
World.content:
Budapest Airport has suffered a sharp fall in direct cargo capacity from China and Hong Kong. According to analysis by Rotate, capacity between 1 and 21 August dropped by 58 per cent compared with June levels, before the European Union’s new tariff regime came into force.

The collapse at Budapest Airport stands out even by European standards. Frankfurt recorded a 16 per cent decline, Amsterdam 28 per cent and Liège 35 per cent. By contrast, Cologne/Bonn increased capacity by 25 per cent and London Stansted by 37 per cent.

The figures underscore the risks when a cargo hub’s growth becomes overly reliant on a single market. Budapest Airport has built up substantial Chinese air freight traffic in recent years, leaving it particularly exposed to shifts in that trade, Budflyer wrote.

BUD Cargo City, Budapest, Hungary. Photo: facebook.com/budapestairport

The coming months could prove decisive. Should the downturn prove persistent, Budapest’s cargo operations may face serious challenges. Moreover, following the introduction of a €3 tariff in July, an additional EU handling fee could be imposed on affected shipments from November. The European Commission will determine the exact amount.

World.title: Central bank chief on the scenario for introducing the Hungarian euro
World.content:
Hungary’s central bank governor has spoken of the pitfalls of euro adoption: this, he says, is how a Hungarian euro can be made to work.

Only one criterion met

The president of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank emphasised that the aim is not a swift, but a successful euro introduction. In his view, three things are needed for this: societal support, a coordinated strategy and a prepared real economy, index.hu writes.

Public backing is already in place: among countries on the verge of adopting the euro, Hungary has the highest proportion of supporters, with roughly four in five Hungarians favouring the single currency. At the same time, an equally large share believe the country is not yet economically ready for it.

The figures so far bear out this caution. According to Mihály Varga, Hungary currently meets just one accession criterion – the inflation reference value. This has, however, already improved the country’s standing in financial markets, while over the past year and a half the forint has become one of the world’s best-performing emerging-market currencies.

Risk from energy dependence and sluggish growth

Hungarian economic cycles move closely in step with those of the eurozone, which is a favourable sign. A more serious risk, however, is inflation: because of the greater energy dependence of central and eastern European countries, prices can more easily diverge from trends seen in the euro area.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

There is also work to be done on catching up. Between 2020 and 2025, Hungary grew by an average of 1.2 per cent a year, while several neighbouring countries expanded more quickly.

On the basis of Mr Varga’s message, then, adopting the euro has again become a more realistic political goal, but actual accession is not yet close. Societal support is strong, certain economic indicators are improving, but significant economic-policy work is still required to meet the necessary convergence criteria.

The European Commission has broken its silence: the Hungarian euro remains light-years away — can Péter Magyar’s plan succeed?

This is what the “Hungarian euro” looks like

As we reported last year, the first Hungarian euro coin is available for purchase on Vatera, and its price was not excessively high at the time. The obverse features King Matthias and Queen Beatrix, while the reverse shows the Phoenix, one of the largest sailing vessels on Lake Balaton, which sailed on the “Hungarian sea” in the ownership of the Festetics family, founders of the Georgikon in Keszthely. Why these particular images appear on the front and back, and why this coin was produced in the first place, can be read in our article.

World.title: PM Magyar’s stern message to Ukraine: no EU accession without progress
World.content:
Ukraine must take concrete steps to secure the rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia before further EU accession clusters can be opened, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told a doorstep press briefing in Bratislava on Thursday.

PM Magyar insists performance-based accession

He said political agreement was reached in June between the Hungarian and Ukrainian governments on the educational, cultural, linguistic and administrative rights of the Transcarpathian Hungarians, but the promised concrete measures had yet to be implemented.

Magyar said the Tisza Party had supported the opening of the first and sixth clusters, but further chapters should only be opened on a performance-based accession.

Péter Magyar and Volodimir Zelensky at the EU Summit on 18 June 2026. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

The prime minister cited Serbia, which started its accession process 12 years ago, yet only two of the six clusters have been opened for it, and noted that nearly 300,000 Hungarians live in Serbia, many of whom commute to Hungary for work or study, often queuing for hours at the Schengen border.

“For this reason … and out of honesty, it isn’t fair that everyone is now demanding that we open clusters for Ukraine, when there has been no progress in the negotiations on the first and sixth clusters.” Magyar said it would be unfair if Ukraine advanced faster in EU accession than candidates that had been fulfilling the conditions for many years. “This is a very long process, and it is by no means certain that it will be successful in the end,” he said.

No progress yet on Slovakia’s Benes Decrees

Magyar said that no progress had been made yet on disputed issues between Hungary and Slovakia such as the confiscation of land without compensation, the threat of imprisonment for expressing opinions, or the Benes Decrees, adding, however, that he was confident this would happen soon.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava after a meeting of Visegrad Four prime ministers and their Irish counterpart, Magyar said he and Slovak PM Robert Fico had previously agreed, and reaffirmed on Thursday, that these issues needed to be prepared at an expert level, but this had not yet happened. “I am confident that, as with any Slovak prime minister, it is in the interest of the Slovak prime minister to find solutions to these issues,” Magyar said.

He added it was clear that progress at the bilateral level could not be made until there was movement on at least the confiscation of land without compensation or the threat of imprisonment for expressing opinions. Last year, Slovakia passed a law that criminalises criticism of the Benes Decrees with up to six months in prison.

If you missed: Hungarian government to fight for annulment of Benes decrees

Potential in central European cooperation greater than current reality

There is greater potential in strengthening cooperation between central European countries than has been exploited so far, Prime Minister Peter Magyar told MTI on Thursday in a press briefing in Bratislava. Speaking about the economic and trade success indicators of Visegrad Four (V4) cooperation, Magyar said he could not specify a concrete target figure for trade growth, but he was interested in growth.

He highlighted the development of north-south transport links, such as the Warsaw-Prague-Bratislava-Budapest high-speed rail project, which could also extend to Vienna, as well as cooperation opportunities in energy, the defence industry, digitalisation, health care, agriculture and the food industry. Magyar said the V4 countries could form the basis of a strong central Europe, to which other countries, including Austria, Romania and the Balkan states, could later join.

World.title: Breaking – Magyar names Tisza’s five Constitutional Court nominees
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar, leader of the Tisza Party, on Thursday announced his party’s five nominees for the Constitutional Court on Facebook.

Magyar named his five Constitutional Court candidates

The nominees are Nóra Chronowski, a university professor, doctor of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and constitutional lawyer; Miklós Ligeti, an ombudsman, criminal lawyer and legal director of Transparency International Hungary; András György Kovács, a Kúria (supreme court) council chair judge and administrative lawyer with a PhD; Árpád Gábor Orosz, former head of the Kúria’s Civil College, a council chair judge, civil lawyer and European legal expert who has taught at the University of Szeged since 1993; and Zsolt Szomora, deputy director of the Institute of Criminal Sciences at the University of Szeged’s Faculty of Law and Public Administration and a habilitated university professor.

Magyar said the nominees’ committee hearings would be held on Monday, and parliament would elect the five new Constitutional Court judges on Tuesday morning.

The Prime Minister added that, true to the Tisza party’s pledge, he would propose Constitutional Court nominees who meet not only the requirements of the Fundamental Law but every professional criterion.He added that over recent weeks the government had held extensive consultations with a number of outstanding jurists, weighing considerations of irreproachability, integrity, independence and genuine professional achievement.Care had also been taken, he wrote, to ensure that the candidates would cover all branches of law: constitutional law, criminal law, administrative law, civil law and fundamental rights.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Background to the vacancies

The mandates of four Constitutional Court judges – among them Péter Polt, the Court’s president – expired on 1 September, after the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, adopted in July, stipulated that “the mandate of a member of the Constitutional Court shall terminate upon reaching the age of 70”.In addition to Mr Polt, this age limit had already been reached by Mária Haszonicsné Ádám, Miklós Juhász and Zoltán Lomnici.

Under the law, the National Assembly has 60 days to elect new Constitutional Court judges to replace those who have left. Parliament elects the new judges by secret ballot, requiring a two-thirds majority of MPs, for nine-year terms. The 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law reduced the length of judges’ mandates from 12 years to nine.

Further changes at the Court

Ágnes Czine, the Court’s vice-president, will see her 12-year mandate as a Constitutional Court judge expire in November.

One judge, Csaba Hende – a former MDF and later Fidesz MP and defence minister – had already left the 15-member body in July, as a result of the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law and the rules of the Constitutional Court Act. In his place, Parliament elected Pál Sonnevend, a university professor and former dean who heads a department at ELTE’s Faculty of Law, as a Constitutional Court judge.

World.title: Hungary shouldn’t be paying EUR 1 m daily to protect Europe’s borders, says PM Magyar
World.content:
It is “not right” that Hungary is paying 1 million euros a day to protect Europe’s common borders, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said at the meeting of Visegrád Four prime ministers and their Irish counterpart in Bratislava on Thursday.

PM Magyar: not a good message from the EU

Magyar said at a press conference in Pozsony/Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia, that he did not want to “bash Brussels”, but it was “unfair” that Hungary was paying daily to protect both its own and the European Union’s borders. “This is not right at all. It is not a good message,” he said, thanking the Czech prime minister for his solidarity on the issue.

Photo: MTI

Concerning illegal migration, Magyar said the world had changed significantly. The position once held only by Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland was now the majority view in the EU, he said. Some 19-20 member states now agreed on the need for consistent, strict action and support for border protection, he added, expressing hope for an agreement at the October European Council meeting.
