World.title: Student-Led Movement Launches Election Challenge to Serbian Government
World.content:
Hundreds gathered in Serbia’s second city Novi Sad on Thursday evening for the first pre-election rally held by the student opposition movement ahead of early parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

Their electoral slate – called Student List – Students are Winning – will include 250 candidates chosen by students involved in the long-running protest movement triggered by the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster.

The student movement has become the strongest opposition force in Serbia, and the decision to participate in the elections represents its first direct entry into electoral politics. It hopes to defeat the Serbian Progressive Party led by Aleksandar Vucic, which has been in power since 2012.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Hungary Begins Clear-out of Russian Spies
World.content:
PM ally elected to constitutional court; Poland deepens US-focused rearmament in $4bn deal

In the latest chapter of Poland’s rule-of-law saga, the parliament on September 4 elected a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal – the body which has been at the centre of a decade-long battle between the ruling KO party and the opposition PiS. Prior to his election, the candidate Maciej Berek – who is a lawyer by training – served until August as a minister in Donald Tusk’s government, and his election reignited questions over the government’s pledge to depoliticise the judiciary. Nine rule-of-law NGOs had urged Berek to withdraw his candidature, arguing that replacing PiS-linked judges with someone so closely associated with the current government would undermine efforts to depoliticise the highest court in the land. His appointment also drew criticism from some lawmakers within the governing coalition, particularly because the government itself previously backed legislation that would have prevented politicians from moving directly into judicial posts. Four coalition MPs, including the speaker of the Sejm, Wlodzimierz Czarzasty, voted against Berek. President Karol Nawrocki also expressed doubts about Berek’s candidacy, saying “the last thing the Constitutional Tribunal needs right now is another politician”. He has not said whether he will swear in Berek, opening up the possibility of another institutional clash over the court. The crisis began after PiS took power in late 2015 and moved to install its own judges, while refusing to recognise some appointments and later some tribunal rulings. Restoring the institution’s independence is a central part of Tusk’s government’s rule-of-law agenda, with the PM announcing in August that he plans to wrest control of the court back from PiS this autumn. “I need to be sure in September that our judges enter that building and that everything is in accordance with the law,” Tusk said. “I take 100 per cent responsibility for it, and I really ask that all criticism be directed at me,’ he reiterated, adding: “Yes, it is controversial, but, as I have already said, I have no intention of capitulating on this.”

Poland secured another 4 billion dollars in US-backed financing for military purchases, in an effort to take “greater responsibility for Europe’s security”, Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Wednesday. It is the sixth agreement Warsaw has signed under the US’s Foreign Military Financing (FMF) scheme, which provides allies with grants and loans to purchase American weapons, defence equipment, services and training. The latest deal brings Poland’s access to FMF financing to almost 20 billion dollars and can be used both for existing contracts and new purchases of US equipment. The agreement fits a broader Polish rearmament strategy in which American arms occupy a central place. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Warsaw has bought or ordered F-35 fighter jets, Abrams tanks, Patriot air-defence systems, HIMARS rocket artillery and Apache attack helicopters from the US. The latest financing should help speed up those purchases. The scale of Poland’s rearmament has turned it into one of the world’s largest weapons buyers; according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer in 2021-25, with imports up 852 per cent from the previous five-year period. The deal comes amid a domestic dispute over whether EU defence financing could constrain Poland’s ability to keep buying heavily from US and South Korean suppliers. Poland is due to receive 43.7 billion euros under the EU’s SAFE program, but Kosiniak-Kamysz rejected the idea of a choice between the two, saying SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Poland’s reliance on Washington and Brussels is not exclusive, as South Korea supplied 47 per cent of Poland’s arms imports during that same period.

World.title: Can Greek PM’s ‘Progress and Prosperity’ Economic Package Deliver?
World.content:
The hall at the Ioannis Vellidis Conference Center in Thessaloniki, northern Greece, was packed on Saturday, September 5. Security lined the corridors as Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was about to begin his speech.

For the eighth time as prime minister, Mitsotakis opened the Thessaloniki International Fair, a major trade fair, which now in its 90th edition has become the country's most important political event of the year.

In a speech seemingly aimed at the 2027 spring general elections, Mitsotakis spoke optimistically and confidently about the Greek economy, claiming that his government had achieved stabilisation and progress after a long period of fiscal crisis, though also noting “the failures that remain to be corrected”. The next step, he said, is for these positive achievements to reach every home.

In this context, Mitsotakis presented his government’s economic programme, which he called an “agreement of progress and prosperity”.

World.title: Intimidation Claims Loom Large as Kosovo’s Thaci Awaits Trial Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip

In its closing statements at the war crimes trial of Hashim Thaci and his co-accused, prosecutors decried what they alleged was an “historic” climate of witness intimidation.

Indeed, just before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers issues its verdict in the trial, it will hear closing statements in a separate - but related - trial in which Thaci, the former president of Kosovo, is accused of obstruction of justice.

The verdict in the first case is due on September 16, some three years after it began.

In that case, Thaci is charged alongside Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi, all of whom played prominent roles in the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, during the 1998-99 Kosovo war before entering politics when the war ended. All have pleaded not guilty.

Of the four, Thaci was the only one also charged with obstruction of justice in 2024, this time alongside four others: former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu. All five defendants have pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Young Guns: Vulnerable Youths, ‘Disposable Goods’ in Balkan Drug Feuds
World.content:
It was a Saturday evening in early December and the Belgrade restaurant was packed. Upstairs, a children’s birthday party was in full swing, while waiters downstairs hurried from one table to the next.

No one paid much attention to the 16-year-old in a hoodie, standing at the bar among customers waiting to be seated. That is, not until he approached a table where two men were sitting, pulled a gun from his jeans and began shooting.

Nine bullets. Five hit a man identified by the initials N.K.; four lodged themselves in the restaurant furniture. The shooter fled and N.K. survived.

The man he was with, Nenad Alajbegovic, walked away unscathed. The leader of a faction of football hooligans, Alajbegovic had been the intended target. The 16-year-old had shot the wrong man.

According to police reports seen by BIRN, which identify the killer by the initials B.R., he was paid 5,000 euros. He fled to neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, laid low for six weeks, but was arrested on his return to Belgrade. Police found an encrypted phone on him; the messages revealed he had been assigned another murder, this time for 150,000 euros.

The boy said he didn’t know who hired him beyond the nicknames they used in encrypted messages.

Poor, gullible, and easily discarded, youths like him are increasingly in demand as hired guns among organised crime gangs in Serbia and Montenegro, according to cases of gang-related killings reviewed by BIRN.

Of B.R., a police source in Serbia said: “I doubt he would ever have actually been paid the 150,000 euros. He was hired as a paid gun, not a professional killer.”

“Many young people disappear without a trace after such jobs,” the source told BIRN on condition of anonymity.

“Sometimes we find out they were killed because it’s cheaper for the clans than paying them. Or the clan itself simply tips off police about where the perpetrators of a hit are, so they get arrested and the case gets ticked off as solved while the trail to those who ordered it goes cold.”

The phenomenon is also now on the radar of the European Union’s policy agency, Europol.

“Organised crime groups increasingly try to create distance between those who order violence and those who carry it out,” said a Europol spokesperson.

“Young perpetrators are often recruited because they may have no established connection to the criminal organisation, and in some cases no prior criminal record either. They’re usually assigned a single task, which makes it harder to link them to the organizers and easier to replace them if arrested.”

World.title: Croatia Buys South Korean Rocket Launchers as Regional Arms Race Accelerates
World.content:
Boo-hwan Lee, chairman of Hanwha’s board of directors (L) and Croatian Defence Minister Ivan Anusic. Photo: MORH/F.Klen.

Croatia signed contracts on Thursday with South Korean company Hanwha Aerospace to buy 18 Chunmoo K239 self-propelled multiple rocket launchers worth 435.2 million euros, excluding VAT, which Hanwha will deliver by 2029. The total cost of the deal, including VAT, training, missiles and spare parts, was not disclosed.

The government in Zagreb previously said the system’s advantages include its ability to use missiles of different calibres, flexibility, strong firepower and a very short reaction time.

The same launchers have already been purchased by Norway, Estonia and Poland, which also produce missiles for the system.

On Thursday, Defence Minister Ivan Anusic also signed a contract with Polish company WB Electronics to deliver and integrate a command-and-control system for the launchers.

“With this type of weaponry, Croatia is gaining capabilities that it does not currently have, or has ever had,” Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said at the contract-signing ceremony.

The Chunmoo K239 launchers “will complement the contracted HIMARS systems, increase the range and firepower of the Croatian Army, diversify supply routes and further strengthen deterrence,” the Prime Minister added, referring to the missile system that Croatia previously ordered from the United States.

Anusic said the Chunmoo launchers, “along with the [French] Rafale [fighter jets] will be the strongest and most striking force” of the Croatian armed forces.

He stressed that this is not a “one-way relationship” with South Korea, as the Croatian company Koncar will also be involved in implementing the project.

The Defence Minister praised the South Korean arms industry for its “very affordable price, top quality and very fast delivery”, which he said was crucial in current geopolitical circumstances.

Boo-hwan Lee, chairman of Hanwha’s board of directors, emphasised that the company wants to “continue and deepen cooperation with Croatia” and “focus on the transfer of technology and knowledge”. He called Croatia a “long-term partner” and expressed hope that South Korea’s defence industry will “find a place” there.

Beside the contract with the Korean company, Croatia’s and South Korea’s defence ministries signed a memorandum of understanding.

Croatia’s eastern neighbour, Serbia, is meanwhile also arming itself, as a kind of arms race continues to develop in the region.

During the official visit of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to Serbia and the Serbia-Uzbekistan Business Forum held in Belgrade on Tuesday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic announced that Serbia will start producing long-range ballistic missiles.

“Within a year, we will start producing long-range ballistic missiles, and we are ready to cooperate with you [Uzbekistan] on that matter as well,” Vucic said to Mirziyoyev, adding that Serbia is already producing shorter-range ballistic missiles.

“We are making progress in our defence industry. We are receiving technology transfers from some powers, while we are providing [technology] to others,” Vucic said.

World.title: Hague Prosecutors Seek Six Years for Kosovo’s Thaci for Obstructing Justice
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Hashim Thaci in court on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo: Screenshot/Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The Kosovo Specialist Prosecutor’s Office in The Hague on Thursday demanded six years’ imprisonment for former President Hashim Thaci on obstruction of justice charges, days before the announcement of the verdict in his other trial for war crimes.

Thaci is being tried alongside four co-defendants in the obstruction of justice case for interfering with witnesses in his war crimes trial.

“The prosecution asks that you impose … nine months of imprisonment for [Hajredin] Kuci; three years for [Fadil] Fazliu; three years for [Isni] Kilaj; three years for [Bashkim] Smakaj; and six years for Thaci,” prosecutor Joshua Hafetz said during closing statements.

The prosecution claims Thaci told the other four defendants to give instructions to certain witnesses in the war-crimes case about to what to say in court. Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

Prosecutor Hafetz highlighted that the prosecution wants the six years in prison for Thaci “to be served consecutively to any sentence that might be imposed” at his war crimes and crimes against humanity trial alongside three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders: Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi.

The verdict in the war crimes case will be announced on September 16. All four have plead not guilty.

Hafetz told the court on Thursday that the evidence of obstruction of justice consists of around 28 hours of recordings of Thaci during nine separate visits over four months at the Detention Centre in The Hague.

“What was important to Thaci and his co-defendants was that the witnesses Thaci had chosen for intervention should say and do what Thaci wanted,” Hafetz told the court.

He added that whenever Thaci instructed Kuci, Fazliu, Kilaj and Smakaj, he “lowered his voice and whispered to give specific instructions on what the visitors should say to the witnesses. He did this for months and his instructions had a similar practice; to dilute the charges in [the war crimes case]”.

Prosecutor Kimberly West told the court during the closing statements that Thaci, “together with his collaborators in this process, attempted to obstruct this process by interfering with the testimonies of these witnesses and was caught. He was caught with many hours of recordings and documents confirming the recordings in question.”

West said the instructions went from asking witnesses to change their testimony to denying Thaci’s presence in a place where crimes were allegedly committed, so that the testimonies fit “his narrative”.

The prosecution claimed that the evidence, parts of which were found at Kilaj’s home in November 2023 less than a month after Kryeziu and Kilaj met Thaci, was printed via the only printer at the detention centre that Thaci could use, and discussed during visits to the same centre.

Hafetz also claimed that Thaci tried to influence two former KLA fighters, Bislim Zyrapi and Rrustem Mustafa, who were testifying in his war crimes case. The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

In his testimony in 2023, former KLA area commander Mustafa claimed that the KLA zone commanders made operational decisions, not the guerrilla force’s General Staff. He said the KLA’s leaders, who included Thaci, did not have control over lower-ranking fighters – testimony that bolstered the defence’s case.

Zyrapi, former chief of the KLA’s General Staff, gave his testimony in 2024.

During defence questioning, he said the General Staff often was not informed of the actions of fighters in the KLA’s operational zones and that, despite attempts, it had not been possible for the KLA to fully exercise control over its lower-level units, partly because of Serbian offensives.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb Wartime Minister Makes New Release Plea
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

A lawyer for the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mico Stanisic has asked the UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in The Hague to free him early on the grounds that he has served two-thirds of his sentence.

Stanisic previously requested early release in November 2024, but was turned down.

His lawyer, Slobodan Zecevic, said the amount of jail time he had served reaches the threshold required for early release under the law in Poland, where Stanisic is serving his sentence.

Stanisic was the interior minister of Bosnia’s Serb-dominated entity, Republika Srpska, during Bosnia’s 1992-5 war.

The Hague Tribunal sentenced him to 22 years in prison for persecution, murder and torture under a final verdict in 2016.

As evidence of Stanisic’s rehabilitation, his submission to the International Residual Mechanism states that Stanisic served his sentence in a multi-ethnic prison and has had friendly relations with inmates of different ethnic backgrounds.

It also notes that during his time in prison no disciplinary proceedings were brought against him.

“The petitioner claims that, especially given the length of his sentence, his behaviour manifests a great level of re-socialisation,” the submission says.

“After almost 20 years from his voluntary surrender, and more than 32 years from the time the crimes were committed, the sentence already served by the petitioner not only reduces the likelihood of further criminal conduct but also contributes to reconciliation within the community where the crimes had been committed,” it adds.

Stanisic voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal in March 2005 and his trial began in September 2009, alongside his co-defandant, Stojan Zupljanin, the wartime head of the regional police centre in Banja Luka. Zupljanin was convicted of persecution, murder, torture and extermination.

According to Stanisic’s application for early release, if he is permitted to leave prison he will live at the family home in Belgrade and has the financial resources – a pension – to support himself.

World.title: Records Broken as Croatia Surpasses 5 Million Arrivals in August
World.content:
September the 11th, 2026 – Records have been broken as Croatia successfully surpasses 5 million arrivals in August alone.

A staggering 17.5 million arrivals and 90.5 million overnight stays were recorded across Croatia during the first eight months of this year. That impressive figure represents a 1% increase in both indicators compared to the same period last year, the Croatian Tourist Board announced. Index reports that of the total number of overnight stays realised, 86.7 million were registered on the coast and islands and 3.8 million on the mainland. Data from the eVisitor system also show that in August alone, for the first time in history, the number of more than five million tourist arrivals in a single month was exceeded. This is according to a statement from the Ministry of Tourism and Sport and the Croatian Tourist Board.

an expectation-shattering august this year

In August alone, more than five million guests arrived in Croatia, which is 2% more than in the same month last year. 31.4 million overnight stays were recorded, or half a percent more than in last year’s August. The most overnight stays in the eighth month were recorded by guests from Germany, Croatia, Slovenia, Poland, Austria, Italy, Hungary and the Czech Republic. By counties, Istria, Split-Dalmatia and Kvarner lead, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin, Umag and Dubrovnik.

“Croatian tourism is competitive, which is evident from all indicators, and we have done our utmost for that. Behind us are an extraordinary eight months and a summer season in which, despite numerous challenges, we achieved growth in key indicators,” said Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina.

“It’s particularly important that we achieved this result in circumstances of changed travel habits. We have constantly said that trips would be shorter and that guests would manage their budgets more rationally, and the difference between the growth in arrivals and the somewhat milder growth in overnight stays precisely confirms this,” he added. The minister thanked the entire tourism sector for their cooperation and readiness to respond to seasonal challenges, especially regarding price competitiveness.

detailed results for the first 8 months of 2026

Looking by counties, in the period from January to the end of August, the most overnight stays were recorded in Istria, 25.4 million. This is followed by Split-Dalmatia County with more than 17 million overnight stays and Kvarner with 15.2 million. The most visited destinations in the year so far were Rovinj, Dubrovnik, Poreč, Split, Umag and Medulin. The most numerous guests in the first eight months were Germans with 16.9 million overnight stays. Domestic guests recorded 11.7 million overnight stays, followed by guests from Slovenia (9.6 million), Austria (6.3 million), Poland (6.3 million), the Czech Republic (4.5 million), Hungary (3.7 million), Italy (3.5 million) and the United Kingdom (3.2 million).

plans for the remainder of 2026

Director of the Croatian Tourist Board Kristjan Staničić emphasized that the results confirm strong interest in Croatia. “As a destination, Croatia has responded very well to market challenges and changes in traveller behaviour, who today make decisions about travel much more carefully. I believe that, in addition to the quality of the offer and the work of the entire sector, the continuity of our promotional activities has also contributed to this,” said Staničić. He noted that the HTZ was active in key markets through digital campaigns, social networks, PR activities and cooperation with carriers and tour operators.

“An important part of the year remains ahead of us and we are very focused on the off-season and the winter period. We want to maintain positive momentum, but at the same time continue working on quality, competitiveness and greater value of Croatian tourism,” concluded Staničić.

World.title: Croatian Government Puts Forward Plan to Handle Lika Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 11th, 2026 – The Croatian Government has put forth its plan to handle the Lika hazardous waste scandal, stating that it will burn 650 tonnes of said waste in cement plants.

The Croatian Government has revealed that it will handle the urgent disposal of around 650 tonnes of waste from the site of the former PPK Velebit in Gospić. This was announced by Prime Minister Andrej Plenković at the beginning of yesterday’s government session. Index reports that the waste will be taken over by two domestic cement plants – Holcim Hrvatska and Nexe – which will energetically recover it, i.e. burn it, within a maximum of 45 days. The value of the job is estimated to stand at a maximum of 357,500 euros.

“When it comes to the hazardous waste in Gospić, we’ve adopted a decision determining the urgent takeover of the removal, transport, recovery or other appropriate waste management procedures for the non-hazardous waste located at the PPK Velebit site. The procedure is carried out for the complete removal of the subject waste from the site, and its lawful and environmentally acceptable disposal,” Plenković revealed.

“we reacted quickly”

The Prime Minister also commented on the failed tender of the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund and the revolt of the residents of Zaprešić, where the waste was originally supposed to go for processing.

“After the Fund annulled the decision on the selection of the bidder for the removal of non-hazardous waste that is in bags, the Government, seeing that this procedure… you saw the reaction in Zaprešić, and then we also looked at the amounts of other offers, a decision was made to annul that procedure,” Plenković said.

“However, we reacted lightning-fast in parallel and agreed that two domestic cement plants, Holcim Hrvatska and Nexe, with whom we held talks these days, will be the ones who will carry out this procedure, and that in a total value of a maximum of 357,500 euros, which was also the offer of the company, i.e. the bidder who ultimately withdrew from the job. And that in a very short deadline, the deadline will be a maximum of 45 days,” the Prime Minister added.

This Government decision comes after the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund officially annulled the public procurement procedure for the removal of waste from the so-called big bag sacks in Gospić. The job was awarded on the 2nd of September to the Tabak group from Zaprešić, which offered 357,500 euros excluding VAT. However, the possibility that the waste would end up in Zaprešić caused protests among the general public, after which the company’s director Ivan Tabak withdrew their offer.

The second offer in that tender was that of the joint bidders CE-ZA-R (part of Petar Pripuz’s CIOS group) and Saubermacher-TS. They requested 578,500 euros excluding VAT, which the Fund rejected because the offer exceeded the estimated value of 400,000 euros. By annulling the tender, the state was left without a contractor, so the Government cut the matter short with a direct agreement with the cement plants.

a further 4,500 tonnes of waste still lies in gospić

These 650 tonnes in bags are only a smaller part of the problem in Gospić. At the same location there are still around 4,500 tonnes of scattered waste for which the Fund is conducting a separate tender, estimated at 4.72 million euros excluding VAT. The Tabak group and CIOS’s CE-ZA-R also applied for that job.

Earlier expert reports commissioned by USKOK showed that there are tens of thousands of tonnes of waste at the locations in Gospić. Analyses established high levels of heavy metals such as copper, lead and antimony, while microplastics and dangerous PFAS compounds, known as “forever chemicals”, were found in the groundwater beneath the landfill. Water in the city water supply, according to findings so far, is not contaminated.

World.title: 1.72 Million People Employed in Croatia in Second Quarter of 2026
World.content:
September the 11th, 2026 – 1.72 million people were registered as employed across Croatia during the second quarter of 2026, with the number of employed individuals rising by 21,000 on an annual basis.

There were 84,000 unemployed people across Croatia during the second quarter of 2026, representing a decrease of 2,000 compared to the same period back in 2025. Poslovni reports that the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) has published data from the Labour Force Survey, according to which it is estimated that in the second quarter of this year there were one million and 723,000 employed people in Croatia, an increase of 21,000 or 1.2 percent, compared to the second quarter of last year.

A comparison of the data collected on those registered as unemployed obtained from the Labour Force Survey with data from the Croatian Employment Service (HZZ) and other statistical monitoring based on administrative sources reveals more. It showed that during the second quarter of this year, the Croatian unemployment rate according to administrative records data of 3.5 percent was lower than the survey unemployment rate (4.7 percent) by 1.2 percentage points.

During that period, the average number of unemployed according to the Labour Force Survey was 21 thousand higher than the data of the Croatian Employment Service. Given that the surveyed persons declared whether they were registered with the employment service, the comparison of data shows that of the total of 84,000 unemployed according to the Labour Force Survey, 50,000 or 59.6 percent were registered with the employment service, while 40.4 percent of the survey unemployed were not interested in registering with that service.

At the same time, of the total of 63,000 people registered with the Croatian Employment Service, 13,000 or 20.2 percent failed to actually meet the international criteria for unemployment. It should also be added that in the second quarter of 2026, the employment rate for persons aged 15 to 64 stood at 69.2 percent, which is an increase of 0.4 percentage points compared to the second quarter of last year.

World.title: Will the New Croatian Toll System End Up Being Delayed?
World.content:
September the 11th, 2025 – In true Croatian form, questions about whether or not the new road toll system will end up being delayed are circulating. Here’s what Croatian Motorways (HAC) have to say in response.

Poslovni reports that the company doesn’t deny that this is a complex process which, among other things, also includes appeal deadlines in tenders. In more recent days, several pieces of information have been circulating in the media according to which the project of introducing a new toll collection system in Croatia will be delayed.

At the end of July, the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures (DKOM) annulled the decision of Croatian Motorways (HAC) on the selection of the contractor for the sales web portal, mobile application and integration data hubs, which form the most important user part of the system. As a result of that Croatian Motorways was approached with a query about what is happening with the deadlines and whether they are in any way at risk.

“Regarding the media reports, we wish to emphasise that the deadline for putting the new Crolibertas toll collection system into operation is determined by the Law on Toll Collection and that all activities are being carried out according to that deadline,” Croatian Motorways then revealed.

The company does not deny that this is a complex process which, among other things, also includes appeal deadlines in tenders. “The establishment of a single electronic toll collection system Crolibertas along all motorways in Croatia, including concession motorways, is an implementation-complex project because it is multidisciplinary and requires the integration of several different and independent segments (e.g. technological, legal and operational).

All implementation activities must be consistently and systematically connected and coordinated, all so that when the system is put into operation it is accessible to users and simple to use,” they’re stated from Croatian Motorways. The cost of the entire project is estimated to stand at a whopping 160 million euros.

World.title: Rimac Has Taken Complete Control of Bugatti
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Croatia’s world famous Rimac has now officially taken complete control over the legendary Bugatti.

An investment consortium led by HOF Capital has completed the takeover of Porsche’s stakes in the Rimac Group and the company Bugatti Rimac. Index reports that the transaction, initially announced back in April this year, has been officially finalised. Through it, the consortium has taken over Porsche’s 21% ownership in the Rimac Group and 45% stake in the company Bugatti Rimac.

The Rimac Group remains the majority owner of the company Bugatti Rimac with a 55 percent stake. The joint company Bugatti Rimac was founded back in 2021, and in the new consortium the largest investor is BlueFive Capital along with other institutional investors from both the USA and Europe. “This is an important step for Bugatti Rimac and the entire Rimac Group. I’m pleased that HOF Capital and their consortium are becoming our partners in the next phase of the Group’s development and I look forward to working together on realising the full potential of our companies. We have achieved strong progress in all parts of the Group and I believe that this partnership will give us additional momentum for continued growth,” said Mate Rimac, founder and president of the Rimac Group and chief executive officer of the company Bugatti Rimac.

management changes

With the new ownership structure now formally and fully established, Bugatti Rimac is also restructuring its management team. This further strengthens the strategic and operational vision that Mate Rimac set for Bugatti when he was appointed chief executive officer in 2021.

Christophe Piochon is leaving the positions of president of the Bugatti Automobiles brand and chief operating officer of the company Bugatti Rimac. His role as president of Bugatti Automobiles is personally taken over by Mate Rimac. Marko Brkljačić, previously chief operating officer at Rimac Technology, becomes the new chief operating officer of the company Bugatti Rimac. Further changes are also planned, so Hendrik Malinowski, previously director of management at Bugatti Automobiles, will be appointed commercial director of the brand.

Rimac thanked Piochon for his contribution to the brand. “With over two decades spent at Bugatti, Christophe has strongly influenced what that brand represents today. From the Veyron to the Tourbillon, he participated in building and preserving the quality and supreme craftsmanship by which all hypercars that leave Molsheim are recognised. On behalf of the entire Bugatti Rimac team, I want to thank Christophe and wish him every success, and at the same time I take the opportunity to welcome Marko,” Rimac stated.

World.title: Will Lika Now Remain Polluted Forever?
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Lika has been at the heart of a terrible hazardous waste scandal, and the findings are leading people to ask whether Lika will remain polluted forever.

The case of the illegal disposal of thousands of tonnes of waste in Lika has in recent weeks raised serious questions about possible environmental pollution, its scale and consequences for people, which is why a large protest was also held on Saturday in Zagreb. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that hazardous waste was being brought to Lika for years from neighbouring Italy and Slovenia under the guise of raw material for the alleged production of construction blocks.

It was then somewhat buried in an uncontrolled manner, and somewhat simply left out in the open. Croatian police, in an international operation with the support of Europol, have since arrested 13 people. Among them are entrepreneur Josip Šincek and his wife Monika, owners of the company Tipos Resur.

After the public was first confronted with findings about so-called “forever chemicals”, and then also microplastics in groundwater, the question opened of how much we actually know about the scale of the pollution and its possible consequences. Professor Branimir K. Hackenberger from the Department of Biology at Josip Juraj Strossmayer University in Osijek spoke out about the details of this awful case.

Hackenberger went through three publicly published expert reports from this specific case from Lika. These are the finding of the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering from March 2026, its supplement from July, and the report of the Josip Juraj Strossmayer Water Institute on microplastics from August, which USKOK published yesterday. He emphasised that he is not a participant in the proceedings nor did he work on those expert reports, but comments on them as an ecotoxicologist.

what exactly are “forever chemicals”?

He explained that PFAS is a collective name for a family of over ten thousand synthetic compounds in which hydrogen on the carbon chain has been replaced by fluorine. This is important because the “hydrogen-fluorine bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry”. One of the consequences of this is persistence, says Hackenberger, “since in the environment there is neither a biological nor a chemical pathway that would break that bond under normal conditions”. Their characteristic is also that they are retained in the organism. For PFOS that time amounts to three to five years, our interlocutor explains.

The PFOS that Hackenberger mentions is one of the best-known and most long-lasting PFAS compounds, which due to its persistence and ability to be retained in the organism is considered particularly problematic. Another of the more problematic PFAS compounds is PFOA. For that “forever chemical” Hackenberger says that the International Agency for Research on Cancer in 2023 classified it among carcinogenic substances for humans, while PFOS was classified among possible carcinogens. As regards health effects, Hackenberger explained the following:

“The European Food Safety Authority has set a tolerable weekly intake of 4.4 ng per kilogram of body weight, and that for the sum of only four compounds: PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and PFOS. The critical effect on which that value was derived is not cancer but a reduced antibody response to vaccination in children, thus an immune effect at very low doses. In addition, elevated cholesterol, changes in liver enzymes, thyroid disorders and lower birth weight have been documented,” he notes.

what was actually find in lika?

Hackenberger underlines that neither PFOA nor PFAS has been confirmed to have been discovered in Lika. According to the sampling by the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering which was on 11 May 2026, and in which 20 compounds were analysed, other “forever chemicals” were found. “PFBS, PFBA, PFPeA and PFHxA are compounds with four to six carbon atoms and industry introduced them precisely as a replacement for PFOA and PFOS. Toxicologically they are milder per unit of mass and accumulate more weakly in the organism, but environmentally they are worse: they are more soluble, bind more weakly to soil, travel faster and, what is decisive for remediation, are significantly harder to remove from water,” he explained.

“Upstream there is nothing, and downstream it is 200.5 ng/L. The ratio is greater than 130 to 1 and cannot be explained by a natural background, because there is no natural background for PFAS; these compounds do not exist in nature,” he says. “To put 200.5 ng/L into perspective: that is twice above the parametric value for drinking water, but it is water from a borehole next to the landfill that no one drinks. No one has been exposed on the basis of that measurement and the expert expressly says so. The value of the finding is therefore not in the exposure but in that it is an early warning: it shows how the path from waste to groundwater is open,” are his words.

antimony was discovered in lika cabbages

He touched on antimony, a metal which in larger quantities can be very harmful to human health, and long-term exposure is associated with damage to the liver, heart and lungs. “The biggest chemical problem that was measured at that location is not PFAS but metals in the soil. Antimony reaches 317 mg/kg, while naturally it is below 1; copper reaches 9,946 with a maximum permitted concentration of 100; lead 1,051 with the same limit of 100. In the eluate of one sample ‘next to the silo wall’ antimony amounts to 499 mg/kg of dry matter with a limit of 0.7 for non-hazardous waste.

Antimony was also found in various plants, a piece of data that the media did not report: 0.28 to 0.34 mg/kg in woody species and around 0.3 mg/kg in cabbage at 20 to 30 metres from the pile. That means that the path from waste to edible tissue is closed, which for residents is a more direct message than any figure about PFAS,” he says.

there has been no pfas analysed carried out in the soil

He explained that by removing the waste the source is removed, but not what has already come out of it. “Exactly how much remains, honestly speaking, we do not know, and the measurement that would say that has not been done. PFAS was analysed in three water samples, while in the soil it was not analysed even once. The stock in the unsaturated zone cannot be estimated differently than by guessing without that, and I will not guess. What can be said as a framework is the following. Short chains, which predominate here, are washed out relatively quickly, realistically in a range from a few years to two decades. Longer chains and precursors, of which there are none in the water now, but which are probably in the waste, remain significantly longer. Remediation is therefore not planned in deadlines of a few years,” he also said.

teflon is also an issue

Hackenberger was then asked about a compound called PTFE, which is better known as Teflon. He says that Teflon, in the report of the Water Institute, appears only in one of six samples, and that in only two particles. They were found in a sample taken from a borehole that is located upstream of the landfill and serves as a reference point, while in the other five samples PTFE was not found. Because of that, he said, that finding is not proof that Teflon from the waste reached the groundwater.

“returning the underground area in the affected areas in lika isn’t realistic”

He warned that the location is not classic open karst, as one might conclude from some claims, but that according to geophysical measurements and drilling there is a poorly permeable base there. As the best solution he sees the removal of the source of pollution itself, that is complete remediation and disposal of the waste, whereby its further release would be stopped. As a temporary measure it is possible to cover the waste impermeably and prevent the penetration of precipitation. He concludes that returning the underground to a completely original state is not realistic, but it is possible to remove the source, prevent further pollution and monitor the state in the long term.

how dangerous are these microplastics?

He notes that nowhere in the world is there a health-based limit value for microplastics in drinking water.

“Back in 2019 and in later reviews, the World Health Organisation concluded that the evidence is not sufficient for deriving a guideline value, and Directive (EU) places microplastics on the watch list and prescribes the measurement methodology, but does not prescribe a limit,” he added. “The greatest value microplastics has here is as a marker, and not as a poison. Polystyrene in the groundwater downstream of the landfill and its complete absence upstream are a feature of a local anthropogenic source. That is how the report itself interprets it and that is logically correct,” he stated.

When it comes to public water supply, Hackenberger says that according to the data available so far there is no reason for the conclusion that it is endangered. “The Mrđenovac and Divoselo intakes are located upstream of the landfill and are hydrogeologically not connected with it, and public water supply is regularly controlled. When it comes to private wells downstream, no one has an answer to that question because no one has measured,” he says.

there can be plenty lying undetected

He was asked about what such analyses can still leave undetected, that is whether we can even ever truly know the full extent of the pollution if we analyse only the substances that we decided in advance to look for. “We cannot know it all, and that’s not a shortcoming of these specific expert reports but a limitation of the method itself. For example, the total PFAS parameter of 500 ng/L was not measured. It is measured as total organic fluorine, by AOF and EOF methods, and would be the only one to show how much fluorine there is in the water at all.

In studies where both are measured, the targeted twenty compounds usually explain between 1 and 30 % of the present organic fluorine. Translated to this case, the real load could be several times greater than the measured 200.5 ng/L, but that is an estimate from the literature, and not a measurement at this location, and that is precisely why it is worth doing that analysis. My own calculation, thus an estimate: on the basis of a base of 1,063 substances that appear in this kind of waste and the list of analyses that were actually carried out at this location, the expected number of substances that would pass unnoticed amounts to around 79%,” he noted. He warned of the fact that individual substances are assessed separately, while their mixture can have a different effect.

World.title: Croatian Motorways: Crolibertas is Being Implemented Within Deadlines
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Croatian Motorways (HAC) has stated that the upcoming Crolibertas system that will replace the current toll system is being implemented within all legal deadlines.

The deadline for launching the new Crolibertas system is set by the Law on Toll Collection, states the simple message from Croatian Motorways, with Boris Huzjan at the helm. Poslovni reports that the company makes no attempt to deny that this is a long and complex process which, among other things, also includes appeal deadlines in tenders.

In recent days, several pieces of information have been published in the media according to which the project of introducing a new toll collection system in Croatia will be delayed. Back at the end of July, the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures (DKOM) annulled the decision of Croatian Motorways (HAC) on the selection of the contractor for the sales web portal, mobile application and integration data hubs, which form the most important user part of the system.

Croatian Motorways was as such approached with a query about what exactly is happening with the deadlines and whether they are in any way at risk. “Regarding all of the media reports, we want to emphasise that the deadline for putting the new Crolibertas toll collection system into operation is determined by the Law on Toll Collection and that all activities are being carried out according to that deadline,” Croatian Motorways revealed, as touched on above.

“The establishment of a single electronic toll collection system Crolibertas along all motorways in Croatia, including concession motorways, is an implementation-complex project because it is multidisciplinary and requires the integration of several different and independent segments (e.g. technological, legal and operational). All implementation activities must be consistently and systematically connected and coordinated, all so that when the system is put into operation it is accessible to users and simple to use,” they concluded.

It should be noted that the cost of the entire Crolibertas project is estimated to stand at 160 million euros.

World.title: With Rijeka Gateway Doing Well, Railway Improvement is Necessary
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Rijeka Gateway is doing excellently, but proper Croatian railway improvement is now necessary to continue the momentum.

At the Rijeka Gateway container terminal, more than 370,000 container units (TEU) were handled in the first year of commercial operations. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that one hundred ships called at the terminal, and it is expected that in 2027 the full capacity of the first phase of investment in the terminal will be achieved, with around 650,000 container units (TEU) handled.

“In Rijeka and the wider region, a technologically advanced terminal like this did not exist. Our jobs and processes are special and very complex, so building a team that can compete at that level with the best terminals is a source of pride not only for all of us at Rijeka Gateway, but also for Rijeka and the whole of Croatia.

new logistics corridors

Important new logistics corridors have connected Rijeka with the region, which is a major value brought by our terminal. The third thing is that we have continued to carefully monitor our impact on the environment and the community with the aim of being a good neighbour to the citizens of Rijeka. We have successfully certified our environmental management system according to the ISO 14001:2015 standard, confirming our commitment to environmental protection, and we continuously communicate with the local community on all topics related to the quality of life of citizens,” said Peter Corfitsen, President of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway. Since its opening, the terminal has received more than a thousand trains and over 80,000 trucks. The current modal split for cargo leaving the terminal is 42 percent by rail and 58 percent by road. The entry and exit process for truck transport has been fully digitalised, which speeds up truck processing and reduces waiting times, thereby reducing the burden on traffic and pollution. The average truck processing time is around 15 minutes, and the shortest time achieved for a truck is ten minutes, on a day when more than 500 trucks were processed.

investment in the local community

“By handling 370,000 TEU of cargo, we have significantly increased the overall capacity of the Port of Rijeka and are rapidly approaching the figures we planned, that is, reaching a throughput of 650,000 TEU and, in the second phase, one million TEU. During the first year of operations, Rijeka Gateway maintained a high level of operational reliability, with 98 percent availability of port equipment and 99 percent availability of key systems on the operational quay and storage areas, which is at the level of the best terminals.

For the full potential of the terminal, the planned increase in railway traffic capacity will be key, and we welcome the activities of the Croatian Government in this regard. We’ll continue to invest in the local community, especially through cooperation with the Faculty of Maritime Studies and the University of Rijeka, through various scholarship and education programmes, as well as through donation programmes aimed at Rijeka kindergartens and primary schools,” said Tomislav Rosandić, Member of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Outgoing defense minister: Intelligence early warning mustn't be a political request
World.content:
The future defense minister should not make what amounts to a political request to the intelligence services to alter their threat assessment of Estonia's security, outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur said.

Defense minister candidate Martin Herem has said in the media that, if he becomes minister, he wants the government to update the wording of its threat assessment because, in his view, the war in Ukraine could end within six months, after which Russia may need only another six months before it could use military force against Estonia.

Pevkur noted that if the threat assessment is changed, the information on which it is based must be objective and politically independent.

"This is one area where I would very, very strongly urge the future defense minister to bear in mind that intelligence early warnings and the information that goes into them cannot be politically commissioned. You cannot tell intelligence officers for political reasons to write a particular intelligence warning or preliminary assessment for you. Professionals do that based on their best judgment and the best information available, gathering intelligence themselves and speaking with partners, and an independent, objective intelligence assessment is then compiled on that basis. If anyone starts interfering with that politically, it is a very, very wrong path to take and so I sincerely hope there will be no political pressure on intelligence officers to describe the situation beyond our borders in a particular way," Pevkur said.

Defense minister candidate Martin Herem told ERR in an interview that a year from now Russia could use military force of an unknown scale against Estonia, but before that happens, Estonia must consider whether its preparations are sufficient to eliminate that force.

"The first step is to consider how quickly the war in Ukraine might come to an end. I would say that could happen within six months. Probably not tomorrow, but we should set some kind of deadline, and I think it could be within six months, though it be within three years. As to what the shortest possible time-frame is, I would say six months.," Herem said.

Pevkur also noted that since the criticism leveled by the National Audit Office over disarray in the Estonian Defense Forces relates to the period when Herem was commander of the Defense Forces, he will now have to address those concerns substantively.

"The accounting of the Defense Forces' stocks and assets definitely needs significant improvement. If you look at who was responsible for these matters at the time, Gen. [Veiko-Vello] Palm (expected to be on Herem's team once he takes office — ed.) was also involved when it came to materiel management and everything related to it. So I very much hope Martin Herem understands that these problems with accounting for the Defense Forces' assets and stocks date back to his time in charge and that he takes very seriously the fact that the National Audit Office's audit report is not simply some accounting issue, but something that needs to be addressed substantively," Pevkur said.

Regarding the departure of Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk, Pevkur said that because the next six to eight months will be extremely critical, with Russia expected to engage in "soft" interference in elections taking place in several European countries, they could not allow a situation in which the future defense minister and the current secretary general could not work together.

"Over these six months, we cannot have a situation where the Ministry of Defense's permanent secretary and minister are glaring at each other from across the room or across the hallway. It is in the interests of Estonia's security to ensure that the Ministry of Defense's leadership functions and that can only happen if the permanent secretary and the minister are in lockstep," he said.

World.title: Incoming defense minister: Russia could use military force against Estonia within a year
World.content:
Incoming Defense Minister Martin Herem says Russia could use an unknown level of military force against Estonia a year from now, meaning Estonia must assess whether its preparations are sufficient.

Herem, former Estonian Defense Forces commander, made the remarks as he prepares to take up the defense minister post following the resignation of Hanno Pevkur and the dismissal of Kaimo Kuusk as defense ministry permanent secretary.

Estonia must be ready to respond if such a scenario materializes, he added.

Is it true that you want a new threat assessment for Estonia and that this should be based on the assumption that Russia will strike Estonia within a year?

No, it is not so drastic as that. Our stance at the moment is that Russia is a threat, but then come all the types of assessments. Some say that could happen within three years of the end of the war in Ukraine, and others say within six months of that. And we all take that very seriously and all nod along. Then in the next moment, we have made our plans and do not take those threat assessments into account at all.

I think this needs to be pinned down somehow. I am not saying it would be inside a year. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said that it could be potentially three years after the war in Ukraine. German or Danish intelligence has stated that it could be possible six months after the war in Ukraine ends.

Everything else we are doing reflects that in no way whatsoever. We need to decide when it might be viable. Then we should review whether we will be prepared by that time, or whether we need to speed up certain processes so that we are prepared by that time. I would argue that this is simply not how we have been planning our activities today.

If a new threat assessment gets drawn up, what assumptions should be made about when Russia might strike Estonia?

The first step is to consider how quickly the war in Ukraine might come to an end. I would say that could happen within six months. Probably not tomorrow, but we should set some kind of deadline, and I think it could be within six months, though it be within three years. As to what the shortest possible time-frame is, I would say six months. The next question is: If all the world events and circumstances align and are amenable, how much time would Russia actually need to ready itself to carry out a military action which would in turn require us to deploy our wartime Defense Forces? In other words, mobilization — so we are talking about a real war. Again, I think it would not require more than six months for that.

This is because everything [Russia] is using up on a daily basis today will start accumulating once the war in Ukraine ends. If it has spent six months stockpiling the things it is currently expending, that will be sufficient to do something militarily against us.

Ministry of Defense building in Tallinn. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

That is why I say that our first deadline is when the war in Ukraine ends. Could it end within six months? Yes. How much time would they need to prepare? Six months? Yes. Fine. So, a year from now, Russia could use a military force of size "X" against us.

Are our preparations matching that? Are we capable of eliminating a military force of that size? And if we are not, then we should make those necessary preparations. Or there is another option: We can all sign off on keeping our fingers crossed that it will not happen and do nothing at all.

The third option is to note that it would be very bad if it were to occur, but we will make an effort, get certain things done and do them faster than we are doing now.

So in drawing up that threat assessment, should it indeed be based on the possible outcome that Estonia could be facing a real military threat within the year?

I am not confirming that one-year time.frame right now. I would like to talk to the intelligence agencies. They should also state that this is viable; I do not want to be doing this alone. That is also why I am not saying today whether we should work on the basis of one year or on three years. We should put this kind of framework down on paper for ourselves. But I have the feeling that this is not how things are being done today. That is completely comprehensible when you look at what politics is currently focused on: Herem as a person, the Reform Party, the prime minister's decisions, granting certain powers. Six officers wrote a long letter about why Herem must not be granted too much power, yet not one of them is talking about the threat.

As of today we would essentially be willing to sacrifice six months, by saying that nothing can be completed in that time-frame anyway. Let's wait for the elections. 'But come on, people, can you not see the threat?' 'Yes, we can see the threat', yet then everything becomes about politics all over again, which I find strange.

This anger towards someone, or the conviction that one's own course of action would be much better, has blinded everyone to the threat. Okay, let's say it happens within a year. At what point within that year would it take place? Ask that of, I don't know, [Isamaa chair Urmas] Reinsalu, [SDE leader Lauri] Läänemets, [Prime Minister Kristen] Michal or [Center Party chair Mihhail] Kõlvart. Ask them within what time-frame it could happen. Let them set the deadline themselves, and then ask whether, based on that stated deadline, we are now acting quickly enough.

But they are not dealing with that today. They are engaged in some kind of politics of principle. I would argue that ministries and government agencies actually operate in much the same way. [Current EDF commander Lt Gen. Andrus] Merilo says Russia could do something in 2027, whatever the basis for his claim may be. And everyone says this is serious, yet there is zero action.

We have been talking constantly, until we are foaming at the mouth, about the Russia threat. This is because talking about the Russia threat is obligatory and fashionable; it keeps you in the spotlight, but you do not actually have to believe in it. I want to change that somewhat.

According to information received by ERR, the disagreement between Herem and recently departed Ministry of Defense permanent secretary Kaimo Kuusk may have arisen precisely over the need to revise the threat assessment. Asked whether this was true, Herem said Kuusk should be asked about that. Kuusk could not be reached by the newsroom for comment as of the time the article was published. Herem declined to discuss Kuusk further.

World.title: Tartu plans larger addition for Miina Härma High School to replace collapsed section
World.content:
Tartu decided to build a new addition more than twice the size of the collapsed section at Miina Härma High School. The plan will cost the city an extra €2.7 million, which officials said will not come at the expense of other school reconstruction projects. Taking out a loan is not off the table.

The school began renovating its technical systems at the start of summer, during which part of a building constructed in 1960 collapsed. Although the city initially considered rebuilding the section to its previous size, officials have now opted for a larger project.

Tartu Deputy Mayor Martin Bek said that after weighing all the pros and cons, the city found it reasonable to move forward with constructing a new building. "We are demolishing the entire 650 square meters of space and replacing it with a new three‑story building with a basement, totaling 1,450 square meters," he said.

School Director Ene Tannberg said the addition will solve several bottlenecks. "We will be able to run all classes in a single shift," she said.

Tannberg added that first and second grade students currently study in a second shift. "This plan will allow us to expand the cafeteria, which is a bottleneck in the main building, and we will get a more modern learning environment," she said.

The school has a memorial to composer Miina Härma (1984, Juta Eskel). Source: Heidi Tooming

The addition is expected to cost €4.2 million, but Bek said the city's extra expense will be €2.7 million.

"It is smaller for the reason that some of the work already contracted was not carried out, and we can use that financial buffer for the new building," he said. "We will reclaim value‑added tax from the full construction and hope that part will also be covered by insurance," Bek said.

He said the money will not come at the expense of other school reconstruction projects. "We have found full coverage for it," Bek said. No cuts have been made elsewhere. "We are looking at the four‑year budget strategy, and we were able to fit this essential work into it," he said.

Tartu Deputy Mayor Martin Bek. Autor/allikas: Airika Harrik/ERR

It is not yet clear whether something else will be left undone as a result. "Our borrowing capacity grows year by year, and that option exists to keep the overall budget balanced," Bek added.

Because of the technical systems renovation, the school will operate in temporary facilities until the start of the next academic year. Tannberg said some students will have to remain in temporary facilities until next Christmas because of the addition. The city council will discuss the plan in October, after which a new procurement will be announced.
