“Regardless of how good a policy is, if its implementation system is weak, people will not feel its impact. That is why strengthening our government employees and the institutions they serve is important to ensure that every law, program and public fund allocated by the government results in services that genuinely benefit the people,” Legarda said.

World.title: Bojie Dy hails Pisa improvement: ‘It’s a welcome news’
World.content:
Speaker Faustino Dy III — Photo from Faustino “Bojie” Dy III/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III welcomed the Philippines’ improved performance in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa), saying the results are fruits of the government’s sustained investments and reforms

Dy credited the gains to a collective effort involving the national government, the Department of Education (DepEd), school leaders and teachers, who he said translate policies and resources into actual learning in classrooms.

“I commend Secretary Juan Edgardo ‘Sonny’ Angara and the entire Department of Education for keeping their focus on improving learning outcomes and addressing the long-standing challenges confronting basic education,” Dy said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bojie Dy says Pisa gains show education reforms yielding results

He acknowledged that improving the country’s education system would take time, noting that the challenges facing Philippine basic education “cannot be solved overnight.”

“But these results tell us that progress is possible when we stay focused on learning outcomes and support our teachers and students,” Dy said.

Dy also lauded President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. for making education a national priority, saying the administration’s continued allocation of resources to schools and young people reflects that commitment.

He stressed that improving education requires sustained government support over several years rather than short-term interventions.

Article continues after this 

Dy emphasized that the latest results should serve as a basis for further reforms rather than a reason for complacency.

“The important thing is that we now have evidence that improvement is possible,” he said. “Our responsibility is to build on these gains and make sure that progress reaches every classroom and every Filipino child.”

Article continues after this 

Dy said Congress would continue supporting education reforms, programs and investments aimed at equipping teachers with the necessary tools and providing Filipino children with quality education.

World.title: Rape suspect wanted in Northern Mindanao caught in Nueva Ecija
World.content:
CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — A 32-year-old man wanted for raping and impregnating his minor stepdaughter in Northern Mindanao was captured in Nueva Ecija on Wednesday, closing out the region’s list of the top 10 most wanted fugitives.

Operatives from the Tagoloan municipal police station in Lanao del Norte and local police intercepted the suspect around 4:50 p.m. on September 9 in Barangay Sampalucan, Bongabon town.

The suspect fled Northern Mindanao after charges were filed against him for rape and violation of Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act or Republic Act 7610. Investigators said the abuse occurred in 2023 while the child was under his care, resulting in her pregnancy.

READ: Rape suspect nabbed in Cavite yields shabu, unlicensed gun

He was arrested by virtue of a warrant issued on October 11, 2024, by the Regional Trial Court of Iligan City under Criminal Case No. 24-30063, with no bail recommended.

Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr, Police Regional Office 10 (PRO 10) director, said intelligence tracking allowed operatives to trace the fugitive across regional borders after months on the run.

“Our trackers remain determined and relentless in pursuing those who have pending cases, guided by intelligence, professionalism, and respect for the law. This arrest is also a clear example of what we can achieve through strong interoperability and coordination among police offices,” Babagay said.

Babagay noted that the operation completes the capture of all 10 individuals listed on the regional police office’s top most wanted list.

The suspect is now detained at the Tagoloan municipal police station in Lanao del Norte pending court proceedings./coa

World.title: SMC backs Dinagat bid to tap Sabang Dam water resource
World.content:
MAP ASSESSMENT. (From left) Atty. Niel Edward M. Demerey, Dinagat Islands Board Member Nilo Marco M. Demerey, Governor Nilo P. Demerey Jr., and San Miguel Corp. (SMC) Chairman and CEO Ramon S. Ang inspect engineering layout maps during a high-level meeting at the SMC Head Office in Ortigas, Pasig City. (Photo courtesy of Dinagat Islands Board Member Nilo Marco M. Demerey)

SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — Conglomerate San Miguel Corp. (SMC) has committed to grant the provincial government of Dinagat Islands access to the Sabang Dam reservoir to resolve the island province’s persistent water supply shortages.

The deal was finalized during a high-level meeting between Dinagat Islands Gov. Nilo P. Demerey Jr. and SMC Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon S. Ang on Thursday at the SMC Head Office in Ortigas, Pasig City, according to a social media update posted by Dinagat Islands Board Member Nilo Marco M. Demerey.

Under the agreement, the province will be allowed to tap the Sabang Dam, located in Barangay Del Pilar in the municipality of Cagdianao, to serve as an additional bulk water source for local communities.

Article continues after this 

READ: Dinagat Islands rolls out measures vs water crisis

Built in the early 1980s by the Philippine Nickel Corporation for industrial mining operations, the dam is the province’s largest man-made reservoir. The dam is a government asset, but it is located within SMC’s massive 25,000-hectare mining concession, requiring corporate clearance, coordination, and right-of-way permissions for municipal water extraction.

The development comes at a critical time for the province. Dinagat Islands was recently placed under a state of calamity due to a severe water crisis triggered by a prolonged dry spell. Rivers and local gravity-fed systems have dried up, leaving over 18,000 residents vulnerable to acute water shortages.

Technical teams from both the provincial government and SMC have begun mapping the infrastructure requirements to utilize the reservoir. The project will entail constructing extensive pipeline networks, treatment facilities, and supporting logistical systems to distribute water to municipal water districts.

To address immediate distribution gaps while the long-term infrastructure is being engineered, Ang committed to donating a brand-new stainless steel water tank truck to the province. The vehicle will ferry potable water to communities currently experiencing acute supply disruptions.

Article continues after this 

READ: Water aid arrives in Dinagat Islands amid severe crisis

Gov. Demerey stated the collaboration provides a critical opportunity to stabilize the province’s water security and build resilience against future climate-induced dry spells.

Article continues after this 

Aside from utility infrastructure, the meeting reopened talks on broader industrial ties between the conglomerate and the local government. In July 2022, Gov. Demerey first announced SMC plans to invest $500 million (approximately ₱27.7 billion) to establish an electric vehicle (EV) battery manufacturing plant within its mining claims in the province, which span across the mineral-rich towns of Cagdianao, San Jose, and Basilisa.

The planned facility aims to tap the island’s vast natural deposits of nickel, manganese, chromite, and iron—the raw materials essential for producing electric car batteries. During Thursday’s high-level huddle, officials touched on prospective SMC investments to further advance local industrialization, including the feasibility of establishing a new agri-industrial zone to stimulate employment and economic growth.

World.title: Ridon: Malicious prosecution rap vs Sara Duterte husband ‘on the table’
World.content:
Rep. Terry Ridon. Screengrab from House of Representatives/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — House impeachment prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said Thursday that lawmakers may file a malicious prosecution case against Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, following the dismissal of Carpio’s complaint against them.

Ridon said the possible legal action would be discussed with his colleagues before any decision is made.

“So, ’yung usapin po ng malicious prosecution, pag-usapan ho namin if kailangan ba naming kasuhan pa si Atty. Mans Carpio dito sa bagay po na ito (we will discuss the issue of malicious prosecution and whether we need to file a case against Atty. Mans Carpio over this matter),” Ridon said during a press briefing at the House of Representatives.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ridon, Diokno to present evidence on alleged Duterte unexplained wealth

“But I think at this point, that is on the table,” he added.

Ridon said he would first consult the other lawmakers involved.

“Well, I have to talk to the other colleagues, no? Kung ano ho ’yung pagtingin nila sa bagay po na ito (to hear their views on this matter),” he said.

READ: Abante: Sara Duterte self-incrimination plea could raise questions

Article continues after this 

“Pero I think very clear ho na walang batayan, basura, panggulo itong kaso na ito (But I think it is very clear that this case has no basis, is baseless and is merely disruptive),” he added.

Carpio filed the complaint after financial records belonging to him and Duterte were discussed during the House Committee on Justice proceedings on the impeachment complaints against the Vice President.

Article continues after this 

He accused Ridon and several other lawmakers and government officials of violating the Bank Secrecy Law, Data Privacy Act and Anti-Money Laundering Act in connection with the disclosure and handling of the records.

The lawmakers were among those who took part in the committee proceedings where the financial documents were discussed.

Ridon said Carpio’s complaint even sought to hold lawmakers liable for failing to object to a motion involving the records.

He maintained that the lawmakers were acting within the scope of their official legislative duties.

“Kasi ang gampanin naman ho namin dito sa House Justice Committee proceeding ay actual na trabaho ng mambabatas (because our role in the House Justice Committee proceedings was part of the actual work of lawmakers),” Ridon said.

“And again, saan ho kayo nakakita ng gustong ipakulong, gustong sampahan ng kaso dahil hindi nag-object sa isang motion? (And again, where have you seen someone being sought to be jailed or charged simply for failing to object to a motion?) Ngayon lang ho talaga kami nakarinig, nakakita ng ganoon pong kaso (This is really the first time we have heard of or seen such a case),” he added.

The Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office dismissed Carpio’s complaint without prejudice on jurisdictional grounds, saying the matter should have been filed before the Office of the Ombudsman.

Carpio’s camp has said the dismissal was not a ruling on the merits of his allegations and that he could refile the complaint with the Ombudsman.

Ridon, however, maintained that the complaint had no basis regardless of where it was filed.

“But again, irrespective of venue, whether Ombudsman or sa piskalya po (whether before the Ombudsman or the prosecutor’s office), tingin po namin no basis (we believe there is no basis),” he said.

Ridon also challenged Carpio to pursue the complaint before the Ombudsman, saying he was confident it would be dismissed again.

World.title: Ridon, Diokno to present evidence on alleged Duterte unexplained wealth
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors Reps. Terry Ridon and Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno will lead the presentation of evidence on Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth when proceedings on Article II of the impeachment complaint begin on Monday, Ridon said Thursday.

Ridon said he and Diokno would alternate in presenting evidence and making legal arguments as the prosecution seeks to establish its allegations against Duterte.

The prosecution has asked the impeachment court to subpoena three witnesses: retired Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang; lawyer Karen Batu, identified by Ridon as officer-in-charge of the Office of the Ombudsman’s records division; and Securities and Exchange Commission Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo F. Del Rosario.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sara Duterte calls on Marcos to resign: ‘You’re a liar, abusive’

Cabotaje-Tang is expected to testify on public accountability, integrity in public office and legal principles involving undisclosed wealth and prohibited business interests, Ridon said.

Batu is expected to testify on Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, particularly those filed with the Ombudsman. Del Rosario is expected to authenticate company records that the prosecution plans to present as evidence.

The prosecution expects Cabotaje-Tang to testify first, followed by Batu and Del Rosario, although the sequence could change depending on the proceedings.

Prosecutors may also call representatives from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, bank managers and personnel from the Philippine National Police firearms division to identify documents relevant to the case.

Article continues after this 

Ridon said the prosecution already has tax records involving Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, as well as bank records linked to the couple and their companies.

The impeachment court has given the defense 15 days to respond to 104 requests for admission involving bank accounts and other records. Matters admitted by the defense may no longer require additional witnesses, but the response period will not delay the prosecution’s presentation of evidence.

Article continues after this 

Ridon said prosecutors had factored in the possibility that the defense would reject the requests and were targeting completion of the Article II presentation by the first or second week of October.

The prosecution may also drop some witnesses if the evidence presented is sufficient to establish its case, he said.

World.title: Measures vs harmful social media content raised at Senate hearing
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—The idea of disabling the automatic promotion and demonetizing violent and sexually graphic content was floated at a Senate hearing on Friday in light of recent incidents of violence in schools allegedly linked to online games.

While tackling the proposed P49.99 million budget of the Movie and Television Review and Classification (MTRCB) for 2027, Sen. Erwin Tulfo raised the August 18 school shooting in Zamboanga City that left two students dead, including the shooter.

READ: 2 reported victims in Zamboanga City school building

Earlier reports said that video games might have influenced the perpetrator, a Grade 8 student, who opened fire on campus while livestreaming the incident through a body camera on a website and social media.

READ: Remulla: Video games led Tacloban, Zamboanga shooters to rabbit hole

“May steps po ba kayo? Are you already talking about this? How do you, your agency will control this?” Tulfo asked during the hearing of the Senate subcommittee on finance.

While explaining that online gaming and video games are not covered by the agency’s mandate, MTRCB Chairperson Diorella Maria “Lala” Sotto-Antonio told the panel that they have been conducting “exploratory research” on the matter.

“We are continuing the discussions on this exploration,” Sotto-Antonio said, before referring the question to MTRCB Executive Director Roberto Diciembre.

Citing global studies on violence in social media, Diciembre said the country could adopt a “do not amplify” policy that would require major social media platforms to block automatic promotions and monetizations of violent content.

“If there will be a law na hahawakan ang mga social media na ito, we can tell them na dapat hindi naka-autoplay ang mga violent content sa mga materials natin,” he said.

(“If there will be a law governing these social media platforms, we can tell them that violent content in their materials should not be set to autoplay.)

“Kung pwede, hindi ma-monetize because sa totoo lang, isa sa mga motivation ng mga content creators, syempre ma-monetize yung gagawin nilang content. If these videos, at yung violent videos, sex videos ay made-demonetize, I think mababawasan yung mga gano’ng materials,” Diciembre added.

(“If possible, they should not be monetized because, to be honest, one of the motivations of content creators is, of course, to monetize the content they produce. If these videos, particularly violent and sexually explicit videos, are demonetized, I think there would be fewer such materials.”)

There should also be stronger protections for minors using these platforms, such as age-gating graphic content and imposing enhanced safeguards for livestreaming.

“Repeated exposure to violent content should trigger additional safeguards,” the MTRCB official said.

Diciembre answered in the affirmative when Tulfo asked whether the MTRCB could do nothing for now in the absence of a law granting it authority over these online platformers.

There are ongoing discussions in Congress on a measure seeking to ban social media use among children under 13.

World.title: Legarda, Leviste did not do anything illegal – spox
World.content:
Sen. Loren Legarda and Rep. Leandro Leviste. INQUIRER PHOTOS / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda’s camp has maintained that she and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, have not “done anything illegal” amid investigations into the latter’s solar panel company.

Tony La Viña, Legarda’s spokesperson, described the allegations against the mother and son as “political persecution,” primarily because no formal charges have been filed against Legarda or Leviste yet.

This comes as the plunder and graft complaint against the two remains under preliminary investigation at the Office of the Ombudsman in connection with Solar Para sa Bayan (SPBC) and Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc., owned by Leviste while he was still a private citizen.

Article continues after this 

“Against that backdrop, the subsequent inclusion of Senator Legarda in an Ombudsman preliminary investigation, and the timing with which that proceeding emerged, inevitably raise questions about whether the scrutiny against her is grounded in evidence of her own acts or is being driven by the wider political issues surrounding her son,” La Viña said in a statement posted on his Facebook page on Friday.

READ: Ombudsman reveals graft, plunder raps vs Loren Legarda, Leandro Leviste

He also said Legarda “does not own, run, or take part” in SPBC or any other solar energy companies. There was also no evidence showing her connection with Leviste’s businesses, rather than simply being his mother.

“Saying she’s connected to the business only because she’s the mother of a private businessman is pure invention. Being a parent and being a senator does not in any way prove she benefited, acted improperly, or committed a crime,” he added.

Legarda and Leviste already filed their counter-affidavit this week as ordered by the anti-graft court, according to the spokesman.

Article continues after this 

He added that he will represent Legarda and her son in cases that may be filed against them.

READ: Ombudsman doubts circumstances of Legarda’s ‘serious’ illness

Article continues after this 

The Ombudsman raised suspicions after Legarda and Leviste flew abroad last August amid an ongoing probe into alleged P10.44-billion irregularities involving Leviste’s solar companies.

Legarda, who is currently on medical leave, filed to extend her absence, while Leviste requested a two-month travel authority from July 26 to Sept. 24.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla insinuated that the two may not return to the country to evade the issue.

“The ombudsman’s public pronouncements convey the unmistakable impression that liability has already been assumed, notwithstanding that the matters involving them remain at the preliminary investigation stage,” La Viña said.

The case stemmed from more than 30 service contracts in the government that Leviste obtained in 2013.

The ombudsman alleged that the number of service contracts “created a virtual monopoly of solar energy projects.”

However, La Viña explained, “Solar Para sa Bayan is one corporation. Other Solar Philippines companies are separate entities. A congressional franchise is different from a renewable energy service contract. Both a service contract and a franchise are not given government funds.”

He dismissed the claim that DOE’s renewable energy service contract is a monopoly, noting the 518 commercial solar energy projects and 1,362 renewable energy projects in the country.

“The franchise was not sold, contrary to what government people have been saying. The franchise could not be fully operationalized because the DOE did not issue the implementing rules and did not identify the areas where the franchise can operate—conditions which the franchise law required,” he added.

He also said that Leviste “should be praised, not punished” for his energy initiatives in the country.

World.title: How Will Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Work? New Rules Set Sessions, Ethics and Penalties
World.content:
ASTANA – Deputies of Kazakhstan’s Kurultai will face new rules governing their conduct inside and outside the legislative chamber, with violations ranging from inappropriate remarks and providing unverified information to breaches of parliamentary ethics that could result in public apologies, restrictions on speaking and other disciplinary measures.

Deputy Chair of the Kurultai Daniya Yespayeva outlined the rules at a briefing for media representatives after the plenary meeting of deputies on Sept. 10.

The new provisions form part of the Kurultai’s approved regulations, which establish the procedures for the legislative body’s work, including parliamentary sessions, the legislative process, government hours, hearings and the activities of parliamentary factions and committees.

Kurultai to meet Wednesdays and Thursdays

Under the new regulations, the Kurultai’s regular session will run from the first working day of September to the last working day of June. Plenary sessions will generally be held on Wednesdays and Thursdays, while hearings will take place on Fridays and government hours on Mondays.

Sessions will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with a break from 1 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. The Kurultai or its Bureau may decide to hold sessions at other times when necessary. A session is valid when at least two-thirds of the total number of deputies are present, meaning at least 97 deputies.

The regulations provide for open sessions as the general rule. Open meetings will be broadcast, including online through Kurultai’s internet resources. The legislative body will maintain transcripts and video recordings, and will also publish transcripts of open sessions on its website.

Between regular sessions, deputies will continue exercising their powers, including initiating legislation, preparing amendments to laws and working with constituents. Deputies may travel to the regions for up to 10 calendar days, and such visits must take place at least twice during a session.

Deputies are required to provide verified information

According to Yespayeva, violations of parliamentary ethics may include unjustified remarks directed at speakers and statements that insult or otherwise affect the honor and dignity of deputies or other individuals.

The ethical requirements will apply not only during Kurultai sessions and meetings of its factions, groups and other bodies, but also to deputies’ conduct outside the legislature. Specific requirements also apply to deputies’ interactions with the media. In public statements, responses and interviews, deputies are expected to provide verified and accurate information.

“Simply saying that something is not being fulfilled, or citing certain facts when they are not reliable, will also constitute a violation of parliamentary ethics,” Yespayeva said.

The provision emphasizes deputies’ responsibility for public statements, particularly because their comments to the media can influence public perceptions of government policies and legislative work.

Disciplinary measures range from reprimands to salary deductions

A Council on Parliamentary Ethics will be established to consider complaints concerning deputies’ conduct. The council will accept appeals from individuals and legal entities and will also conduct educational work on parliamentary ethics.

The council’s regulations were adopted the day before the briefing. Several types of disciplinary measures are available for violations. A deputy may receive a reprimand or be required to issue a public apology.

More serious measures include being prohibited from speaking at one Kurultai session or, in more severe cases, at three sessions. The law also provides for a deputy to be removed from one or three Kurultai sessions.

The most severe sanction among those outlined by Yespayeva is the withholding of one day’s salary. However, the Council on Parliamentary Ethics will not decide on sanctions independently. It will consider the alleged violation and issue a decision, after which the matter will be considered at a Kurultai session.

Council to focus on both enforcement and prevention

Yespayeva stressed that the Council on Parliamentary Ethics will have a broader role than simply reviewing complaints. It will also conduct explanatory work to help deputies understand the rules and standards governing their conduct.

The emphasis on guidance reflects the significant renewal of the Kurultai’s current composition. According to Yespayeva, nearly 70–80% of the deputies are new, meaning that many are working within the legislative framework for the first time.

The council’s explanatory function is therefore intended to help deputies understand the boundaries of acceptable conduct and their responsibilities before violations occur.

New regulations define Kurultai’s legislative work

The regulations also establish the procedures for considering draft laws. Most bills will be considered in three readings, while legislation on the ratification or denunciation of international treaties will be considered in two readings.

The first reading will focus on a bill’s goals, objectives and main provisions, as well as its potential social, economic, legal, environmental and other consequences. The second reading will consider amendments submitted by deputies, committees and party factions. The third reading will generally be limited to amendments needed to bring a draft law into compliance with the Constitution and legislation, eliminate contradictions and address editorial or legal-technical issues. Substantive changes will not be introduced at this stage.

Parliamentary opposition receives procedural guarantees

The regulations also establish procedures for the parliamentary majority and opposition. A political party holding the largest number of deputy mandates is recognized as the majority. Political parties represented in the Kurultai but not part of the majority may form a parliamentary opposition.

The opposition will have specific procedural rights. It may initiate hearings at least once during each session and determine the agenda of a government hour at least twice per session. The regulations also provide for opposition representation in the leadership of permanent committees.

The framework also regulates the work of party factions and deputy groups, requiring at least 15 deputies to establish a deputy group. The new rules thus combine procedures governing legislative work with requirements concerning deputies’ individual conduct and accountability.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Security Council’s Focus to Cybersecurity, AI and Economic Crime
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Security Council is expanding its focus to a broader range of national security risks, including information and cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, personal data protection, economic crime and civil protection, under new regulations approved by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Sept. 11.

Tokayev signed a decree approving the regulations on the Security Council and its Apparatus and defining the powers of the deputy chair of the Security Council. The Security Council and its Apparatus will be responsible for comprehensive analysis of global threats and challenges, as well as current aspects of the domestic situation.

The new framework also strengthens coordination and oversight of measures related to national security, defense capability, legality and public order.

Expanded powers of the Deputy Chair

The deputy chair of the Security Council will oversee the full and unconditional implementation of acts and instructions issued by the Chair of the Security Council President Tokayev, as well as decisions adopted by the Security Council, including those made at operational meetings.

According to the new regulation, the deputy chair will coordinate the activities of state bodies and organizations in implementing measures related to national security and the country’s defense capability, as well as maintaining legality and public order.

The responsibilities also extend to emerging and cross-cutting security issues. These include information and cybersecurity, including the use of artificial intelligence, protection of personal data, combating corruption and economic crime, and civil protection. The deputy chair will coordinate the work of government bodies and organizations in these areas, conduct international cooperation and coordinate the activities of the Security Council Apparatus.

Apparatus to operate under direct presidential accountability

Under the decree, the Security Council Apparatus is defined as an independent state body directly subordinate to and accountable to the President. Its activities aim to strengthen and improve control over national security risks, ensure the resilience of public administration, and provide institutional support for implementing decisions of the President, the chair of the Security Council, and the council itself.

The new provisions are intended to strengthen the protection of Kazakhstan’s sovereignty and independence, territorial integrity and national interests in the international arena, as well as the foundations of the constitutional order.

The changes follow Tokayev’s Aug. 28 decree and were accompanied by changes in the Security Council’s leadership. Aida Balayeva was appointed Deputy Chair, while Gizat Nurdauletov was relieved of his position as Secretary of the Security Council.

World.title: Electrification is Reshaping Global Economy and Kazakhstan Has Lot at Stake
World.content:
ASTANA – The global energy transition is often discussed through the language of climate targets, emissions cuts and renewable energy. Yet the next stage of the transformation may be defined by a more practical question: how much economic activity can countries run on electricity, and how efficiently can they do it?

According to Clem Perry, global lead for clean energy supply at the World Resources Institute (WRI) Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, electrification is moving beyond a climate strategy to become a question of affordability, competitiveness, energy security and resilience to volatile fossil fuel markets. The shift is visible in electric buses, heat pumps, electric vehicles and increasingly electrified industrial processes, but its implications extend far beyond individual technologies.

The global economy still has a long way to go. According to WRI, electricity accounts for about 20% of final energy use globally, with the share approaching 30% in China, compared with roughly 22% in the United States and 21% in the European Union. Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency (IEA) says global electric car sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with electric cars accounting for one in four new cars sold worldwide.

These figures point to a structural change rather than a temporary technology trend. More economic activity is shifting from direct fossil-fuel combustion toward electricity, from transport and buildings to industrial equipment. But electrification does not necessarily mean consuming more energy. Its economic logic lies partly in efficiency.

Perry notes that combustion engines can waste as much as 80% of the energy contained in fuel, while electric motors can convert around 80% of electrical energy into motion. Heat pumps can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity consumed. This means an economy can use more electricity while using less energy overall to achieve the same output.

This creates a second, less obvious transformation: as households and businesses electrify transport and heating, electricity consumption may rise while overall energy costs can fall because electric technologies are more efficient. Avoided fossil-fuel costs can offset higher electricity costs, although the scale of savings varies by market and technology. WRI cites an analysis estimating that fully electrifying a typical European household’s heating and transport could cut its overall energy bill by more than half.

But the transition also exposes a new constraint: electricity networks. The challenge facing many economies will not only be whether they can generate enough power, but whether their grids can deliver it at the right place and at the right time. Electric vehicles, industrial facilities, data centers, cooling systems and new housing are all adding demand to networks that in many countries are already under pressure.

This is where the next phase of electrification becomes more sophisticated. Not every new megawatt of demand requires another megawatt of generation. Some consumption can be shifted in time. Electric vehicles can charge overnight, buildings can pre-heat or pre-cool, and batteries, water heaters and certain industrial processes can respond to periods of grid congestion. Smart controls can automate much of this without requiring consumers to change their daily routines.

Why electrification matters for Kazakhstan’s competitiveness

For Kazakhstan, this global trend is becoming increasingly relevant. The country is seeking to expand industrial production, transport, digital infrastructure and data centers — all areas that depend on reliable and increasingly large amounts of electricity. As economist Ruslan Sultanov, author of the Tengenomika channel, notes, the issue should be considered not only in terms of electricity generation but also in terms of economic efficiency. The key question is not simply how many kilowatt-hours Kazakhstan can produce, but how much industrial output and added value the economy can generate from each megawatt.

For Kazakhstan, this could change how we define energy competitiveness. Generating more electricity will remain important, but generation capacity alone will not be enough.

Sultanov points to the importance of networks, storage, demand management and the ability to connect new industrial consumers quickly. The ability to move electricity to where it is needed and manage demand when networks are under pressure could therefore become nearly as important as the amount of power produced. This is particularly relevant as Kazakhstan seeks to expand industrial production and other electricity-intensive activities.

Sultanov also raises a broader industrial question: how much of the investment generated by a more electrified economy can remain inside Kazakhstan through domestic production, construction, technology and services? In that sense, electrification could become an opportunity to deepen domestic value creation rather than simply increase electricity consumption.

At the same time, electrification has clear limits. Steelmaking, chemical production, aviation and shipping remain harder to electrify directly, while hydrogen, synthetic fuels and other low-carbon alternatives may be more suitable for some applications. As Perry notes, the practical objective is not to “electrify everything” regardless of cost, but to electrify directly where it makes the most economic and efficiency sense while reserving other technologies for harder-to-electrify sectors.

For Kazakhstan, that distinction matters. The country does not need to replicate the energy pathway of China, Europe or the United States. It needs to identify where electrification can generate the greatest economic return — from urban transport and industrial processes to buildings, digital infrastructure and new manufacturing.

The global energy transition is therefore moving into a new phase. The question is no longer simply how to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources of power, but how to build an economy that uses electricity more efficiently, connects new demand faster and converts additional power capacity into greater productivity. Perry’s analysis highlights the importance of grid expansion, smarter demand management and coordination between power, transport, buildings and industry, while Sultanov’s Kazakhstan-focused argument emphasizes the economic value created from electricity.

For Kazakhstan, that may ultimately be the more important measure of the transition: not simply how many kilowatt-hours the country produces, but how much economic value it can generate from each megawatt. Sultanov’s central argument is that the focus should increasingly be on the amount of industrial output and added value the economy can derive from its electricity resources.

World.title: China-Central Asia Trade Surpasses $100 Billion as SCMP Hosts Landmark Conference in Astana
World.content:
ASTANA – Trade between China and the five Central Asian states has surpassed $100 billion, highlighting the region’s growing economic importance, as the South China Morning Post (SCMP) convened policymakers, business leaders, investors and innovators in Astana on Sept. 7 for its China Conference: Central Asia 2026.

Co-hosted by SCMP and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the conference focused on capital, resources and the digital Silk Road and examined deepening economic, technological and capital links between Greater China and Central Asia.

The event marked the first time a Hong Kong media organization has brought an event of this scale to Central Asia, following Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee’s official visit to the region in June.

Connecting capital and innovation

The conference explored capital pathways and dual listings, intelligent mining and energy transition, the digital Silk Road, and healthcare and talent development. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee highlighted the city’s role as a bridge between China and global markets.

“Hong Kong stands ready as your trusted partner, connecting markets, financing sustainable growth and driving seamless cross-boundary trade,” he said.

Former Hong Kong Chief Executive CY Leung described Central Asia as a “key BRI [Belt and Road Initiative] region” and Kazakhstan as a “key BRI country,” saying the conference could identify opportunities for broader economic cooperation through Hong Kong, “the super-connector.”

Strengthening financial ties

AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said China is one of Kazakhstan’s key strategic partners and stressed the potential for greater two-way capital flows and closer market connections.

“Our focus is on turning this strong relationship into greater two-way capital flows, closer connections between our markets, and tangible investment opportunities,” he said.

SCMP Publisher Tammy Tam said Hong Kong is “uniquely positioned to connect Central Asia’s rising dynamic with global capital and influence.”

She noted that the conference brought together delegates, industry leaders and representatives from more than 100 companies spanning Hong Kong, the Greater Bay Area, mainland China and ASEAN.

Healthcare cooperation

CY Leung also announced that the GX Foundation, together with Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Healthcare and Nazarbayev University, will co-host a seminar on Global Medical Frontiers at Nazarbayev University on Oct. 5.

The seminar will cover clinical technology, health system management and traditional medicine, vector-borne diseases, habitat and disaster response, medical education and humanitarian talent.

World.title: From National SDGs to Regional Delivery: Central Asia’s Next Step
World.content:
Central Asia has entered a new phase of regional cooperation. The question is no longer simply whether the five countries can work together. Increasingly, it is whether growing political trust can be converted into practical institutions, shared measurements and tangible results for the people of the region.

The Sustainable Development Goals offer an important test.

Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan have each incorporated the 2030 Agenda into national development policies to varying degrees. Yet some of the region’s most difficult development challenges cannot be solved within national borders.

Water flows across them. Energy systems increasingly depend on regional balancing and trade. Climate change affects shared river basins, glaciers, pastures and ecosystems. Transport corridors only deliver their full economic value when they function across several countries. Air pollution, desertification and food security similarly have a regional dimension.

This creates a fundamental mismatch: many challenges are regional, while most mechanisms for implementing and measuring the SDGs remain national.

A foundation already exists

Central Asia is not starting from zero.

In 2021, the European Union and UNDP launched a Regional SDG Platform designed to work with governments and civil society in all five Central Asian states. The initiative supported knowledge exchange, policy analysis, monitoring and SDG financing. In 2024, a Regional SDG Monitoring Panel was launched to provide an integrated regional view of trends, policies, interlinkages, financing and data gaps.

Kazakhstan has played an important role in this process.

More significantly, Almaty is becoming home to the United Nations Regional Centre for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan. In August 2025, UN Secretary-General António Guterres and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev witnessed the signing of the host country agreement. Guterres said the Centre could help translate stronger political relations in Central Asia into deeper economic integration.

The opportunity now is to turn that institutional foundation into measurable results.

Start with a limited number of shared priorities

Regional cooperation does not require Central Asian countries to create a second set of 17 SDGs or duplicate national institutions. A more realistic approach would be to identify a small number of issues where regional action clearly adds value.

Water and energy should be among the first.

Upstream and downstream interests have historically made this one of Central Asia’s most complicated policy areas. Climate change is making coordination increasingly unavoidable. Changes in glaciers and river flows affect agriculture, hydropower generation, ecosystems and drinking-water security across borders.

Instead of addressing water, energy and climate adaptation through separate policy tracks, countries could gradually develop shared indicators covering water efficiency, seasonal energy exchange, ecosystem resilience and climate risks.

Transport connectivity provides another opportunity. Governments understandably measure new roads, railways, border facilities and trade volumes nationally. But the real economic value of a corridor depends on the performance of the entire route.

Regional indicators could therefore measure border-crossing times, logistics reliability, digital customs interoperability and the environmental footprint of major corridors.

From data exchange to shared accountability

A regional approach also requires better data.

Central Asian governments already collect large volumes of statistics for national SDG monitoring. The challenge is not necessarily to create more indicators, but to make selected data comparable and useful for joint decision-making.

The existing regional SDG monitoring experience provides a starting point. The next step could be a compact regional dashboard focusing only on cross-border challenges. Governments, research institutions, civil society and international organizations could jointly review progress on a limited set of indicators each year.

This would not replace national reporting to the United Nations. It would complement it.

The difference is important. National reports ask: How is our country progressing? A regional mechanism would ask another question: Where can cooperation produce an outcome that no country can achieve alone?

The political moment is favorable

There is also a broader political reason to move now.

On 20 May 2026, the UN General Assembly adopted without a vote Resolution 80/260, “Strengthening regional cooperation and economic integration to ensure sustainable development in the Central Asian region.” The resolution encourages closer coordination among Central Asian states and calls on UN agencies, funds and programmes to align their activities with regional priorities.

This provides political legitimacy for moving from general commitments toward practical regional instruments.

The UN Regional Centre in Almaty could become an important platform for this work — not as a supranational institution, but as a neutral facilitator of data exchange, policy dialogue, expertise and joint initiatives.

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, as the region’s two largest economies, have a particular opportunity to support this transition. But sustainable regionalism cannot be built around two countries alone. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are indispensable to water and energy cooperation; Turkmenistan is critical to connectivity, energy and engagement with Afghanistan.

The principle must therefore remain inclusive: five countries, shared ownership and practical benefits for all.

A Central Asian contribution to the global SDG debate

The implications could reach beyond the region.

The 2030 Agenda was designed around universal goals implemented primarily through national frameworks. Yet many of today’s development challenges — climate change, water scarcity, migration, energy transition, ecosystems and transport connectivity — are inherently transboundary.

Central Asia could help demonstrate how the gap between national commitments and regional realities can be narrowed.

The region does not need grand new structures. It needs a disciplined transition from dialogue to delivery: a few shared priorities, comparable indicators, regular review and joint projects where cooperation produces demonstrably better outcomes.

The political rapprochement of recent years has created an opportunity. The institutional foundations are beginning to emerge.

The next measure of Central Asian cooperation should therefore be not how often countries meet, but what they can achieve together.

The author is Jakhongir Isaev, the head of Department at the Center for Sustainable Development in Uzbekistan.

World.title: Kazakh Businesses to Trade Carbon Units on AIFC Exchange
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh businesses implementing environmental projects will be able to trade carbon units on the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) exchange under a planned agreement with the international carbon standard Verra, AIFC Product Director Zhanbolat Kakishev said at Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026.

“We will sign an agreement with the Verra standard. This will allow us to trade carbon units. Verra is one of the largest standards in this field. We will introduce it on our exchange, enabling entrepreneurs involved in environmental projects to trade carbon units directly on our exchange platform,” Kakishev said.

The agreement is expected to be signed during the AFD, taking place on Sept. 9-10.

The initiative is designed to expand access to the international carbon market for businesses implementing projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions.

Verra is an international nonprofit organization that develops standards for verifying greenhouse gas emission reductions and removals. Its Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) enables independently verified environmental projects to issue carbon units.

One carbon unit generally represents one metric ton of greenhouse gas emissions reduced or removed from the atmosphere, measured in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e). Such units can then be traded with companies and other carbon market participants.

AFD participants also discussed Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop new asset classes and expand the country’s digital financial infrastructure, reflecting a broader push to modernize its capital markets.

AFD 2026 is held under the theme Delivering Impact. Capital in Action has attracted more than 8,000 registered participants, including representatives of major international investment companies and funds managing nearly $26 trillion in assets.

World.title: AFD 2026 Delivers New Agreements, Market Instruments for Regional Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026: Delivering Impact. Capital in Action concluded with a series of agreements and new financial instruments to strengthen regional financial cooperation, sustainable finance, digital assets, aviation finance and access to capital.

Held on Sept. 9-10, the forum brought together 8,000 participants from 90 countries, including representatives of major global financial institutions and asset managers collectively managing more than $26 trillion. The forum also featured renowned Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.

Expanding regional financial cooperation

Several agreements signed during the forum focused on regulatory cooperation and improving cross-border access to financial markets.

The Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the National Bank of Georgia on mutual access and recognition in financial services. The agreement establishes a framework for closer regulatory cooperation between the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Georgian financial markets in selected areas.

AFSA also signed an MoU with the Croatian Financial Services Supervisory Agency (HANFA) to strengthen regulatory cooperation and further develop cooperation between the two authorities.

The agreements complement discussions held during the forum on reducing fragmentation between regional financial markets and facilitating cross-border capital flows.

The Astana International Exchange (AIX) and the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange (KSE) also agreed to strengthen cooperation and engagement between Kazakhstan’s and the Kyrgyz Republic’s capital markets.

New instruments for sustainable finance

A major development on the second day was AIX’s launch of trading in voluntary carbon credits verified under the international Verified Carbon Standard (VCS).

AIX became the first exchange in Central Asia to provide its own infrastructure for trading voluntary carbon credits. London-based Valor Carbon became the first supplier, with Standard International Market, an AIX broker and Trading Member, facilitating transactions.

The new exchange-based model is designed to provide transparent trading rules and market-based price discovery for carbon credits, creating an additional mechanism for climate projects in the region to access financing.

The initiative builds on the AIFC Carbon Platform and expands AIX’s environmental products, following the earlier introduction of I-REC renewable energy certificates.

The forum also advanced cooperation in sustainable finance through agreements involving the AIFC Green Finance Center, First Carbon Group, Green Investment Group and HYT-CAPITAL. The agreements aim to support sustainable projects, develop financial instruments and attract investment through capital markets in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

Aviation and digital assets

Aviation finance was another area where discussions moved toward practical cooperation. The AIFC and Development Bank of Kazakhstan agreed to cooperate on projects related to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The forum also highlighted the development of Kazakhstan’s aviation finance ecosystem. Jupiter Jet completed its first aircraft leasing transaction with an American lessor with support from the AIFC Aviation Finance Hub.

Digital finance and tokenization featured prominently throughout AFD 2026. Tech Hub Ltd. and ōzen signed a framework cooperation agreement to develop a music royalty tokenization platform in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Other agreements involving CodeCoin Tech Ltd., Delta DA Ltd. and Altyn Bank focused on cross-border financial services, fintech, asset management, trade finance and payment infrastructure.

From discussion to implementation

The agreements signed at AFD 2026 reflect the forum’s broader focus on turning investment opportunities into practical projects and market infrastructure.

The first day centered on sovereign and institutional capital, financial infrastructure, tokenization and the transformation of global finance. The program also included the launch of the AIFC Junior Mining Platform’s investor activities, with 23 early-stage mining projects presented to potential investors.

On the second day, the focus shifted further toward implementation – from carbon-credit trading and aviation finance to regional regulatory cooperation and new digital instruments.

As AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said at the opening of the forum, competition for capital increasingly depends on the ability to transform opportunities into real projects and investments.

Against this backdrop, the agreements and market initiatives announced during AFD 2026 demonstrate the AIFC’s efforts to position Astana as a platform connecting international capital with investment opportunities in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

World.title: Dimash Calls for Investment, Infrastructure to Unlock Kazakhstan’s Creative Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer, composer and producer Dimash Qudaibergen called for greater investment, infrastructure and legal support for Kazakhstan’s creative industries during the opening ceremony of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 on Sept. 9.

AFD 2026 is a two-day event bringing together more than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries to discuss capital markets, investment, artificial intelligence, innovation, real-economy financing and cross-border capital.

While on stage, Qudaibergen performed “Aqerke,” “Stranger” and “Weekend,” as well as the traditional Kazakh kui “Adai” on dombra.

Following the performance, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov spoke with Qudaibergen about the potential of Kazakhstan’s creative economy, attracting investment to the sector, intellectual property protection and the challenges artists face when entering international markets.

Qudaibergen said the development of the creative industry requires not only investment, but also stronger legal protection for artists and mechanisms to connect creators with investors.

“Artists need legal protection and support from creative industry development funds. These funds can become a bridge between investors and new creative projects,” Qudaibergen said.

Bekturov noted that Kazakhstan’s creative sector brings together thousands of companies and more than 140,000 people, while its contribution to the economy remains relatively small, highlighting the need to develop the sector as a source of future growth.

When asked why investors should consider creative industries, Qudaibergen pointed to Kazakhstan’s culture, history and music as assets with strong international appeal.

“Our culture, our history and the music are truly unique, and that makes them interesting to an international audience,” he said, drawing on his experience of performing around the world.

Protecting creative independence

For Qudaibergen, attracting investment should not come at the expense of an artist’s independence or ownership of intellectual property.

He said the decision to share rights with investors or business partners is ultimately personal, but artists should understand the financial and contractual side of their profession before making such decisions.

“I choose the second option, because for me it is essential to keep both creative independence and ownership of my intellectual property,” he said.

Qudaibergen stressed that financial literacy is part of an artist’s professional responsibility, allowing creators to better understand contracts, finances and the business side of the industry.

“Education everywhere is very important,” he said, adding that understanding contracts, finances and the business side of the industry allows artists to make informed decisions and retain control over their work.

He also cited his own career as an example of how an artist can gradually move from performer to producer and entrepreneur.

Qudaibergen said he now works directly with business partners and operates his own label, established by his father, which promotes not only his work but also young artists.

His transition into production included an international vocal project on China’s Hunan TV, where he first gained international recognition through “I’m a Singer” show. Returning to the network as a producer, he said, gave him an opportunity to introduce other Kazakh talents to a global audience.

From Kazakh roots to global audiences

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s cultural identity can become a competitive advantage internationally when traditional heritage is combined with contemporary approaches.

“Our uniqueness comes from combining respect for our roots with a desire to innovate,” he said. “We can make traditional things feel fresh and turn something authentic into a modern trend.”

During his tours, Qudaibergen has introduced audiences to musicians from his team and traditional Kazakh instruments, including dombra and kobyz. He said some international fans also became interested in Kazakhstan’s history, language and traditional music.

He also encouraged young Kazakh artists to remain connected to their identity while pursuing international careers.

“To become an international artist, you have to follow your own path, first of all. And then you need to believe in yourself,” he said.

He warned young artists against changing direction simply because of short-term financial opportunities.

“Professional career management means thinking long term,” he said. “You shouldn’t accept every offer just because it looks profitable today. You always have to remember the goal you are moving towards.”

Building a system for young talent

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s creative sector needs a more systematic approach to developing talent, particularly in management, professional training, broadcasting and distribution.

He identified a shortage of qualified professionals as one of the industry’s key challenges, arguing that talented artists need more than opportunities to perform.

“We have not yet become a full-fledged industry with a clear system. So, we need to do our best to train professionals,” he said.

He also pointed to the limited presence of creative projects across television, radio and large-scale distribution platforms.

“The main task is to build professional infrastructure and create a clear, systematic path to international markets,” Qudaibergen said.

Qudaibergen said this was particularly important because young artists should not have to rely on chance encounters or simply hope that someone will discover them.

“This is exactly what I was missing when I started,” he said, recalling his own experience as a young artist from Aktobe who had little understanding of how to build an international career.

“Right now, it has become one more mission,” he said. “Young talents should grow inside a real creative development system, instead of simply hoping that one day they will get lucky and someone will invite them somewhere.”

Qudaibergen’s own career, from a young performer in Aktobe to an internationally recognized artist and producer, illustrates the potential of such opportunities. Reflecting on his journey, he emphasized that talent alone is not enough to build a lasting career.

“Hard work is also very important. It’s the most important thing,” he said. “When the universe turns to your side, you need to be ready.”

Qudaibergen is now preparing his new Dimensions world tour, continuing his international career while expanding his work as a producer and supporting young Kazakh artists.

World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Property prices in Armenia rise again: new wave of emigration from Russia and other factors
World.content:
Armenia is seeing another wave of people relocating to the country, amid reports over the past two months of a possible mobilisation in Russia. As a result, both rents and property prices have risen again. On average, prices for rentals and properties for sale have increased by 20%.

At one point, prices were rising almost every day. This was evident from listings on popular online property sales and rental platforms. The biggest boom has been in the rental market. Activity is also increasing in cities near Yerevan, including Abovyan, Masis and Nor Hachn.

Most of those arriving are Armenians who had been living in Russia. They say they are moving to avoid being called up for military service and because of the uncertainty they have faced in recent months.

Amid the large influx, it has become difficult to find affordable and mid-range rental properties. This is also linked to students from the regions moving to the capital as the new academic year begins.

A Russian man found a job but cannot find a flat

Dmitry Popov arrived in Armenia with friends three weeks ago. They first stayed in Yerevan, then moved to Lori Province, where they found jobs in the towns of Alaverdi and Tumanyan.

He decided to stay in Yerevan, where he has acquaintances who offered him a place to stay. He has already found a job as a courier with one of Yerevan’s companies. He is now negotiating his pay with his employer. Meanwhile, Dmitry has been looking for a one- or two-bedroom flat in the outer districts of the capital. He cannot afford a place in the city centre because rents there are very high.

“At first, I was looking for a place for up to $500. Now I’m looking for one for $700. I still haven’t found anything because I need basic amenities — furniture and household appliances. Even when I find a flat with an average-quality renovation, it turns out there is no fridge, washing machine or comfortable sofa,” the young man explains.

He knows that the latest influx of migrants from Russia is largely driving the rise in prices.

After the initial influx and surge in prices during the first months of the Russia-Ukraine war, the property market began to stabilise. Prices fell slightly as many Russians returned home or moved to other countries. Now they have risen again.

“To be honest, I really like Yerevan. The city has its own rhythm, an interesting cultural scene, good food, friendly people and convenient public transport. I managed to find a job within a few days. Now I just need to find a flat. If I can’t find one in Yerevan, I’ll look in nearby towns. I’m asking local people how public transport works in the suburbs, what rental options are available and how lively those places are,” Dmitry says.

He says he did not have many options: he could either move to Yerevan or Tbilisi:

“I’ve visited both cities many times and had already been considering moving to one of them before the recent tensions in Russia. My friends who have lived in both cities recommended Yerevan, even though it is more expensive than Tbilisi. They said people in Yerevan are friendly, welcoming towards Russians and willing to help. They also said it would be easier to find a job here. By the way, they also suggested moving to other Armenian cities, such as Gyumri, Dilijan and Vanadzor.”

He says relatives in Russia call him to ask whether they should move to Armenia for the long term. He recommends it, although he also tells them about the problems.

He has already decided that if he manages to earn more in the future, he will buy a one-bedroom flat in Yerevan.

Factors affecting prices

Andranik Harutyunyan, director of Silver REA real estate agency, says apartment rents have risen by around 15% compared with last year. This is an average estimate, as prices vary significantly between different parts of the city and types of apartments.

The same applies to the property sales market. According to the estate agent, it is difficult to establish a single rate of price growth and compare it with last year’s figures:

“It is quite difficult to assess price changes in the primary market because developers sell apartments in residential complexes at different prices depending on the stage of construction. The secondary market is also seeing a noticeable increase in demand.”

Harutyunyan notes that members of the Armenian diaspora are showing greater interest in apartments on the secondary market. For them, buying property is a form of business investment. By renting out a property, they can earn a higher annual return than they would by keeping the same amount of money in a bank.

“Those who moved to Armenia after the Russia-Ukraine war began are also active. Some have been living here for about a year and have decided to settle permanently. Another group consists of people who had ties to Armenia in the past but have now decided to move their businesses and families here.

Interest is also being driven by the growing value placed on property assets in Armenia in recent years. As a result, demand for housing remains high in both the primary and secondary markets,” the real estate agency director says.

Apartment price trends by administrative district

According to data from the Cadastre Committee, property prices continued to rise across all of Yerevan’s administrative districts in the second quarter of 2026. However, the pace of growth varied. The biggest increases came in Nork-Marash, Shengavit and Ajapnyak.

Nork-Marash recorded the sharpest increase, with the average price reaching 553,000 drams ($1,527) per square metre. Compared with last year, this represents a 24% rise.

Apartment prices in Shengavit rose by around 19% over the same period, while prices in Ajapnyak increased by 16%. More construction and relatively affordable prices have helped drive demand in these districts.

Price changes were more moderate in other parts of the city. Growth has been relatively slow in the Small Centre and neighbouring Arabkir, largely because prices there were already high.

Overall, property prices in Yerevan continue to rise. However, the strongest growth is occurring in districts with development potential and relatively more affordable prices.

Property prices in Armenia rise again

World.title: How does Georgia’s parliament work? SJC analyses current legislative processes
World.content:
The Social Justice Center (SJC) analyses the work of Georgia’s 11th Parliament between 25 November 2024 and 26 June 2026. It notes that the parliament’s work has, on the one hand, undermined democratic institutions and rights and, on the other, expanded the executive branch’s discretionary powers and strengthened the centralisation of power.

The organisation’s director, Tamta Mikeladze, published the report’s main findings:

During this period, parliament adopted 276 legislative packages or initiatives. Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives.

Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives. During the same period, the parliament, which was almost entirely made up of members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, did not adopt a single opposition legislative initiative , including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously.

, including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously. The quality of the legislative process is also problematic. Explanatory notes generally did not indicate that broad consultations had taken place and often lacked relevant sectoral or comparative legal analysis. Of the 276 initiatives, local or international experts took part in only six cases, while just eight initiatives provided for the harmonisation of Georgian legislation with legal instruments of the Council of Europe, the EU or the UN.

Against this backdrop, the parliament’s work can be divided into several main areas:

● Restrictions on civil society and repressive controls – 7 legislative changes. Alongside the laws on “transparency of foreign influence” and “registration of foreign agents”, parliament amended the law on grants. These changes effectively placed civil society organisations under full state control and criminalised certain forms of their activity. Parliament also created an Agency for the Management of State Grants, restricted NGOs’ participation in state decision-making, tightened the rules for issuing and receiving grants, broadened the legal definition of a grant, and introduced new criminal and financial sanctions.

● Media and freedom of expression – 6 direct changes: rules on foreign funding changed, the Communications Commission gained wider powers, new requirements for broadcast content were introduced, coverage of court proceedings was restricted, and financial oversight mechanisms were strengthened.

● Five separate changes concerned freedom of assembly and expression, increasing administrative and criminal liability for actions related to protests.

● Public service – 8 changes. Institutional safeguards for civil servants were weakened, while political appointments and the discretion of senior officials gained greater importance. The Civil Service Bureau was abolished, and opportunities for employment under administrative contracts were expanded. At the same time, new financial benefits and mechanisms for obtaining permission to engage in certain activities were introduced, with access to them largely dependent on decisions by senior officials. This creates a risk of not only politicisation but also clientelist governance.

● Education and academia also became targets of centralisation. Changes adopted in 2025-2026 strengthened the government’s influence over university funding, student numbers, academic programmes, and the reorganisation and institutional structure of universities. The limited involvement of academics in the process points to a broader problem with academic freedom.

● Ideological and propaganda-related measures – 7 major legislative changes. These included the introduction of a new crime, “treason against the state”; the removal of the term “gender” from legislation; tougher drug policies; changes to labour and immigration rules for foreigners; and expanded mechanisms of state control. What these changes have in common is not only tougher policies in specific areas, but also the incorporation of political and ideological concepts into the legal framework.

It is also important to look not only at what parliament adopted, but at what it left off its agenda. During the reporting period, issues concerning the rights of children and prisoners, public procurement and corruption prevention, environmental protection and civil safety, healthcare, urban planning and construction, education, regional policy, agriculture and tourism were pushed into the background or postponed. As a result, parliament’s agenda was clearly dominated by restrictive and controlling legislation. At the same time, its positive legislative agenda, covering a broad range of public interests, was significantly weakened.
