World.title: They were frightening days: September 11 and the first draft of history
World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor They were frightening days: September 11 and the first draft of history Jordan Baker September 11, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Back in 2001, the Tuesday night ritual for those of us working in the Canberra Press Gallery was to settle back with a cup of tea and watch our favourite US political drama. The Senate wing of Australia’s parliament, which is home to the press gallery, was not nearly as exciting as The West Wing, but we related to the fictional drama nonetheless. Tuesday, September 11, had been a particularly busy day. We’d been reporting news that one of Australia’s two main airlines, Ansett, was on the brink of collapse; it would implode the following day, with enormous consequences for its workers and the aviation industry. For many of us, the moment we heard about the September 11 attacks is seared into our memory. Getty Images The gallery bigwigs were in Washington with then prime minister John Howard, who was due to address a joint sitting of Congress on September 12 (Howard reflected on the experience to James Massola in this piece published on Friday). Michelle Grattan, who was The Sydney Morning Herald’s political correspondent, was in Washington with Howard, as was Peter Hartcher, who then worked for The Australian Financial Review and is now, of course, the Herald’s political and international editor. In fact, it had been a busy few months. In July, as a baby journalist for Australian Associated Press, I’d been trusted with my first reporting round: immigration. In August, I found myself covering the biggest story in the country after the prime minister refused to allow the MV Tampa, a Norwegian ship that had rescued 433 asylum seekers from Afghanistan, to enter Australian waters – a drama that dominated headlines and still shapes immigration and refugee policy in Australia and around the world.



So, late on Tuesday, September 11, many of us escaped into an imaginary political drama on TV. Until a news update at about 10.45pm, which showed footage of a plane crashing into the World Trade Centre in New York. We madly messaged each other on our Nokia phones. Was it an accident? An attack? We put down the tea, and drove to work. When a story like that breaks, whenever it breaks, heading to the newsroom is an involuntary reflex. Almost our whole bureau converged on the office. We did it again and again too many times over the following years and decades – after a series of explosions in Bali in 2002, and following the tsunami in South East Asia in 2004. We did it again last December, dropping everything to head to work when the news of a shooting at Bondi broke. Our sacred duty as journalists is to keep the public informed, and that responsibility is even more profound when the news is so horrendous, and so consequential. At the Herald, the presses ran hot with special editions (online news was in its infancy). It was all hands on deck in Sydney, and editors desperately tried to reach reporters already in the danger zones (including our US correspondents, our editor-at-large – who happened to be in New York – and Grattan, who ended up flying out of the United States with Howard on Air Force Two, escorted through closed airspace by fighter jets). They were frightening days – buildings teetering, people jumping, figures walking on the streets of New York covered in ash.



The Herald’s then editor, Robert Whitehead, had just arrived in North Queensland with his wife and newborn for a holiday, which he had postponed due to the Tampa incident; as soon as the news broke of the attacks, he was booked a 6am flight back to Sydney. They were frightening days – buildings teetering, people jumping, figures walking on the streets of New York covered in ash. Desperate searches for loved ones. The shock turned into aching grief, mingled with fear – of more attacks, of impending war. Travel writer Lee Tulloch was living in New York, and this week recalled the confusion of those days. Some 3000 people died in the attacks. Ten of them were Australians. For many of us, the moment we heard about the September 11 attacks is seared into our memory. Others were too young to remember, and know it only through stories. It was disturbing, this week, to read Michael Koziol’s story on how some of those who were too young to witness the attack are already beginning to doubt it, despite all the footage, photographs and living memory. As we look back, 25 years on, I am reminded of the role of journalism as the first draft of history. I’ve pored over the pages of the Herald from September 11, and reflected again on the importance of having experienced and highly trained journalists from trusted news organisations both at the coal face and back in the newsroom during events of this magnitude.



It is difficult to report chaos and tragedy, but bringing these events to you, our readers, with speed, empathy and insight is a responsibility we take extremely seriously. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Building, sport and community services helped this school hit a 100 per cent VCE completion rate
World.content:
NationalVictoriaSchools that excel Building, sport and community services helped this school hit a 100 per cent VCE completion rate Caroline Schelle September 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jonah Heta was struggling just to get to classes at Gleneagles Secondary College last year; now he’s first to arrive each morning. Since finishing school, the 19-year-old has taken a job maintaining the Endeavour Hills campus thanks to the building and construction course he took in year 12 which helped turn things around. Principal Jo Sayer and former student Jonah Heta, who now works at the school. Eddie Jim “[The course] helped me engage in school, and it was a tool that helped me finish,” he said of his experience with the VCE Vocational Major certificate. “I was really struggling in my attendance, and it pulled me in, and helped me understand why I needed to go to school and finish my program.”



Back on the school grounds five days a week, the former student credited a great building and construction teacher with paving the way for him to succeed in the course and gain an understanding of the industry. Heta’s story is part of a broader pattern of strong vocational performance at Gleneagles, propelling the school into the VET winner’s spot in The Age’s 2026 Schools that Excel. The annual series celebrates schools that have achieved outstanding advancement in their VCE results over the past decade. Max Williams, Maddie Harrington and Sanika Kulkarni (left to right) doing CPR exercise which is part of the community service VET. Eddie Jim Principal Jo Sayer said the school’s building course had become increasingly popular, and Heta’s pathway showed how it could be used to re-engage students in education.



“Having a hands-on course that will lead to a pathway that the traditional VCE wouldn’t give a student helps,” she said. VET was more practical and hands-on for students than the academically focused VCE, and very helpful to kids who already had ideas for their future career, she said. “Not all students like sitting in a classroom learning in the traditional way at schools,” Sayer said. The principal pointed out that Heta may not have graduated from high school if not for the building course, and said that many students took a VET course to complement their traditional VCE subjects. In each year since 2022, Gleneagles has improved its VET completion rates, recording 85 per cent completions in 2023 and 97 per cent in 2024. Last year, the school reached 100 per cent.



In 2022, 169 students Gleneagles students enrolled in a VET certificate and 69 per cent of VET units were completed. Last year, all of its 212 VET students completed their units, as the school hit an all-time high for VET enrolments. “Our school has 100 per cent completion rate in VCE, and we’re pretty proud of that,” Sayer said. “It is amazing, and that’s partly because a lot of our students do VET, and that adds to their engagement,” she said.



Among those set to graduate this year is school captain Maddie Harrington, who is studying a course in community service that she hopes will help in her future employment. “I’d like to do something in law and social work, like youth justice,” the 17-year-old said. Harrington said the VET course aligned well with her subjects, which include legal studies, and gave her a greater understanding of communities and their needs. Sanika Kulkarni, another school captain who is also studying the same course, said she wanted to go into social work. “I wanted a subject that would lead to that, and it was the perfect one,” she said.



It meant she and other students worked with Friends of Ermera, a local aid agency operating in Timor-Leste. Max Williams, 16, is studying the sports and recreation VET at Gleneagles and is eager to go into sport teaching when he finishes high school. “I thought it would really help my leadership and coaching skills,” he said. World.title: ‘You just have a lot more to lose’: How fatherhood has centred Swans star Grundy
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans ‘You just have a lot more to lose’: How fatherhood has centred Swans star Grundy Jonathan Drennan September 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brodie Grundy became a father for the first time at the start of August, when the Swans ruckman and his partner Rachael welcomed a baby boy, Darcy, into the world. The experience has proved invaluable in helping him stay grounded during the drama that beset the club later that month, when the Swans suspended five key players for the rest of the season for breaching behavioural standards, and the stunning qualifying final win over Brisbane that followed last weekend. Swans ruckman Brodie Grundy. Steven Siewert Grundy has always sought balance in his life and career, grappling with ruckmen in his day job while earning degrees in human physiology and business administration in his spare time. Fatherhood has given Grundy less sleep and an aching lower back, but also a sense of what really matters. “You just have a lot more to lose,” Grundy said. “I just put so much energy and emphasis on showing up as a husband and a father in the best way that I can and pouring everything into that.



“I know I’ll be a footballer for a short period in my life, but I’m going to be a father and a husband for hopefully the best part of my life. “It’s about valuing that and seeing the long-haul perspective of it. That’s probably why I’m trying to show up as best as I can and really throwing the kitchen sink at that role, despite what’s a really important time as a footballer. Brodie Grundy was one of the senior Swans who fronted the cameras along with skipper Callum Mills after the suspensions of the ‘Pullman Five’. Getty Images “It’s been really challenging to hold those things, really important parts of my identity as a footballer and then as a husband and as a father, finding the space for those parts of me at different times. I’m not always getting it right, but that’s just what it means to be a human.” Grundy shared the devastation of all at the club when Callum Mills ruptured the ACL in his right knee during the first quarter of last weekend’s epic against the Lions. He had been one of the senior Swans players who stood to support the club captain as he addressed the media after the suspensions of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Riley Bice, James Jordon and Nick Blakey.



Grundy hasn’t thought of taking on the armband himself, but is focusing on the legacy of Mills’ captaincy through what has been one of the most turbulent periods in the club’s history. Like Grundy, Mills is a young father, and the injured captain’s ability to put his teammates before himself has resonated with the ruckman. Dane Rampe and Brodie Grundy embrace after winning against North Melbourne in August. Getty Images “Cal just wants to do the very best he can, he puts a lot of pressure on himself and has the weight of the world at times on his shoulders,” Grundy said. “I was just so proud of him in what has been an unprecedented time for the club. He’s just leading through his values, and that’s all you can ever do ... when he puts his head on the pillow at night, he’s himself and that’s what we encourage all our people to do when they come and play for the Swans.



“They’re the best version of themselves, and I think Cal’s doing that beautifully as a captain. We’re going to have an enormous hole in the next 12 months to fill without him, but true to his character and his values, he will no doubt still have his fingerprints all over this year and next year.” Related Article Sydney Swans ‘It doesn’t matter who puts the jumper on’: How the Swans replaced the irreplaceable Grundy is playing some of the best football of his career and has benefited from the new rules in 2026 where rucks are forbidden from crossing the centre line before engaging with their opponents, and umpires throw the ball up rather than bouncing it. According to Champion Data the ruckman boasts the highest hitout-to-advantage rate in the AFL, with 43 per cent for the season. At 32 years old and in one of the most physically demanding positions in the league, Grundy is reluctant to take on the extra responsibility of the captaincy, and is instead focused on leading by his actions.



“Honestly, I’ve been just thinking about being Dad and getting through training, to be honest, I’ve got the ‘Dad Back’ already,” Grundy joked. “It’s just been getting my body right, looking after the family … that’s sort of been my No.1 priority. “Obviously, it’s been a really exciting but challenging time here at Swans, and I’m just trying to lead as best as I can on the field and leading through my actions. “I’m just trying to add to the mix in there without feeling like I need to put the Superman cape on or anything. It’s just about playing my role and stepping up in moments when I feel like I need to.”

I’ve pored over the pages of the Herald from September 11, and reflected again on the importance of having experienced and highly trained journalists from trusted news organisations both at the coal face and back in the newsroom during events of this magnitude.



It is difficult to report chaos and tragedy, but bringing these events to you, our readers, with speed, empathy and insight is a responsibility we take extremely seriously. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: On algorithms, agency must be returned to people
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters On algorithms, agency must be returned to people September 11, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Critics calling the federal government’s proposed algorithmic opt-out ″⁣censorship″⁣ are misrepresenting the fundamental mechanics of media choice. Censorship requires a central authority to restrict access to information. The only people restricting their feeds will be the users themselves. Reverting a social media feed to a chronological stream of followed accounts removes no content from the public sphere. It simply returns agency to the individual.

The real distortion occurring on tech platforms isn’t government overreach; it’s algorithmic injection. Recommender systems systematically push hyper-targeted, rage-inducing content onto users to maximise engagement – a form of covert, automated propaganda disguised as an organic feed. An opt-out mechanism doesn’t suppress speech; it halts forced exposure. Choosing what to read from sources you explicitly follow is no more ″⁣censorship″⁣ than selecting a book from a shelf.

Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen We should have freedom of choice

Waleed Aly (Comment, 4/9) both correctly predicts and skewers the government’s “My Feed, My Way” legislation, which proposes that users can opt out of social media algorithmic content. I agree the laws wrongly frame the response in terms of individual rights. This assumes that users are not addicted to the content and ignores the wider harm to society and democracy.

The prime minister’s assertion that “if people want to doomscroll ... that’s fine” assumes this is a right and those doing it are free to choose. Do we make the same assumptions about gambling addicts sitting in front of poker machines?

Founder and CEO of Teach Us Consent, Chanel Contos, makes a convincing argument that algorithms should be opt in, so that social media apps have them off by default. Her proposal that feeds be limited to the pages deliberately followed by users and presented chronologically dovetails nicely with Aly’s Back To The Future II metaphor about fun and harmless tech. As pop group Devo sang: “Freedom of choice/Is what you got/Freedom from choice/Is what you want”. With opting-out provisions we have freedom from choice set as the status quo. But we should have freedom of choice.

Greg Williams, West Footscray Crackdown should have occurred earlier

The new crackdown on addictive algorithms can’t come soon enough. Future generations will gasp at how we enabled social media companies to run amok. Much of the issues we face as a society, including significant declines in youth mental health, coincide directly with the beginning of this increased daily exposure to the unregulated minefield that is social media. Bravo for this regulation, if only it could have happened over a decade ago.

Roan Plotz, Preston



THE FORUM Look after your pets

How sad to read of the plight of the Lost Dogs’ Home (″⁣Lost Dogs’ Home trapped in limbo as facility decays″⁣, 9/9). It is incredible to believe that there has been 160 per cent increase in the surrender of animals in the past four years. Sadly, this is likely to increase unless we have compulsory desexing of companion animals (cats and dogs), ban backyard breeding and have only shelters or registered breeders to sell animals. In many cases, these poor surrendered animals have ended up in the shelters because of irresponsible human behaviour.

Tess Vietz, Kew Unacceptable delay

The government’s six-year delay in finding a new site for the Lost Dogs’ Home is unacceptable. This vital organisation is being forced to spend scarce charitable funds maintaining facilities it cannot properly upgrade, while the government offers no clear solution.

But relocation alone will not address the crisis. How can we justify continuing to breed animals for profit while shelters are overflowing with unwanted dogs and cats, some of whom may ultimately be euthanised when homes cannot be found?

The solution must be threefold: urgently provide the Lost Dogs’ Home with a purpose-built site that prioritises animal welfare; introduce mandatory desexing; and undertake a review of legislation governing the breeding and sale of animals.

Commercially producing more animals while charities struggle to care for those already here is unconscionable. If we are serious about animal welfare, we must stop simply accommodating the consequences and confront the system that creates them.

Amy Grossbard, Caulfield Grounded name

As I recall, in 1967 when postcodes were brought in it was necessary to look them up in a booklet. The suburb name appeared first, then words like east or west. To my amusement and amazement, I noticed that people came to believe that there were suburbs called Templestowe Lower and Balwyn North, but they were always called Lower Templestowe and North Balwyn when I was a kid. There was at least one exception though: Airport West was always Airport West.

Simon Thornton, Alphington



Toorak calling

The question was raised (Letters, 11/9) whether those taking a Balwyn tram from Collins Street end up in Balwyn or the less socially elevated Balwyn North. Those old enough to remember the Ben Bowyang cartoons by Alex Gurney might recall that Ben’s mate, Bill Smith, had a cousin who was so stuck up that he took a train from the city to Toorak and then walked home to Richmond each night.

Arthur Roberts, Elwood Security-based win

Prior to the 9/11 attacks on the United States, the Coalition government in Australia was suffering from severe unpopularity and trailed heavily behind Kim Beazley’s Labor Party in the opinion polls.

The national security shock immediately saw a five-point boost in the polls for the Coalition and ultimately led to an unexpected victory in November 2001. There is little doubt that Howard would not have become the second-longest-serving Liberal prime minister behind Robert Menzies without the Twin Towers terrorist attack.

Phil Alexander, Eltham Achieved nothing

John Howard has said that ″⁣it was only right″⁣ that Australia joined the US in Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks. Only right to take part in a fruitless 20-year war that achieved absolutely nothing?

Reg Murray, Glen Iris Heed Rudd’s warnings

Kevin Rudd spoke at the Press Club this week, and made significant warnings about Australia’s complacency. His key issues were China’s rise, AI and accelerating climate change (″⁣Rudd warns nation on borrowed time″⁣, 11/9).

All these are related, and require integrated planning. China has been successful economically for decades, choosing priorities and co-ordinating policies. This has not always worked, but picking winners in specific industries like solar panels and EVs has been successful. Manufacturing industry increased China’s carbon emissions, but by using low-emissions technology China is on track to reach net zero emissions by 2060.

Politically, China is a brutal communist dictatorship, but we have much to learn from it on Rudd’s priorities on industry policy and climate change.

John Hughes, Mentone No longer a beacon

Isn’t paying people to vote for you weakening democracy (″⁣Trump pledges $US5000 to all US adults if his party wins midterms″⁣, 11/9)?

Many people who are struggling financially might take up this offer. If this happens what a tragic end to the US as a beacon of democracy. But let us hope that somehow Donald Trump will cease his presidency at the end of his two terms – unless he changes the rules to limit presidency to that period.

No. We must not give up hope. Anyway, he will be 82 years old then. Surely in need of slowing down. Then the US could again be a democratic beacon and Australia’s reliable and powerful friend.

Marguerite Marshall, Eltham



Respect teachers

The adage ″⁣It takes a village to raise a child″⁣ places teachers in a central and tough role. Parents can be reluctant or blundering in their responsibilities. Home environments can be chaotic for some children. Teachers are expected to cope with and ″⁣fix″⁣ behaviour that doesn’t fit with co-operative learning in large groups. Parents can be aggressive in their complaints. So teachers still need to influence the values and behaviours of their students but they need more respect and resources to do so. Countries such as Finland and Japan weave these life lessons into their classrooms from school entry. Their teachers are well-supported. We need to learn from them.

Glenda Johnston, Queenscliff Tough challenges

Correspondents applauding the idea that the onus to raise children well should be on parents, would do well to consider the circumstances that many children face. A significant cohort of parents are not merely poor at parenting, they are entirely incapable of providing a functional family setting. At one time, I taught in a regional primary school and one in five children in the class were being managed by government agencies and homed by relatives. These children in some cases had been seized from a dangerous or drug-affected parent.

Simply calling on parents to do better misunderstands the challenges our society face.

Patrick Hockey, Clunes Man in the mirror

The downfall of Alonso Quijano, the Man of La Mancha, came about when the Knight of the Mirrors causes Alonso to look at his aged true self through a polished shield acting as a mirror. For such a mirror to be trained on Donald Trump so that he sees the reality of his self-deluded identity. Sadly, I’m not sure that Trump would resile from this image as did Alonso.

Graeme Rose, Wangaratta Parallel lines

Re your correspondent’s views (Letters, 11/9) on Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories in which they mentioned Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus. My father’s village of Morphou is there so I have a more than passing interest in the history of the Cyprus tragedy. Your correspondent claims it is a different circumstance than what is happening in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

But the situation is remarkably the same for both these oppressed peoples and others living under military occupation, that is displacement, ethnic cleansing, seizure of houses and land, destruction of villages and towns and being replaced by settlers and illegal settlements.

Steven Katsineris, Hurstbridge Sizzling affair

The highly marketed NFL game provided more sizzle than sausage.

Mark Hulls, Sandringham



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING AI

An Anthropic researcher believes AI will potentially kill us all. When the time comes can’t we just pull out the plug?

Layla Godfrey, Parkdale What Anthropic is really saying about AI superintelligence is super stupidity, as we hurtle towards the end of humankind. Why do I keep having visions of The Terminator?

Pepe Salvatore, Fitzroy North Human behaviour may be the cause of our extinction, but now we have a choice of climate change or AI.

Kevan Porter, Alphington



Trump

Donald Trump must really be worried about losing the midterms if he’s resorting to promising $5000 to each adult citizen (″⁣Trump pledges $US5000 to all US adults if his party wins midterms″⁣, 11/9). Voters should be very wary of this presidential con artist.

George Djoneff, Mitcham I cannot believe Donald Trump is bribing people or in other words buying their vote. Do they really think if the Republicans win he will give them the money?

Jane Cheong, Aspendale Gardens Donald Trump is using America’s poor to buy the upcoming midterm elections. Pauline Hanson’s superannuation “policy” could effectively work the same way and produce the same result.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton It’s said that ″⁣everybody has their price″⁣. In the case of US voters, Trump puts it at $5000.

Malcolm Cameron, Camberwell Donald Trump has taken the term ″⁣buying an election″⁣ to a new level.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick



US democracy for sale. Disgusting.

Michelle Leeder, Trentham A man who is so vain, who believes he is so beloved, yet doesn’t seem to see the irony of having to bribe Americans to vote for him. It’s so odd.

Brendan O’Farrell, Brunswick Finally

Whether an issue passes the pub test appears to depend in which electorate the pub resides.

Arthur Pritchard, Ascot Vale

World.title: Building, sport and community services helped this school hit a 100 per cent VCE completion rate
World.content:
NationalVictoriaSchools that excel Building, sport and community services helped this school hit a 100 per cent VCE completion rate Caroline Schelle September 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jonah Heta was struggling just to get to classes at Gleneagles Secondary College last year; now he’s first to arrive each morning. Since finishing school, the 19-year-old has taken a job maintaining the Endeavour Hills campus thanks to the building and construction course he took in year 12 which helped turn things around. Principal Jo Sayer and former student Jonah Heta, who now works at the school. Eddie Jim “[The course] helped me engage in school, and it was a tool that helped me finish,” he said of his experience with the VCE Vocational Major certificate. “I was really struggling in my attendance, and it pulled me in, and helped me understand why I needed to go to school and finish my program.”



Back on the school grounds five days a week, the former student credited a great building and construction teacher with paving the way for him to succeed in the course and gain an understanding of the industry. Heta’s story is part of a broader pattern of strong vocational performance at Gleneagles, propelling the school into the VET winner’s spot in The Age’s 2026 Schools that Excel. The annual series celebrates schools that have achieved outstanding advancement in their VCE results over the past decade. Max Williams, Maddie Harrington and Sanika Kulkarni (left to right) doing CPR exercise which is part of the community service VET. Eddie Jim Principal Jo Sayer said the school’s building course had become increasingly popular, and Heta’s pathway showed how it could be used to re-engage students in education.



“Having a hands-on course that will lead to a pathway that the traditional VCE wouldn’t give a student helps,” she said. VET was more practical and hands-on for students than the academically focused VCE, and very helpful to kids who already had ideas for their future career, she said. “Not all students like sitting in a classroom learning in the traditional way at schools,” Sayer said. The principal pointed out that Heta may not have graduated from high school if not for the building course, and said that many students took a VET course to complement their traditional VCE subjects. In each year since 2022, Gleneagles has improved its VET completion rates, recording 85 per cent completions in 2023 and 97 per cent in 2024. Last year, the school reached 100 per cent.



In 2022, 169 students Gleneagles students enrolled in a VET certificate and 69 per cent of VET units were completed. Last year, all of its 212 VET students completed their units, as the school hit an all-time high for VET enrolments. “Our school has 100 per cent completion rate in VCE, and we’re pretty proud of that,” Sayer said. “It is amazing, and that’s partly because a lot of our students do VET, and that adds to their engagement,” she said.



Among those set to graduate this year is school captain Maddie Harrington, who is studying a course in community service that she hopes will help in her future employment. “I’d like to do something in law and social work, like youth justice,” the 17-year-old said. Harrington said the VET course aligned well with her subjects, which include legal studies, and gave her a greater understanding of communities and their needs. Sanika Kulkarni, another school captain who is also studying the same course, said she wanted to go into social work. “I wanted a subject that would lead to that, and it was the perfect one,” she said.



It meant she and other students worked with Friends of Ermera, a local aid agency operating in Timor-Leste. Max Williams, 16, is studying the sports and recreation VET at Gleneagles and is eager to go into sport teaching when he finishes high school. “I thought it would really help my leadership and coaching skills,” he said.
